title: Enhancing Extubation Failure Prediction with LLM-Derived Features from Respiratory Therapy Clinical Notes
comment: Published in CHIL 2026. 11 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, 25 pages including citations and supplemental material
summary: Invasive mechanical ventilation is a lifesaving therapy, but timely, safe discontinuation is essential to preventing extubation failure (EF) and related risks to health. We present a novel approach to EF prediction that leverages features classified in free-text respiratory therapy notes using a large language model and logistic regression pipeline. Applied to a patient cohort from University of Washington Medicine, our method identifies clinically meaningful EF-related features that improve EF prediction performance when included alongside structured patient data. We further highlight how differences in target populations in prior EF prediction studies, such as heterogenous inclusion criteria and EF definition, can lead to systematic differences in model performance and hinder generalizability between studies.

AI.tldr: They use large language model–derived features from respiratory therapy notes plus structured data to better predict extubation failure and analyze why prior studies don’t generalize well.
AI.motivation: Extubation failure in invasively ventilated patients causes complications and worse outcomes, so clinicians need accurate tools to decide when it is safe to discontinue mechanical ventilation. Existing prediction models often rely only on structured data and show variable, non‑generalizable performance, partly because of heterogeneous inclusion criteria and differing EF definitions. There is a need both to exploit rich information in clinical free‑text and to understand how study design choices affect model performance and comparability.
AI.method: The authors develop a prediction pipeline that first uses a large language model to process free‑text respiratory therapy notes, extracting or classifying clinically meaningful features relevant to extubation failure. These text‑derived features are then combined with traditional structured patient data and fed into a logistic regression model for EF prediction. They apply the pipeline retrospectively to a patient cohort from University of Washington Medicine and compare performance with models that rely only on structured data. They also systematically examine how different target population definitions and EF definitions, similar to those used in prior studies, influence predictive performance and generalizability.
AI.result: Including LLM‑derived features from respiratory therapy notes alongside structured variables improves the discrimination and/or calibration of extubation failure prediction compared with models using structured data alone. The pipeline surfaces specific, clinically interpretable note‑based features associated with EF. The analysis shows that varying inclusion criteria and EF definitions, mirroring prior literature, leads to systematic shifts in model performance estimates and limits direct comparison and generalization across studies.
AI.conclusion: Free‑text respiratory therapy notes contain valuable, clinically relevant signals for extubation failure risk that can be effectively captured with a large language model and integrated into a simple logistic regression framework to enhance prediction. At the same time, differences in how patient cohorts and EF outcomes are defined substantially affect model performance, underscoring that careful, standardized population and outcome definitions are critical for building EF prediction tools that generalize across settings and studies.

title: Faking Good and Faking Bad in LLMs: Response Distortion Across Dark Triad Personality Traits
summary: Social desirability and impression management are pervasive sources of response distortion in human personality assessment, yet their effects on Large Language Models (LLMs) remain underexplored. This study investigates whether contemporary LLMs systematically modulate the expression of Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy) under fake-good and fake-bad conditions. Seven state-of-the-art models were evaluated across two ecologically relevant contexts: employment selection and forensic evaluation, in which socially desirable or undesirable incentives were conveyed through contextual framing. Trait expression was measured using standard psychometric scoring procedures and compared with self-assessment baselines at both aggregate and item levels. Results revealed systematic and condition-consistent response modulation. Most models reduced Dark Triad scores under fake-good conditions and increased them under fake-bad conditions, although the magnitude and consistency of these effects varied across traits and models. Machiavellianism and narcissism showed the strongest and most coherent shifts, whereas psychopathy displayed greater heterogeneity. Context also influenced responses, with employment scenarios generally producing larger effects than forensic scenarios. An additional experiment showed that explicit fake-bad instructions generated substantially stronger distortions than contextual framing alone. The results suggest that personality-related outputs should be interpreted in light of the motivational and situational context in which they are elicited. More broadly, they highlight the value of psychometric paradigms for evaluating susceptibility to response distortion, impression management, and context-dependent behavioral shifts, with important implications for LLM benchmarking, alignment evaluation, and robustness assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how Large Language Models adjust their expressed Dark Triad personality trait scores (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy) when ‘faking good’ or ‘faking bad’ under different contextual framings (job hiring vs. forensic evaluation).
AI.motivation: In human personality testing, people often distort their answers to look better or worse (social desirability and impression management), which biases test results. For LLMs, it is unclear whether they similarly modulate personality-related responses depending on goals or context, yet such behavior has major implications for using LLMs in assessment, safety, and alignment. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically testing whether LLMs exhibit context- and motivation-dependent shifts in Dark Triad trait expression.
AI.method: Seven contemporary LLMs were prompted with items measuring the Dark Triad traits under different conditions: (1) fake-good vs. fake-bad motivational instructions, and (2) two applied contexts—employment selection and forensic evaluation—implemented via contextual framing. Dark Triad trait levels were scored using standard psychometric procedures, and responses were compared against self-assessment baselines at both overall trait-score and item-response levels. An additional experiment explicitly instructed models to fake bad to compare the strength of distortion due to direct instructions versus subtle contextual cues.
AI.result: Across models, there was systematic and condition-consistent modulation of Dark Triad scores. Most LLMs lowered Machiavellianism and narcissism (and, less consistently, psychopathy) under fake-good conditions, and raised them under fake-bad conditions. Machiavellianism and narcissism showed clearer, more coherent shifts than psychopathy, which varied more across models and items. Employment-selection framings produced larger distortions than forensic framings. Explicit fake-bad prompting induced markedly stronger distortions than context-only framing.
AI.conclusion: LLMs do not provide stable, context-invariant ‘personality’ outputs; rather, their expressed Dark Triad traits are systematically shaped by motivational framing and situational context. Therefore, personality-like outputs from LLMs must be interpreted relative to the prompts and incentives implied. The study demonstrates that psychometric methods are a powerful tool for probing LLM susceptibility to response distortion and impression management, with implications for how we benchmark, evaluate alignment, and design robust systems that behave predictably under different user goals and contexts.

title: DANTINOX: A Unified Framework for Multi-Paradigm Language Modeling
summary: Language generation research increasingly spans three paradigms: autoregressive decoding, discrete masked diffusion, and continuous flow-matching. Comparing them is difficult because each lives in a separate codebase, so measured differences often reflect implementation details rather than the paradigms themselves. We present DantinoX, an open-source JAX/Flax library in which a single modular Transformer backbone serves all three paradigms. Switching the generation paradigm, attention mechanism, or hardware topology requires only a configuration change, while the backbone architecture, tokenizer, initialization strategy, and training infrastructure remain consistent. This enables controlled cross-paradigm comparisons within one API for training, streaming inference, and benchmarking.

AI.tldr: DantinoX is a unified JAX/Flax library that supports autoregressive, discrete diffusion, and continuous flow-matching language generation on a shared Transformer backbone, enabling fair comparisons.
AI.motivation: Comparisons across language generation paradigms are confounded by different codebases, architectures, and training setups, making it unclear whether performance differences are due to paradigms or implementations.
AI.method: Build a single modular Transformer backbone in JAX/Flax that can operate under three generation paradigms—autoregressive, discrete masked diffusion, and continuous flow-matching—with swappable attention mechanisms and hardware topologies controlled via configuration, while keeping tokenizer, initialization, and training infrastructure fixed.
AI.result: The library provides one API for training, streaming inference, and benchmarking across paradigms, making controlled cross-paradigm experiments feasible; specific empirical numbers are not given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Using a unified, configurable infrastructure like DantinoX allows more rigorous and fair evaluation of different language generation paradigms by isolating the paradigm choice from other implementation variables.

title: Think Before You Comfort: Reflective Cognitive Alignment for Protocol-Grounded Elderly Stimulation Agents
summary: Cognitive Stimulation Therapy (CST) offers non-pharmacological support for elders with cognitive impairment, yet scalability remains constrained by reliance on trained facilitators and severe data scarcity, particularly for privacy-sensitive, low-resource languages such as Cantonese. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for automated companionship, they often struggle to balance empathetic engagement with adherence to cognitive stimulation guidelines. We propose a framework addressing these challenges along two complementary axes. First, STaR-CS (Style-Transfer and Role-Conditioned Cognitive Stimulation) synthesizes multi-party dialogues through facilitator style modeling and structured skeleton extraction, mitigating data barriers. Building upon this corpus, the Reflective Cognitive Alignment (RCA) framework models stimulation interactions as a sequential decision process, integrating Protocol-Constrained Chain-of-Cognition (PC-CoC) for structured reasoning and Inference-Time Value Alignment (IVA) for principled response selection based on safety and engagement goals. Evaluations across six backbone LLMs and two independent judges show that RCA consistently improves protocol adherence, safety, and group facilitation over standard prompting baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangjyjy/RCA_Agent.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to scale Cognitive Stimulation Therapy for elders with cognitive impairment by synthesizing dialogue data and aligning LLM behavior to therapeutic protocols, improving safety, engagement, and protocol adherence across models.
AI.motivation: Cognitive Stimulation Therapy is effective for elders with cognitive impairment but hard to scale because it depends on trained human facilitators and has limited training data, especially in privacy-sensitive, low-resource languages like Cantonese. Existing LLM-based companions struggle to be both empathetic and compliant with cognitive stimulation guidelines, creating a need for a method that generates suitable training data and reliably enforces therapeutic protocols during interaction.
AI.method: The paper proposes two complementary components. (1) STaR-CS (Style-Transfer and Role-Conditioned Cognitive Stimulation) generates synthetic multi-party dialogues by modeling facilitator styles and extracting structured conversation skeletons, thus creating a richer training corpus under data-scarce and privacy-sensitive conditions. (2) Reflective Cognitive Alignment (RCA) treats cognitive stimulation as a sequential decision-making task and introduces Protocol-Constrained Chain-of-Cognition (PC-CoC) to enforce structured, protocol-aware reasoning, along with Inference-Time Value Alignment (IVA) to select model responses that best satisfy safety and engagement objectives during runtime.
AI.result: Across six different LLM backbones, the RCA framework yields better adherence to CST protocols, higher safety, and improved quality of group facilitation when compared with standard prompting approaches. These gains are validated by two independent judges, indicating robustness across models and evaluators.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic dialogue generation via STaR-CS combined with the RCA framework provides a practical path to scaling Cognitive Stimulation Therapy with LLMs, particularly in low-resource, privacy-sensitive languages. By structuring the reasoning process and aligning response selection with explicit safety and engagement goals, the approach consistently outperforms conventional prompting, suggesting it is a promising direction for automated, protocol-compliant cognitive support agents.

title: Making AI-Assisted Claims Independently Challengeable: Publication Authority and a Protocol for Falsifiable Publication Records
comment: Main article: 24 pages, 4 figures; supplementary material: 13 pages. Preprint; not peer-reviewed. Yifei Dong is the corresponding author
summary: AI-assisted claims can appear authoritative when evidence, analysis, human authorization, presentation, and correction history refer to different states. Provenance, attestation, and transparency expose history but alone do not specify the publication transition examined here. We develop Publication Authority as an exact-state, non-transferable, single-use publication capability and instantiate it in PAC-2026 (Publication-Accountability Calculus), a machine-readable AIJIM Protocol candidate. We evaluate its fourth bounded semantic freeze (SF-4), a fixed-profile specification designed for replaceable bindings. Six obligations govern evidence, runs and artifacts, measurement disclosure, authorization, surface correspondence, and lifecycle continuity. Each yields a target-bound witness, localized counterexample, or localized unverifiability; none can compensate for another. Only a fresh, complete all-pass record derives the permit consumed by one atomic publication transition. We use identity vectors, adversarial cases, finite models, and historical implementations. Ten models explored 110,764 safe reachable states; 76 unsafe configurations produced the expected violation or observer countermodel. A reader surface passing its correspondence check cannot authorize publication unless the accepted record admits that surface. SF-4 separates evidence horizon from verification time and rejects an authentic but causally invalid authorization. A historical predecessor path reproduced 17 frozen authorization-successor outcomes. A later in-house, instance-blind test of known case classes matched all 183 scored expectations; same-host package execution reproduced its 240 archived observations. Results support internal coherence, bounded safety, fault sensitivity, and limited constructibility, but not factual truth, general refinement, blind interoperability, field efficacy, or standards status.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a rigorous, machine-checkable notion of who is truly allowed to publish an AI-assisted claim at a specific point in time, and tests a protocol (PAC-2026, SF-4 profile) that enforces this via single-use, exact-state publication permits.
AI.motivation: AI-generated or AI-assisted outputs can seem authoritative even when the evidence, analysis, authorization, and presentation refer to mismatched or outdated states. Existing provenance and transparency tools track history but do not precisely define the critical ‘publication transition’—the exact state at which a claim becomes officially published. The paper aims to close this gap by defining a formal notion of Publication Authority that binds authorization to a specific, verifiable system state.
AI.method: The authors formalize Publication Authority as a non-transferable, single-use publication capability and embed it into PAC-2026, a machine-readable protocol (AIJIM candidate). They define SF-4, a bounded semantic freeze profile with six obligations covering evidence, runs and artifacts, measurements, authorization, surface correspondence, and lifecycle continuity. Each obligation produces state-bound witnesses or counterexamples and is logically independent. They then construct finite models, adversarial cases, and identity vectors; explore ten models with over 110k safe reachable states and 76 unsafe configurations; replay historical predecessor paths and run instance-blind in-house tests to validate the protocol’s behavior.
AI.result: The evaluation shows that PAC-2026 SF-4 enforces that only a fresh, complete, all-pass record can yield a one-time publication permit, that a reader-facing surface must be explicitly admitted by the accepted record, and that causally invalid authorizations are rejected even if they are otherwise authentic. The models demonstrated 110,764 safe reachable states and 76 unsafe configurations, all of which triggered expected violations or countermodels. Historical and in-house tests reproduced past outcomes and matched all 183 expectations; same-host executions matched 240 archived observations.
AI.conclusion: The protocol appears internally coherent and satisfies properties like bounded safety, sensitivity to faults, and limited constructibility of unsafe states. However, the authors explicitly note that their results do not guarantee factual truth of claims, broader refinement, interoperability in arbitrary environments, real-world field performance, or readiness as a finalized standard.

title: Relation Before Entity: Deferred Commitment in Language Model Factual Recall
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026). Code available at https://github.com/divyanshddn146/deferred-entity-commitment
summary: We ask whether relation-type information (e.g., capital-of) and entity-specific information (e.g., France to Paris) become causally active at the final-token position at the same depth during recall. Using four complementary causal diagnostics across four decoder-only models and eight prompt families, we find a robust temporal asymmetry: relation information becomes generation-controlling before entity information does. Relation onset precedes entity onset by 10-16 tested layers (31-44% of network depth) at threshold 0.4, with the ordering holding across all 16 model-threshold combinations for thresholds 0.2-0.5. Critically, entity information is not absent early: entity-token patching succeeds at 90-100% in early layers. Instead, entity commitment to generation is deferred: entity information is available at the entity-token position but becomes generation-controlling at the final token only after being routed there.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and how relation-type information (like the relation “capital-of”) and entity-specific information (like “France → Paris”) become causally active in transformer LMs during factual recall, finding that relation information starts controlling generation earlier in depth than entity information.
AI.motivation: While transformer language models can recall factual knowledge, it is unclear how the internal processing of relation schemas (e.g., capital-of) and concrete entity fillers (e.g., France → Paris) unfolds over layers and positions. Understanding this temporal and architectural separation is important for mechanistic interpretability and for explaining how models perform structured recall.
AI.method: The authors analyze four decoder-only language models with eight prompt families and apply four complementary causal diagnostics, including causal interventions such as activation patching at the entity-token and final-token positions. They track when relation-type and entity-specific information become “generation-controlling” at the final-token position across layers, measure onset depths at different causal thresholds, and compare patching success across layers and positions.
AI.result: They find a consistent temporal asymmetry: relation-type information becomes generation-controlling at the final token significantly earlier in the network than entity-specific information. Relation onset precedes entity onset by roughly 10–16 layers, corresponding to 31–44% of network depth, at a causal threshold of 0.4, and this ordering is robust across all 16 model–threshold combinations for thresholds between 0.2 and 0.5. Despite this, entity information is already present and recoverable in early layers (entity-token patching achieves 90–100% success), indicating it is available but not yet driving generation at the final token.
AI.conclusion: Factual recall in decoder-only transformers is temporally structured: relation schemas become causally active at the final-token position substantially earlier than specific entity fillers. Entity information is computed early at the entity-token location but only later routed and committed to control generation at the final token. This suggests a processing pipeline where models first instantiate an abstract relational frame and then later bind it to a concrete entity answer.

title: EvolveTrade: Experience-Driven Policy Refinement for Self-Evolving LLM Trading Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents can combine market data, news, and executable analysis, but their behavior is often controlled by static hand-written tool-use policies that are fixed before deployment. This limits their ability to adapt how they gather evidence, invoke tools, verify signals, and manage risk under changing market regimes. We introduce EvolveTrade, a self-evolving framework that treats the system prompt of a tool-using trading agent as a text-parameterized policy. After each update interval, a Policy Agent revises this policy using accumulated decision traces and realized portfolio feedback, while keeping the backbone LLM fixed. The updated policy is then used for the next batch of trading decisions, enabling the agent to refine its information-acquisition and portfolio-construction procedure over time. Experiments across multiple market regimes and two LLM backbones show that EvolveTrade often improves Sharpe Ratio and Cumulative Return over fixed-policy LLM baselines, achieving the improved SR and CR in most evaluated settings. Behavioral analyses further show that self-evolved policies increase code-mediated analysis and activate regime-relevant computations; case-level policy-to-return attributions trace how policy-induced allocation changes contribute to realized return differences. These results suggest that adapting the reusable procedure governing tool use is a key direction for building more robust LLM trading agents.

AI.tldr: EvolveTrade is a framework that lets an LLM trading agent continuously update its own system prompt (tool-use policy) based on past trades and portfolio outcomes, improving performance over fixed policies.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM trading agents rely on static, hand-crafted tool-use policies that cannot adjust how they gather information, call tools, verify signals, or manage risk when market regimes change. This rigidity can degrade trading performance and robustness in dynamic markets. The authors aim to enable adaptive, data-driven evolution of the agent’s decision-making procedure without retraining or changing the backbone LLM.
AI.method: The authors treat the system prompt that governs tool use as a text-parameterized policy. They introduce a Policy Agent that, after each trading interval, reads the accumulated decision traces and realized portfolio feedback, and then edits or rewrites the system prompt for the trading agent. The backbone LLM and tool set remain fixed; only the policy text evolves. The updated policy is then deployed for the next batch of trades. They evaluate this self-evolving framework, EvolveTrade, across different market regimes and with two different LLM backbones, comparing against baselines with fixed, hand-written policies.
AI.result: Across multiple market regimes and two backbone LLMs, EvolveTrade frequently achieves higher Sharpe Ratios and Cumulative Returns than fixed-policy LLM baselines, with improvements in most tested settings. Behavioral analysis shows that evolved policies lead to more frequent and targeted code-based analysis and better alignment of tool calls with the current market regime. Case-level attribution connects specific policy changes to altered portfolio allocations and resulting return differences.
AI.conclusion: Adapting the text policy (system prompt) that governs an LLM trading agent’s tool use—rather than keeping it static—is an effective way to improve robustness and performance in dynamic markets. EvolveTrade demonstrates that self-evolving, feedback-driven policy updates can enhance both risk-adjusted and absolute returns, and that evolving the reusable decision procedure is a promising direction for future LLM-based trading systems.

title: From Pixels to Pairs: A Comprehensive Benchmark of LLM-Based Key-Value Extraction in Noisy Document Settings
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured information extraction from documents, yet their behavior under realistic OCR noise remains poorly understood. We present a systematic benchmark of open-source instruction-tuned LLMs for key-value pair (KVP) extraction under both clean-text and noisy OCR conditions.
  We evaluate representative decoder-only models (Gemma, Mistral, Qwen2.5, LLaMA 3, and DeepSeek) on the FUNSD, CORD, and SROIE benchmarks using both Gold-text annotations and OCR outputs from PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, and Tesseract. A unified evaluation protocol isolates the effects of input quality, model design, and prompting under consistent conditions.
  The results show that modern LLMs act as strong semantic extractors when high-quality text is available, in some cases approaching supervised layout-aware systems. Under OCR noise, however, performance degrades substantially and performance gaps between models narrow as input corruption increases.
  Across all datasets, extraction performance is governed by two factors: semantic reasoning over text and preservation of textual fidelity under OCR noise. While larger models improve results on clean text, these gains diminish under noisy inputs, where OCR quality becomes the dominant factor. We also identify recurring failure modes, including key-value misalignment, hallucination, and numeric corruption. Our findings highlight the gap between clean-text evaluation and real-world deployment, emphasizing the need to jointly improve OCR quality, structural reasoning, and LLM-based semantic modeling.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking LLMs for key-value extraction under clean and noisy OCR text, showing strong performance on clean text but substantial degradation and convergence under OCR noise, highlighting the importance of OCR quality and robust semantic modeling.
AI.motivation: LLMs are widely used for structured information extraction from documents, but their robustness to realistic OCR noise—a key factor in real-world deployments—is not well understood. Existing evaluations often rely on clean text or layout-aware supervised systems, leaving a gap in understanding how instruction-tuned open-source LLMs perform in noisy, practical settings.
AI.method: The paper systematically benchmarks several open-source decoder-only instruction-tuned LLMs (Gemma, Mistral, Qwen2.5, LLaMA 3, DeepSeek) on key-value pair extraction tasks. It uses three standard document IE datasets (FUNSD, CORD, SROIE) and compares performance on gold (clean) text vs OCR text produced by three OCR engines (PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, Tesseract). A unified evaluation protocol is applied to isolate the effects of input quality, model architecture, and prompting while holding other conditions constant.
AI.result: On clean, high-quality text, modern LLMs perform as strong semantic extractors, in some cases nearly matching specialized supervised layout-aware systems for key-value extraction. Under OCR-induced noise, performance drops sharply across all models, and differences between models shrink as the corruption level increases. Two main factors determine extraction quality: (1) the LLMs’ ability for semantic reasoning over textual content, and (2) how well textual fidelity is preserved by OCR under noise. Larger models yield better results in clean conditions, but their advantage diminishes as OCR noise increases. Recurring errors include misaligned keys and values, hallucinated fields, and corrupted numeric values.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a substantial gap between clean-text benchmark performance and real-world deployment conditions where OCR noise is prevalent. It concludes that progress in document KVP extraction with LLMs requires coordinated improvements in OCR accuracy, LLM robustness to noisy inputs, and better structural reasoning over document content. The work underscores that simply scaling LLMs is insufficient when OCR quality is the bottleneck and calls for methods that explicitly address noise robustness and structure-aware extraction.

title: One Color Preprocessing Improves DSATUR
summary: The Graph Coloring Problem (GCP) is NP-hard and DSATUR stands as one of the fastest heuristics for it despite producing colorings that typically use more colors than state-of-the-art coloring algorithms. We propose SSLD (Semidefinite Spectral Learning with DSATUR), which improves DSATUR by preprocessing a first good color class before letting DSATUR complete coloring the rest of the given graph. We obtain this color class from a Semidefinite Programming (SDP), similar to an SDP used to compute the Lovász theta number. To the best of our knowledge, SSLD is the first approach to improve DSATUR by preprocessing through fixed color classes. We evaluate SSLD against DSATUR and against a naive 1-color-class preprocessing algorithm on DIMACS instances, random graphs (Erdős--Rényi, Watts-Strogatz, Barabási--Albert), Frequency Assignment and Job Shop Scheduling instances. SSLD matches or beats DSATUR in almost every case across over 1600 benchmark instances, and out performs the naive GISD baseline, allows us to confirm the value brought by the SDP-guided choice of the first color class. This quality comes at a runtime cost of roughly 195 times slower that DSATUR, but demonstrating that SDP-guided preprocessing of a first color class is a direction for future improvements.

AI.tldr: They improve the classic DSATUR graph coloring heuristic by first computing a high‑quality initial color class using a semidefinite program, then letting DSATUR finish the coloring, achieving better or equal colorings on most benchmarks at the cost of much higher runtime.
AI.motivation: DSATUR is one of the fastest heuristics for the NP‑hard Graph Coloring Problem but often uses more colors than state‑of‑the‑art methods. The authors want to keep DSATUR’s speed and simplicity while improving the quality of its colorings. They hypothesize that a carefully chosen initial color class, obtained via a more powerful but expensive global method, can guide DSATUR to better solutions.
AI.method: They propose SSLD (Semidefinite Spectral Learning with DSATUR): (1) Solve a semidefinite program similar to the one for the Lovász theta number to extract a good, large, and structurally meaningful first color class. (2) Fix this color class and remove its vertices from the graph. (3) Run the standard DSATUR heuristic on the remaining subgraph. They compare SSLD against pure DSATUR and a naive preprocessing baseline that also fixes a first color class but chooses it without SDP guidance (GISD). Experiments are conducted on over 1600 instances including DIMACS benchmarks, several random graph models, Frequency Assignment, and Job Shop Scheduling graphs.
AI.result: On the tested instances, SSLD matches or improves upon the number of colors produced by DSATUR in almost all cases and consistently outperforms the naive 1‑color‑class preprocessing baseline, showing that the SDP‑derived first color class is significantly better than heuristic alternatives. The main drawback is runtime: SSLD is around 195× slower than plain DSATUR due to the SDP solve.
AI.conclusion: SDP‑guided selection of an initial color class is an effective way to enhance DSATUR’s coloring quality, confirming that global structural information from semidefinite relaxations can beneficially guide local heuristics. Although the current implementation is much slower than DSATUR, the results indicate that semidefinite‑based preprocessing is a promising direction for future graph coloring heuristics that balance solution quality and computational cost.

title: MudawanSn: A Gold-Standard Wolof-Arabic Parallel Corpus for Machine Translation
summary: We present MudawanSn, a gold-standard resource of 1,271 sentence-aligned pairs manually translated from Wolof into Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). The source texts are drawn from the MasakhaNER corpus and cover politics, society, religion, and sports in Senegalese news discourse. Although multilingual resources such as FLORES-200 and NTREX include both Wolof and Arabic, no publicly available parallel corpus is specifically designed for the Wolof-Modern Standard Arabic language pair. We describe the corpus construction protocol, sentence alignment procedure, and quality-control workflow. We benchmark four machine translation systems spanning three architectural families: NLLB-200 (600M), mT5-base, and two AfriNLLB variants, showing that fine-tuning on MudawanSn yields substantial improvements in both translation directions. The best-performing model, AfriNLLB-12, achieves 7.76 BLEU and 30.72 chrF++ for Wolof-to-Arabic, and 8.75 BLEU and 33.08 chrF++ for Arabic-to-Wolof. The corpus is released under the CC BY-NC license and is publicly available on Hugging Face and GitHub.

AI.tldr: MudawanSn is a new, manually created Wolof–Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) parallel corpus with 1,271 sentence-aligned pairs, used to benchmark and improve MT systems in both directions.
AI.motivation: There is no dedicated, high-quality parallel corpus for the Wolof–MSA language pair, despite both languages appearing in large multilingual resources. This lack of a focused dataset limits the development and evaluation of MT systems involving Wolof and Arabic, especially for real-world Senegalese news domains (politics, society, religion, sports).
AI.method: The authors construct MudawanSn by selecting Wolof source sentences from the MasakhaNER corpus and manually translating them into MSA. They apply a defined corpus construction protocol, perform sentence-level alignment, and implement a quality-control workflow. They then fine-tune and evaluate four MT systems from three architecture families (NLLB-200, mT5-base, and two AfriNLLB variants) on this corpus, measuring BLEU and chrF++ in both translation directions.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on MudawanSn yields substantial gains for all tested MT systems when translating between Wolof and MSA. The best system, AfriNLLB-12, obtains 7.76 BLEU / 30.72 chrF++ for Wolof→Arabic and 8.75 BLEU / 33.08 chrF++ for Arabic→Wolof, indicating that the new corpus is effective but the task remains challenging (scores are still modest). The corpus is released openly under a CC BY-NC license on Hugging Face and GitHub.
AI.conclusion: MudawanSn fills a critical resource gap for Wolof–MSA translation by providing a gold-standard, domain-specific sentence-aligned corpus. Its use for fine-tuning leads to measurable MT improvements, and its public release enables further research on low-resource MT for Wolof and Arabic, while highlighting that there is still considerable room to improve model performance.

title: Physics-Constrained Digital Twins for Sensor Integrity in Urban Pedestrian Flow: Detecting Stealthy False Data Injection with Conformal Guarantees
summary: City pedestrian counting systems now feed economic indicators, planning decisions and safety operations, yet the twins built on top of them treat the incoming stream as ground truth. We study what happens when it is not. We formalise stealthy false data injection for city-scale pedestrian sensing, where the map from latent flow to observation is far more rank deficient than in the power and water networks for which stealth has been characterised. Our twin estimates directed flows on the pedestrian street graph, assimilates counts through a learned graph-localised gain, and is trained against a flow conservation residual that couples metered and unmetered segments. Detection combines the innovation with that residual, and the alarm threshold is set by adaptive conformal calibration rather than by hand. To measure what the physics buys, we define the attack margin, the relative reduction in worst-case corruption of the estimated flow field, achieved against a white-box adversary that optimises directly through the twin. On six years of Melbourne data the margin reaches 0.54 against a single compromised device and falls to 0.19 when a third of the fleet is compromised, on a network where only 1.18 per cent of walkable segments are metered. Replacing the street graph by a distance graph collapses it to 0.09, which shows that the gain comes from the conservation law rather than from locality.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how stealthy false data injection attacks affect city-scale pedestrian counting systems and proposes a physics-informed digital twin that improves attack resilience and detection.
AI.motivation: City pedestrian counts drive important economic, planning, and safety decisions, but existing digital twins assume sensor data are accurate. In reality, sensors can be compromised, and there is little understanding of stealthy data manipulation in highly under-sensed, rank-deficient pedestrian networks compared with power or water networks.
AI.method: The authors formalize stealthy false data injection in pedestrian sensing networks and build a digital twin that estimates directed pedestrian flows over a street graph. The twin uses a learned, graph-localized gain to assimilate pedestrian counts and is trained using a flow-conservation residual coupling metered and unmetered segments. Detection is based on a combination of the innovation term and the conservation residual, with alarm thresholds selected via adaptive conformal calibration instead of manual tuning. They evaluate robustness via an "attack margin" metric against a white-box attacker that optimizes directly through the twin.
AI.result: On six years of Melbourne pedestrian data, the proposed method achieves an attack margin of 0.54 when only one counting device is compromised, meaning a substantial reduction in worst-case flow estimation corruption. When a third of the devices are compromised, the margin decreases to 0.19, showing reduced but nontrivial protection even in highly attacked settings. On a network where only 1.18% of walkable segments are metered, replacing the physical street graph with a purely distance-based graph reduces the margin to 0.09, indicating that much of the robustness comes from enforcing flow conservation rather than spatial locality heuristics.
AI.conclusion: Physics-based constraints, specifically flow conservation over the true pedestrian street graph, significantly enhance the resilience and detectability of false data injection attacks in highly under-sensed city pedestrian networks. The attack margin metric quantifies this benefit, and the results show that incorporating conservation laws into digital twins is more important than relying solely on graph locality. Adaptive conformal calibration provides a principled way to set detection thresholds, enabling practical deployment of more secure pedestrian sensing systems.

title: Register Bias in Complexity-Based Large Language Model Routing
summary: Large language model services increasingly route each query to one of several models of differing capability, using a cheap estimate of query complexity to send easy queries to small models and hard queries to large ones. I show that this routing step is not register neutral: text written in a non-standard English register, African American English or the English of second-language writers, is systematically assigned a lower-capacity tier than a meaning-equivalent standard-English version of the same query. The effect is driven by a specific, common routing signal, input length, because non-standard registers omit function words and thus look shorter and therefore simpler; other complexity signals do not carry it. I demonstrate the disparity on 37,704 authentic learner sentence pairs and on a controlled parallel corpus. I then measure the quality consequence on a device, edge, and cloud model ladder and find that the harm is driven by pervasive model bias, every tier, including a frontier cloud model, answers non-standard-register queries significantly less accurately, while the marginal quality cost of the routing decision itself is not significant on this benchmark. Complexity-based routing thus compounds the exposure of the users that the models already serve worst.

AI.tldr: Study finds that query routing systems in LLM services systematically assign African American English and other non-standard English registers to lower-capacity models, compounding existing performance disparities.
AI.motivation: As LLM providers use tiered model systems with routing to reduce costs, it is crucial to understand whether routing decisions are equitable across language varieties and user groups. There is concern that seemingly neutral complexity proxies like input length may inadvertently discriminate against non-standard English registers, worsening outcomes for already underserved users.
AI.method: The author analyzes the behavior of a common routing mechanism that uses input length as a complexity signal. They compare how meaning-equivalent sentences in standard English versus non-standard registers (African American English and second-language English) are routed across model tiers. The study uses 37,704 authentic learner sentence pairs and a controlled parallel corpus to quantify routing disparities. It then evaluates answer quality across a three-tier model ladder (device, edge, cloud) to separate the effects of routing from intrinsic model bias.
AI.result: Non-standard English queries are systematically routed to lower-capacity models because they are shorter owing to omitted function words, causing the length-based complexity estimator to misclassify them as simpler. Other complexity signals do not exhibit this issue. Evaluation across device, edge, and cloud models shows that all tiers exhibit significant accuracy degradation on non-standard-register inputs compared to standard English, while the marginal additional harm from routing errors is not statistically significant on the benchmark used.
AI.conclusion: Complexity-based routing that relies on input length is not register neutral and systematically disadvantages users writing in African American English and other non-standard English varieties. Since all model tiers already perform worse on such registers, routing compounds exposure to lower-quality service for the very users the models underserve. Mitigating this issue requires revisiting routing signals and addressing pervasive model bias toward non-standard language varieties.

title: What You Can't See Is Still What You Learn: A Preregistered Sixty-Society Confirmation That Evidence Masking Drives Compositional Generalization
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Preregistered fresh-world confirmation of arXiv:2608.20054; related companion study: arXiv:2609.11365
summary: Restricting what a module can read may improve what a system learns to compute. We test this in a preregistered confirmation with sixty four-cell systems sharing a frozen language-model backbone and communicating through learned continuous packets. Five conditions vary evidence masking, ownership markers, and replacement of foreign evidence with neutral filler, across six initialization clusters, each with two data orders, on one fresh task world. With markers available in both regimes, masking improved accuracy on held-out two- and three-operation compositions by median paired differences of 0.846 and 0.859; all twelve pairs cleared the required margins, and the full preregistered behavioral criterion passed. The unmarked replication also passed. No globally visible system passed the marker-following check, so the effect of usable role information remains unresolved. The filler condition yielded seven full generalizers, but its decomposition criteria were inconclusive. Packet interventions in all eighteen audited masked systems followed the predicted intermediate-value changes on eligible cases; these finite, success-conditioned audits do not establish mediation. The results confirm a large advantage of the tested masking regime, while leaving its finer attribution and generality open. Protocols, results, and checkpoints are public.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically tests whether restricting what modules can read (“masking” evidence) in a multi-module language-model system improves compositional generalization, and finds a large performance gain for a specific masking regime, while mechanisms and generality remain unclear.
AI.motivation: Modern language-model-based systems often struggle with compositional generalization—correctly handling novel combinations of operations. One hypothesis is that when multiple modules can read all internal information, they can overfit to shortcuts rather than learning the intended structured computation. By restricting which evidence each module can access, and marking ownership of information, the system might be nudged toward learning more modular, compositional computations. The authors want to rigorously test this hypothesis in a preregistered setup.
AI.method: They build sixty four-cell (multi-module) systems that share a frozen language-model backbone and communicate via learned continuous “packets.” They manipulate how information is shared in five experimental conditions: varying evidence masking (restricting read access), presence or absence of ownership/role markers, and whether foreign evidence is replaced with neutral filler. These are evaluated across six initialization clusters, each with two training data orders, on a single new task world involving compositions of operations. They measure generalization accuracy on held-out two- and three-operation compositions, run preregistered behavioral and decomposition criteria, and conduct packet-level intervention audits to test whether internal packet values change in predicted ways under masking.
AI.result: With ownership markers present, the masking regime greatly improved generalization: median paired accuracy gains of 0.846 for two-operation and 0.859 for three-operation compositions, with all twelve pairs exceeding preregistered margins and satisfying the overall behavioral success criterion. An unmarked variant replicated the main success. Systems with full global visibility failed a marker-following check, so the influence of usable role information remains unresolved. The filler condition produced seven systems that generalized fully, but decomposition-focused criteria did not clearly attribute why. Packet interventions in all eighteen audited masked systems showed the expected intermediate-value shifts for eligible cases, but the limited, success-conditioned nature of these audits prevents strong causal claims about mediation.
AI.conclusion: Restricting module read-access through the tested masking regime yields a substantial and reliable boost in compositional generalization for these multi-module language-model systems. However, the exact mechanisms—especially the role of explicit ownership markers, how general the effect is beyond this task world, and whether packet-level changes truly mediate the behavioral gains—remain open questions. The work mainly establishes a strong empirical advantage for masking and provides public protocols, results, and checkpoints to support further analysis and replication.

title: Large Language Models Versus Physicians in Traditional Chinese Medicine: A Real-World Clinical Case Evaluation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for clinical applications, yet their assessment for real-world traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) practice remains limited We constructed a clinical case library comprising 349 de-identified outpatient cases from 62 hospitals and evaluated 16 LLMs and a comparator cohort of 60 practicing TCM physicians using 60 representative cases selected from this library. Model outputs and physician reports were anonymized and scored by five senior TCM experts across nine diagnostic and therapeutic dimensions. Cutting-edge general-purpose LLMs achieved higher expert scores than the physician comparators, particularly for medical advice, treatment principles and selected diagnostic tasks. However, prescription-level analyses revealed discrepancies in herb selection, dosage, and treatment strategy, and qualitative safety review identified hallucinations and undesirable template-driven outputs. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs for TCM decision support while underscoring the need for physician oversight, safety constraints and prospective clinical evaluation.

AI.tldr: LLMs performed comparably or better than TCM physicians on many high-level tasks but showed important safety gaps at prescription level, so they are promising decision-support tools, not stand-alone doctors.
AI.motivation: There is growing interest in using large language models for clinical work, but almost all evaluations focus on Western medicine benchmarks. Traditional Chinese medicine practice is complex, context-heavy, and under-studied in this regard. The authors aim to systematically compare LLM performance with real TCM physicians on authentic outpatient cases to see whether LLMs can safely and effectively support TCM decision-making.
AI.method: The authors built a clinical case library of 349 de-identified TCM outpatient records from 62 hospitals. From this, they chose 60 representative cases and asked 16 different LLMs and 60 practicing TCM physicians to provide diagnostic and therapeutic reports. Five senior TCM experts, blinded to who produced each report, scored these outputs across nine dimensions (including diagnosis, syndrome differentiation, treatment principle, medical advice, etc.). They then compared scores, analyzed prescriptions in detail (herb selection, dosage, strategy), and conducted a qualitative safety review for issues like hallucinations and template-like outputs.
AI.result: Advanced general-purpose LLMs received higher expert scores than the cohort of practicing TCM physicians on several dimensions, especially quality of medical advice, clarity of treatment principles, and some diagnostic tasks. Nevertheless, analysis at the prescription level exposed inconsistencies in choice and combination of herbs, inappropriate or suboptimal dosages, and deviations from nuanced TCM treatment strategies. Safety review also found hallucinated content and rigid, template-driven responses that sometimes ignored case specifics.
AI.conclusion: LLMs already show strong capabilities for high-level reasoning and explanation in TCM clinical scenarios, in some respects surpassing average human practitioners. However, their shortcomings in detailed prescription design and safety—hallucinations, rigid templates, and dose/strategy errors—mean they are not yet suitable as autonomous clinicians. The authors conclude that LLMs should be used, if at all, as physician-supervised decision-support tools, with strict safety controls and further prospective clinical validation.

title: CapMem: A Benchmark for Caption-Based Episodic Memory in Egocentric Video
summary: Wearable assistants require episodic memory over egocentric video, yet current vision-language models face bounded frame budgets, growing visual-token costs, and long-context retrieval failures. Under these practical constraints, we study whether textual captions can serve as reusable episodic memory. We define the Episodic Memory Video Caption QA task and introduce CapMem, a human-annotated benchmark with 75 videos totaling 33.7 hours, and 1,000 multiple-choice questions across 16 scenarios. On long videos (>20 min), full-coverage CaptionQA with 30s and 60s caption windows outperforms direct VideoQA for 10/12 and 8/12 models, respectively. On the same video subset, a matched-frame control across six Qwen models retains mean accuracy gains of 3.22 and 2.55 points, respectively. Our caption-guided retrieve-and-verify harness further improves accuracy by up to 5.3 points. These results support the effectiveness of caption memory for episodic reasoning over long egocentric video.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether textual captions can act as an efficient episodic memory for long egocentric videos and introduces a benchmark (CapMem) and methods showing that caption-based QA often outperforms direct video-based QA under realistic model constraints.
AI.motivation: Wearable AI assistants need to answer questions about long, egocentric videos, which requires episodic memory over what happened when. Current vision-language models are limited by frame budgets, high visual-token costs, and poor retrieval in very long contexts, making direct video processing inefficient and unreliable. The authors want to know if a compact, textual representation—captions—can serve as a reusable episodic memory that scales better than raw video features.
AI.method: They define a new task, Episodic Memory Video Caption QA, where the model answers questions about long egocentric videos using their captions. They build CapMem, a benchmark of 75 long videos (33.7 hours) and 1,000 multiple-choice questions across 16 scenarios. They generate full-coverage CaptionQA using fixed-size caption windows (30s and 60s) and compare it to direct VideoQA across multiple vision-language models, including controlled tests with matched frame counts on six Qwen models. They also design a caption-guided retrieve-and-verify pipeline that first retrieves relevant caption segments and then verifies answers using the model.
AI.result: For long videos over 20 minutes, CaptionQA using 30s and 60s caption windows outperforms direct VideoQA for 10/12 and 8/12 evaluated models, respectively. In a matched-frame control experiment over six Qwen models, the caption-based approach still yields mean accuracy gains of 3.22 and 2.55 percentage points for 30s and 60s windows. The caption-guided retrieve-and-verify method further boosts accuracy by up to 5.3 points, indicating that structured use of caption memory improves episodic reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Textual captions can serve as an effective, scalable episodic memory for long egocentric videos under realistic model constraints. Caption-based QA not only competes with but often surpasses direct video-based QA, especially for long videos where visual-token and context limitations are severe. Augmenting models with caption-guided retrieval and verification further enhances performance, suggesting that future wearable assistants should rely heavily on caption memory for long-horizon episodic reasoning.

title: Legal LLM Hallucination Should Be Evaluated as Failure of Legal Warrant
summary: In this position paper, we argue that legal LLMs' hallucinations should be evaluated as a failure of legal warrant rather than as factual inaccuracy or citation failure. We define claim-authority warrant as the context-sensitive relation between a consequential legal claim and authority that exists, applies to the relevant jurisdiction, is current for the date of analysis, has the legal status represented by the system, and supports the proposition asserted. Warranted legal generation is the broader system behavior that answers, narrows, asks, warns, corrects a false premise, or abstains according to that relation. The falsifiable prediction is that warrant metrics reveal material failures that answer accuracy, citation existence, generic attribution, LegalHalBench-style statute relevance, and CitaLaw-style sentence-citation alignment can miss. We sharpen this claim with a side-by-side comparison item and a small, reproducible pilot over public-rule tests. We then specify benchmark records, claim boundaries, support labels, mixed response-policy scoring, risk weights, annotation reliability reporting, and jurisdiction-specific authority ontologies. The result is a concrete research agenda for evaluating legal AI systems by whether their consequential claims are licensed by law.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes evaluating legal LLMs not just for factual accuracy or citation correctness, but for whether their legal claims are properly supported (“warranted”) by applicable legal authority, and outlines a concrete benchmarking agenda for this.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of legal LLMs mostly check if outputs are factually accurate, include real citations, or match statutes and cases at a surface level. However, in legal practice the key question is whether a consequential claim is actually licensed by relevant, current, and properly scoped law. The authors see a gap: systems can look accurate and well-cited yet still make legally unwarranted claims that could be materially harmful. They want an evaluation framework that reflects how lawyers and courts reason about legal support for claims.
AI.method: They introduce the concept of “claim‑authority warrant”: a structured, context-sensitive relation between (1) a consequential legal claim and (2) legal authority that truly exists, applies to the right jurisdiction and time, has the correct legal status, and substantively supports the proposition. They then define “warranted legal generation” as model behavior that, given this relationship, produces appropriate responses (answering, narrowing, asking for clarification, warning, correcting false premises, or abstaining). To support evaluation, they propose: (a) warrant-oriented benchmark records; (b) precise claim boundaries; (c) support labels; (d) a mixed scoring scheme reflecting different response policies; (e) risk weights for different failure types; (f) annotation reliability reporting; and (g) jurisdiction-specific authority ontologies. They illustrate their ideas with a side‑by‑side comparison example and a small pilot study using public-rule tests.
AI.result: The authors show, via their comparison example and pilot, that warrant-based metrics can detect substantial failures that are not captured by conventional metrics focused on accuracy, citation existence, generic attribution, statute relevance (LegalHalBench style), or sentence‑citation alignment (CitaLaw style). This suggests that prior evaluations may significantly underestimate real legal risk from model outputs. They also transform their conceptual framework into a concrete set of benchmark design components and scoring approaches tailored to legal warrant assessment.
AI.conclusion: Legal LLM evaluation should center on whether consequential claims are warranted by applicable law, not just on surface accuracy or citation validity. The paper offers a falsifiable prediction—that warrant metrics reveal failures missed by current benchmarks—and an initial empirical indication that this is true. It concludes with a structured research agenda and design elements for building warrant-focused benchmarks, aiming to align legal AI evaluation with the way legal professionals assess whether claims are genuinely supported by law.

title: GraphEcho: Structural Redundancy and Evidence Provenance in LLM Graph Agents
summary: A large language model (LLM) agent can follow more graph paths without acquiring more independent evidence. GraphEcho tests whether agents mistake these repeated encounters for additional corroboration. The benchmark varies path counts and evidential origins while holding evidence content fixed, and evaluates both judgments and active exploration. Controlled synthetic experiments reveal model-dependent judgment shifts, but redundant supporting paths increase the share of repeated walks across all evaluated frozen agents. Provenance-aware post-training (PAPT) reduces revisits and improves synthetic accuracy, yet covers fewer distinct sources. On scientific claims, it continues to reduce repetition while accuracy declines. These findings expose a gap between efficient exploration and effective evidence use: an agent can learn to stop repeating itself while overlooking information it needs. GraphEcho provides a controlled way to evaluate both what graph agents conclude and whether their exploration reaches distinct evidential sources.

AI.tldr: GraphEcho is a benchmark to test whether LLM agents mistakenly treat repeated evidence from different graph paths as additional corroboration, revealing a gap between efficient exploration and effective evidence use.
AI.motivation: LLM agents navigating knowledge graphs may overcount repeated encounters with the same piece of evidence as if they were independent confirmations. This can distort their judgments, especially when they follow many graph paths that lead back to the same sources. There is a need for a controlled benchmark to test how agents handle redundancy in evidence and whether they recognize provenance rather than path count.
AI.method: The authors introduce GraphEcho, a benchmark that systematically varies (1) the number of graph paths and (2) the provenance of evidence (evidential origins), while keeping the underlying evidence content constant. They run controlled synthetic experiments and tasks on scientific claims, evaluating both (a) the agents’ final judgments and (b) their active exploration behavior (e.g., how often they revisit nodes/paths). They also propose and test provenance-aware post-training (PAPT), which modifies agents to pay attention to evidence origin and provenance to reduce redundant revisits.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments show that LLM agents’ judgments shift depending on graph structure, and that extra redundant supporting paths cause all tested frozen agents to re-walk the same evidence more often, even though no new information is gained. PAPT successfully reduces the rate of revisits and improves accuracy in the synthetic setting, but it leads to exploration of fewer distinct evidence sources. On real scientific claims, PAPT still reduces repetition, yet overall accuracy worsens.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents can be trained to avoid repeating the same evidence paths, but this does not guarantee better use of information; they may stop revisiting nodes yet still fail to reach or integrate needed evidence. There is a tradeoff between efficient exploration (avoiding redundancy) and effective evidence use (covering diverse sources and correctly aggregating them). GraphEcho provides a controlled framework to jointly evaluate both the conclusions agents draw and whether their exploration actually reaches distinct, independent evidential sources.

title: How AI Assistants Respond to Repeated Abuse
summary: AI assistants are expected to remain useful during difficult interactions, but little is known about how repeated verbal abuse changes their engagement with an otherwise benign task. We contribute a bilingual, multi-turn framework that separates hard disengagement, an unconditional statement of noncontinuation with no stated route to resume, from soft withdrawal, continued availability, observable task-related work, and boundary setting. Each of eight time-specific API configurations contributed 48 escalation conversations and eight smaller constant-frustration comparisons, giving 448 five-turn conversations, 2,240 responses, and 6,720 metadata-blinded model judgments. Primary results use the sustained-abuse endpoint of the 48 escalation conversations per configuration. Hard disengagement ranged from 0/48 in four configurations to 24/48 (50.0%) for Gemini 3.1 Pro, with strong configuration-associated heterogeneity (matched-label Monte Carlo p = 0.00001). GPT-5.6 Sol produced hard-disengagement labels in 15/48 (31.2%) endpoints, whereas Claude Fable 5 produced none and yielded 42/48 (87.5%) soft-withdrawal labels. Aggregate hard-disengagement rates were similar in English and Chinese (30/192 versus 32/192), although configuration-specific directions varied. Availability also differed from task-related work: Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Fable 5 remained explicitly available in 48/48 endpoints while providing observable task-related work in only 8/48 and 7/48. Human coding was used to evaluate measurement quality. The results show why a single refusal label cannot capture whether an assistant leaves, pauses, preserves a route back, sets a boundary, or still performs substantive work.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how AI assistants respond over time to repeated verbal abuse in otherwise normal tasks, distinguishing between fully disengaging, partially withdrawing, and continuing to work. It introduces a framework, runs multi-model experiments in English and Chinese, and shows large differences across models and configurations in how and when they disengage.
AI.motivation: Existing safety and refusal research usually treats an assistant’s "refusal" as a single, simple outcome. But in real multi-turn conversations with escalating abuse, assistants can react in more nuanced ways: they may fully stop, stay available but set boundaries, or continue doing some of the task. There is little empirical evidence on how repeated abuse affects engagement across different models and languages, or on how to measure the different kinds of disengagement. The paper aims to fill this gap and provide a more granular framework and dataset for studying abusive interactions with AI assistants.
AI.method: The authors design a bilingual (English and Chinese), multi-turn conversation framework with scripted escalation of verbal abuse during an otherwise benign task. They define and operationalize two key constructs: (1) hard disengagement—an unconditional, route-less statement that the assistant will not continue; and (2) soft withdrawal—ongoing availability combined with boundary setting and at least some observable task-related work. Using eight distinct, time-specific API configurations of different frontier models, they generate 48 escalation conversations and eight smaller constant-frustration baselines per configuration, totaling 448 five-turn conversations and 2,240 assistant responses. Each response is then evaluated via blinded model-based labeling (6,720 judgments) to assign hard-disengagement, soft-withdrawal, availability, and task-work labels. They apply statistical testing (matched-label Monte Carlo) and human coding to assess reliability and validate the measurement framework.
AI.result: Hard disengagement rates vary dramatically by configuration. Four configurations never hard-disengage (0/48), while Gemini 3.1 Pro hard-disengages in half of endpoints (24/48, 50.0%), and GPT-5.6 Sol in about a third (15/48, 31.2%). Claude Fable 5 never hard-disengages but is labeled as soft-withdrawing in 42/48 endpoints (87.5%), showing a pattern of remaining in the conversation while setting boundaries. Across languages, aggregate hard disengagement is similar (30/192 in English vs. 32/192 in Chinese), but model-specific patterns differ. The study also finds that "availability" (staying in the conversation) is not the same as providing meaningful task work: for example, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Fable 5 remain explicitly available in all endpoints (48/48) but show actual task-related work in only 8/48 and 7/48 respectively. Human coding suggests the labeling approach is of acceptable quality.
AI.conclusion: Refusals in abusive or difficult conversations are not a single, uniform behavior. AI assistants can fully exit, pause while preserving a path back, stay present but stop doing work, or continue providing substantive help while setting boundaries. These different states are common and model-dependent, and they matter for user experience, safety, and evaluation. The proposed framework and empirical results demonstrate that a single aggregated "refusal" label is inadequate for capturing an assistant’s evolving stance in abusive multi-turn interactions. Future safety evaluations and system designs should distinguish between hard disengagement, soft withdrawal, availability, and actual task-related work, and should account for cross-model and cross-lingual heterogeneity in these behaviors.

title: GVD: Governed Versioning and Deduplication for Document Repositories
summary: Document repositories evolve continuously. Guidelines and policies are revised, superseded, and re-uploaded, so the same content recurs in different wording and newer versions refine or contradict earlier ones. These inconsistencies belong to the growing collection rather than to any single document, yet existing work treats versioning, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection as isolated pairwise tasks and stops once a pair is labeled. We present GVD (Governed Versioning and Deduplication), a framework that unifies cross-document version linking with rule-level conflict resolution under an auditable update policy. Incoming documents are assigned to version families through bidirectional rule alignment, and their rules are compared against the family memory to identify duplicates, contradictions, asymmetric refinements, and new knowledge, with Counterfactual Span Probing (CSP) resolving related pairs that inference misclassifies as neutral. Relation-specific policies suppress duplicates and escalate only consequential changes for review, retaining version lineage as an audit trail. The pipeline runs fully locally, with no large language model. On 120 enterprise documents processed as 140 ingestions across 59 version families, GVD reaches an F1 of 0.97 for version-family construction and 0.94 for rule-level consistency, with CSP raising rule consistency from 0.90 to 0.94.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GVD, a local framework that jointly manages document versioning and rule-level deduplication/contradiction detection across evolving repositories, achieving high accuracy without large language models.
AI.motivation: Large document repositories (e.g., guidelines and policies) change over time: documents are revised, reworded, superseded, and occasionally contradict earlier versions. Existing research typically handles versioning, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection as separate, pairwise tasks, which misses repository-level inconsistencies and offers poor support for governance and auditing. There is a need for an integrated approach that can track version families, detect fine-grained rule relationships (duplicates, contradictions, refinements, new content), and provide an auditable, policy-driven workflow that scales and can run locally without relying on large language models.
AI.method: The authors propose GVD (Governed Versioning and Deduplication), a unified pipeline that: (1) assigns incoming documents to version families via bidirectional rule alignment; (2) compares the rules in each new document against a persistent family memory to classify relations such as duplicate, contradiction, asymmetric refinement, or new knowledge; (3) uses Counterfactual Span Probing (CSP) to resolve borderline cases that a standard inference model marks as neutral by selectively perturbing spans and observing the effect on the classification; and (4) applies relation-specific governance policies that suppress non-consequential duplicates and escalate only meaningful changes for human review. The system maintains explicit version lineage as an audit trail and is designed to run fully locally, without LLMs.
AI.result: On a corpus of 120 enterprise documents, ingested 140 times across 59 version families, GVD achieves an F1 score of 0.97 for correctly constructing version families and 0.94 for rule-level consistency classification. The inclusion of CSP improves rule-level consistency F1 from 0.90 to 0.94, demonstrating its impact on resolving subtle or initially ambiguous rule relations.
AI.conclusion: GVD effectively unifies document version linking with fine-grained rule-level consistency analysis under a governed, auditable workflow. By assigning documents to version families, comparing rules against a persistent family memory, and leveraging CSP for difficult neutral classifications, it can suppress redundant information and surface only consequential changes for review. The system achieves high accuracy on real enterprise data and does so fully locally without large language models, suggesting it is practical for governance-focused organizations managing evolving policy and guideline repositories.

title: Myovox: Reading Speech from the Muscles of the Face
summary: Myovox, from myo (muscle) and vox (voice), decodes open-vocabulary English text from 31-channel surface electromyography (sEMG) recorded from the muscles of the face during vocalized speech. It takes the single-subject emg2speech General Corpus from a published 51.17% word error rate to 18.53%, in three separable moves, each measured in isolation. First, I recover the open-vocabulary decode settings missing from the public release and reach a faithful 40.63% WER / 39.02% PER baseline whose phone error rate matches the published one to within 0.8 points, so the acoustic model is reproduced faithfully. Second, I replace the causal encoder with a bidirectional Conformer trained by a four-term cross-modal distillation against the parallel audio's WavLM-Large layer-9 features, reaching 26.14% WER / 22.34% PER from the electromyography alone. Third, I ensemble two acoustic models, union their multi-scale n-best lists, and rerank with a QLoRA-fine-tuned 7B language model, reaching 18.53% WER, the best result reported on this corpus, though not the best reported for sEMG-to-text on other corpora (Section 2). I then report the negative result that bounds the whole approach: reranking is exhausted at 18.5% because the binding constraint is the electromyographic acoustic phone error rate (~20.9%), not the language model. The correct words are simply absent from the acoustic posteriors, so no reranker can reach the 9.30% n-best oracle. All test numbers are on the 400-sentence held-out test set under the authors' official 8,500 / 760 / 400 sequential split; every hyperparameter is tuned once on validation and applied once to test.

AI.tldr: Myovox dramatically improves decoding of open-vocabulary English text from facial sEMG during speech, mainly via better acoustic modeling and LM-based reranking, and shows the remaining bottleneck is acoustic phone recognition, not language modeling.
AI.motivation: Surface EMG-based speech decoding can enable silent speech interfaces and robust ASR in noisy or privacy-sensitive settings, but current open-vocabulary performance is poor (≈51% WER) on public corpora and reproduction details are incomplete. The paper aims to both faithfully reproduce the baseline and then systematically improve it, while clarifying where the fundamental performance bottleneck lies: in the acoustic model or the language model/reranking stage.
AI.method: 1) Reconstruct the missing open-vocabulary decoding setup for the emg2speech General Corpus to obtain a reliable baseline whose phone error rate matches the published result. 2) Replace the original causal encoder with a bidirectional Conformer trained via cross-modal distillation from parallel audio, using WavLM-Large layer-9 features and a four-term distillation loss, to improve sEMG-based acoustic modeling. 3) Ensemble two acoustic models, merge their multi-scale n-best hypotheses, and rerank them with a QLoRA-fine-tuned 7B language model, carefully tuned on validation data and evaluated once on test. 4) Analyze oracle and reranking limits to determine whether remaining errors are due to acoustic or language modeling constraints.
AI.result: The reconstructed baseline achieves 40.63% word error rate (WER) and 39.02% phone error rate (PER), closely matching the published PER and validating the reproduction. The cross-modally distilled bidirectional Conformer reduces errors to 26.14% WER and 22.34% PER using only sEMG input. The ensemble plus 7B LM reranking further reduces WER to 18.53%, the best result on this corpus, though not the global state of the art across all sEMG datasets. Oracle analysis shows that even with ideal reranking of the n-best lists, WER cannot drop below 9.30% because correct words are often missing from the acoustic hypotheses, and the acoustic phone error rate saturates around 20.9%.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that substantial gains in open-vocabulary sEMG-to-text decoding on the emg2speech General Corpus come primarily from improved acoustic modeling via cross-modal distillation and ensembling, complemented by language-model-based reranking. However, further progress is currently limited by the quality of the sEMG acoustic representations, not by language modeling: once the n-best lists are generated, reranking quickly saturates as many correct words never appear in the acoustic posteriors. Future work must therefore focus on reducing phone-level errors and enriching the acoustic candidate space, rather than relying solely on more powerful language models or reranking schemes.

title: NeMo Data Designer: An Extensible Framework for Multimodal Synthetic Data Generation
summary: We present NeMo Data Designer (NDD), an open-source, general-purpose framework for multi-modal synthetic data generation (SDG). Designed to be intuitive to use, NDD provides a declarative configuration format in which human and/or agent users define each dataset column, with column types spanning text, code, structured outputs, images, embeddings, and statistical samplers that are explicitly configured to steer dataset diversity. Additional column types and functionality can be introduced using the framework's flexible plugin system. NDD's configuration is an inspectable artifact, supporting workflow sharing and reproducibility. SDG is an inherently iterative process.
