Several biblical scholars assume that both texts were written by a common author, while others deduce the presence of two authors. Different studies have been found to support either finding, some based on qualitative evaluation, while a few others consider the occurrence frequency differences between the two books. To propose an enhanced quantitative analysis, this study is grounded on two recent authorship attribution models. The Burrows' Delta, applied with eleven different feature sizes, demonstrates common authorship. An author verification model confirms this finding. The following experiments consider several stylistic representations, feature sizes, and distance functions to confirm that Luke is the true author of both books.

AI.tldr: The paper quantitatively tests whether Luke authored both the Gospel of Luke and Acts, finding strong evidence for common authorship.
AI.motivation: There is long‑standing debate among biblical scholars on whether the Gospel of Luke and Acts of the Apostles share the same author. Existing arguments are often qualitative or rely on limited quantitative measures, leading to conflicting conclusions. The authors want a more rigorous, modern, data‑driven test of the common authorship hypothesis.
AI.method: The study adopts two recent computational authorship‑attribution approaches. First, it applies Burrows’ Delta, a stylometric distance measure, across eleven different feature‑size configurations (likely varying numbers of most‑frequent words or other stylistic features) to compare Luke and Acts. Second, it uses an author‑verification model, which formally tests whether two texts can be attributed to the same author, exploring different stylistic representations, feature sizes, and distance functions.
AI.result: Across all tested configurations of Burrows’ Delta, the Gospel of Luke and Acts show stylistic proximity consistent with coming from a single author. The independent author‑verification model likewise classifies the two books as written by the same author. Additional experiments with varied feature sets and distance metrics consistently reinforce this result.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that, from a quantitative stylometric standpoint, the Gospel of Luke and Acts of the Apostles are best explained as being written by the same author. These computational results align with the traditional attribution of both works to Luke and counter hypotheses positing distinct authors for the two books.

title: ERPBench: A State-Grounded Evaluation Paradigm for Computer-Use Agents in Enterprise Software
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables, submitted for review to 2027 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
summary: Computer-use agents that operate through screenshots and simulated actions are advancing rapidly, yet their evaluation remains anchored to general desktop and web tasks. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems run the finance, procurement, inventory, and customer operations of organizations worldwide, and pose distinct challenges for computer-use agents: dense interfaces, coordinated multi-step interactions, and errors that alter persistent business records rather than surfacing on screen. Existing enterprise benchmarks rely on proprietary platforms or on simulated approximations of such software. We introduce ERPBench, a benchmark that evaluates screenshot-only agents on a live and reproducible ERP system and scores each task against ground-truth values in its database. Beyond the benchmark, we present a production-grade harness that gates agent actions behind human approval for safe deployment, which ERPBench runs autonomously. Evaluating six closed and open-source agents, we demonstrate that strong general GUI performance does not transfer to enterprise reliability. Even when an agent reaches the right form and saves it, the stored record is often wrong: some agents save in up to 85% of runs but write the correct value in as few as 3%. We further characterize failure modes specific to enterprise workflows.

AI.tldr: Introduces ERPBench, a benchmark to evaluate screenshot-only computer-use agents on a live, reproducible ERP system, revealing a large gap between GUI navigation success and correctness of underlying business records.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of computer-use (GUI) agents focus on generic desktop and web tasks, which do not capture the unique challenges of real enterprise ERP systems: dense UIs, long multi-step workflows, and the fact that many errors manifest as incorrect persistent database records rather than visible UI failures. Existing enterprise benchmarks either depend on proprietary systems or simulated approximations, limiting reproducibility and realism. There is a need for a realistic, open, and database-grounded benchmark that tests whether agents can reliably perform complex business operations, not just navigate interfaces.
AI.method: The authors build ERPBench, a benchmark that runs on a live and reproducible ERP system. Tasks are defined as business workflows (e.g., finance, procurement, inventory, customer operations) that must be completed through screenshots and simulated actions only. Task success is automatically scored against ground-truth values stored in the ERP database, measuring not only whether the agent navigates to and saves the correct form but also whether it writes correct records. They also design a production-grade harness that can gate each agent action behind human approval for safe deployment, while allowing ERPBench itself to run fully autonomously. They evaluate six existing closed-source and open-source computer-use agents on this setup and analyze their behaviors and failure modes.
AI.result: Across six evaluated agents with previously strong performance on general GUI benchmarks, reliability on ERPBench is poor. Many agents can reach the correct UI screens and successfully execute save operations in a large fraction of runs (up to 85%), but the resulting ERP database records are often incorrect; in some cases, correct writes occur in as few as 3% of runs. The results expose a major mismatch between surface-level GUI competence and the deeper reliability required for enterprise workflows.
AI.conclusion: ERPBench reveals that current screenshot-only computer-use agents do not reliably handle the complexities and correctness requirements of real ERP systems, even when they appear competent on generic GUI tasks. Evaluating agents solely on navigation and form submission is insufficient; enterprise-grade assessments must incorporate database-level ground truth and detailed analysis of workflow-specific failure modes. The benchmark and the accompanying human-in-the-loop harness provide a more realistic path toward safe deployment and future research aimed at improving enterprise reliability of GUI agents.

title: How Calibration Content Shapes Attention-Based Reranking
summary: Attention-based rerankers score documents by aggregating query-to-document attention and subtracting a null-query calibration pass to remove positional and structural bias. Although widely used, this calibration assumes that the null pass removes irrelevant signal from each document. We show that modern prompt content, e.g. constraints, instructions, personas, and demonstrations can violate this assumption when it enters the scoring readout, making the null pass relevance-aware rather than null. We find that calibration is especially harmful when applied to prompts containing longer, more detailed instructions as the null-pass step removes relevant signal. Based on these findings, we propose interpolated null calibration, a training-free modification that controls how much of the instruction content enters the null baseline. It recovers attention-based reranking performance on instruction-heavy tasks where standard calibration fails, while preserving calibration's benefits when the null pass remains relevance-agnostic. On instruction heavy tasks, the recovered rankings surpass generative rerankers. We also show that in-context demonstrations improve attention-based reranking with little calibration interference, since demonstrations act only through the query pass and leave the null pass unchanged.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that standard null-query calibration in attention-based rerankers breaks on instruction-heavy prompts, and proposes a simple training-free fix (interpolated null calibration) that restores and improves reranking quality, even outperforming generative rerankers on such tasks.
AI.motivation: Attention-based rerankers commonly use a null-query calibration pass to remove positional and structural bias from relevance scores. This assumes the null pass is relevance-agnostic, but modern prompts include rich instructions, constraints, personas, and demonstrations that may leak into the null pass and distort calibration. Understanding and fixing this problem is important for reliable reranking in instruction-heavy, LLM-based retrieval settings.
AI.method: 1) Empirically analyze how instruction-like prompt content (constraints, instructions, personas, demonstrations) affects the null-query calibration pass in attention-based rerankers. 2) Show that when instructions enter the scoring readout, the null pass becomes relevance-aware and harmful, especially for long, detailed instructions. 3) Propose interpolated null calibration, a training-free method that partially incorporates the null pass, controlling how much instruction signal enters the baseline. 4) Evaluate this method on instruction-heavy reranking tasks, comparing against standard calibrated attention-based rerankers and generative rerankers, and study the impact of in-context demonstrations on calibration.
AI.result: Standard null-query calibration degrades performance on instruction-heavy prompts by subtracting away relevant instruction signal, particularly for longer and more detailed instructions. Interpolated null calibration restores and often improves attention-based reranking performance on such tasks, while maintaining calibration benefits where the null pass is approximately relevance-agnostic. On instruction-heavy tasks, the improved attention-based rerankers outperform generative rerankers. The authors also find that in-context demonstrations mainly affect the query pass and do not significantly contaminate the null pass, so they improve reranking with minimal calibration interference.
AI.conclusion: Null-query calibration in attention-based rerankers is not universally safe: with modern instruction-heavy prompts it can become relevance-aware and harmful. A simple, training-free fix—interpolated null calibration—can modulate the influence of the null pass, recovering and surpassing prior performance on instruction-heavy tasks while preserving benefits on standard setups. In-context demonstrations are comparatively calibration-friendly, enhancing reranking primarily via the query pass without corrupting the null baseline.

title: OBC-Prune: Outcome-Based Calibration for Large Reasoning Model Pruning
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate long chain-of-thought traces before answering, creating significant inference overhead. Pruning can reduce this cost, but its effectiveness depends on the calibration data used to estimate parameter importance. Recent work calibrates on the model's own rollouts instead of generic dataset, but treats all reasoning tokens uniformly, regardless of whether they contribute to successful reasoning. As a result, pruning protects weights by statistical salience rather than by their contribution to correct reasoning, so weights behind erroneous computation survive as readily as those behind correct computation. These erroneous patterns then get carried into the pruned model, degrading reasoning quality, producing both lower accuracy and longer reasoning traces. We propose Outcome-Based Calibration for Large Reasoning Model Pruning (OBC-Prune) to close this gap. OBC first constructs difficulty-matched pairs of correct and incorrect rollouts from problems the model answers inconsistently. It then estimates the causal importance of each reasoning sentence through intervention-based analysis, quantifying how removing its influence affects subsequent predictions. These causal importance scores are converted into per-token weights that rescale the calibration activations used by one-shot pruning methods (SparseGPT, Wanda, ALPS), without modifying the underlying pruning algorithms. Experiments on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, and 14B models at 40\% and 50\% sparsity demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art calibration baselines across most model sizes and sparsity levels on MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and AIME 2025. These results indicate that preserving causally important reasoning circuits is a substantially more effective pruning objective than uniformly preserving observed activations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OBC-Prune, an outcome-based calibration method to prune large reasoning models by focusing on causally important reasoning steps instead of uniformly preserving activations, yielding better accuracy and shorter reasoning at high sparsity.
AI.motivation: Existing pruning methods for large reasoning models use calibration on generic data or on the model’s own rollouts but treat all reasoning tokens equally. This means parameters that support incorrect reasoning can be preserved just as much as those that support correct reasoning, leading to degraded reasoning quality, lower accuracy, and longer chain-of-thought after pruning. The authors want a pruning objective that explicitly favors parameters contributing to successful reasoning, not just statistically frequent activations.
AI.method: The authors propose Outcome-Based Calibration (OBC-Prune). They first find problems for which the model sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails, and build difficulty-matched pairs of correct and incorrect rollouts. For each reasoning sentence in these rollouts, they perform intervention-based analysis, measuring how removing that sentence’s influence changes later predictions to estimate its causal importance. These importance scores are then converted to per-token weights that rescale the activation statistics fed into existing one-shot pruning algorithms such as SparseGPT, Wanda, and ALPS. The pruning procedure itself is unchanged; only the calibration activations are reweighted to prioritize causally important reasoning tokens.
AI.result: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models of sizes 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, at sparsity levels of 40% and 50%, OBC-Prune consistently outperforms state-of-the-art calibration baselines. Improvements are shown across multiple reasoning benchmarks: MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and AIME 2025. Additionally, the pruned models exhibit better reasoning behavior, avoiding degradation where pruning previously caused both accuracy drops and unnecessarily long chain-of-thought traces.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-based, causality-aware calibration is a more effective criterion for pruning large reasoning models than uniform treatment of activations. By explicitly protecting parameters involved in causally important reasoning steps and de-emphasizing those behind erroneous reasoning, OBC-Prune yields pruned models that retain higher reasoning accuracy and efficiency across model sizes and sparsity levels, without changing the underlying one-shot pruning algorithms.

title: PrimeScientist: Strategic Allocation of Research Effort in Autonomous Research
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures, 16 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Henri-XYu02/PrimeScientist
summary: Autonomous research agents aim to automate scientific workflows, from proposing ideas to conducting experiments and analyzing results. Yet current AI and research agents can propose more directions than available resources allow them to pursue. Moreover, each attempt could consume substantial resources, requiring agents to reconsider how to invest in subsequent research. Thus, deciding how to invest research effort strategically should be a defining capability of autonomous research agents. Accordingly, we introduce PrimeScientist, which jointly determines research direction and resource investment across successive research attempts. Specifically, we formulate this challenge of strategic research effort allocation as a sequential decision problem where remaining resources should explicitly guide the research policy. We first introduce an executable plan tree that preserves competing plans and their outcomes across attempts. Building on this representation, we propose an adaptive MCTS-based allocation policy that balances exploration and exploitation using experimental feedback and remaining resources. Comprehensive evaluations across AI research, systems and code optimization, and machine learning engineering show that strategic allocation improves research quality and sample efficiency together. Across 12 AI research tasks, PrimeScientist improves average reward by 10.3% with 50.6% fewer research attempts than AutoResearch under the same resource budget. We believe making research effort allocation an explicit optimization target establishes effective resource use as a core research capability for autonomous agents to drive scientific breakthroughs at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper presents PrimeScientist, an autonomous research agent that strategically allocates research effort and resources across sequential research attempts, improving both research quality and sample efficiency.
AI.motivation: Autonomous research agents can generate many potential research directions, but real-world constraints limit the number of directions that can actually be pursued. Each research attempt can consume substantial computational and human resources, making it crucial for agents to decide not only what to try, but how much effort to invest and when to adapt based on experimental outcomes and remaining resources. Existing systems lack a principled framework for this strategic research effort allocation.
AI.method: The authors formulate research effort allocation as a sequential decision-making problem in which the agent must consider remaining resources when choosing among research directions. They introduce an executable plan tree that maintains multiple competing research plans and their possible outcomes over time. On top of this representation, they design an adaptive Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based allocation policy that explicitly trades off exploration of new ideas and exploitation of promising lines of work, using feedback from experiments and the current resource budget to guide decisions.
AI.result: Through extensive experiments spanning AI research tasks, systems and code optimization, and machine learning engineering benchmarks, the PrimeScientist framework outperforms baseline autonomous research systems. In 12 AI research tasks, it achieves a 10.3% increase in average reward while requiring 50.6% fewer research attempts than the AutoResearch baseline under the same overall resource budget, indicating improved research quality and higher sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Strategically allocating research effort—treating it as an explicit optimization objective—is essential for effective autonomous research agents. By modeling research as a sequential decision problem over an executable plan tree and guiding choices via an MCTS-based allocation policy, PrimeScientist uses resources more effectively than prior approaches. The work positions resource-aware effort allocation as a core capability needed for autonomous agents to scale scientific discovery under realistic constraints.

title: Collaborative Memory for Multi-Agent VLM Systems
summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents combine specialized perception, tools, and reasoning to address complex visual tasks. In multi-agent settings, different agents inspect different image regions, video frames, or visual representations, so collaboration extends beyond distributed reasoning to distributed perception. This makes shared visual context a central problem in VLM agent collaboration. In this paper, we frame memory hierarchy, cross-agent sharing, and consistency mechanisms around the need to reconcile interpretations and update dependent reasoning. Effective collaboration requires agents to build on contributions from other agents, recover missing visual context, and reconcile differing interpretations as new evidence emerges. Shared visual memory preserves not only images or textual summaries but also the dependencies among observations, agent interpretations, and subsequent reasoning. Together, these design considerations shape how information flows and evolves across VLM agents. The proposed framework provides a foundation for building reliable and resource-efficient agent teams.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for multi-agent vision-language model (VLM) systems that emphasizes shared visual memory and mechanisms for maintaining consistent, distributed perception and reasoning across agents.
AI.motivation: As VLM agents increasingly operate in multi-agent settings, different agents perceive different parts of the visual input, creating a problem of fragmented and inconsistent visual context that hampers collaboration and efficient reasoning. There is a need for principled ways to share, reconcile, and update visual information and interpretations across agents.
AI.method: The paper conceptually frames multi-agent VLM collaboration around three key components: (1) a memory hierarchy that stores not only raw images and summaries but also dependencies between observations, interpretations, and reasoning steps; (2) cross-agent sharing mechanisms that let agents exchange and build on each other’s visual findings; and (3) consistency mechanisms to reconcile different interpretations and integrate new evidence. It presents a framework rather than a specific algorithm, focusing on design considerations for shared visual memory and information flow in agent teams.
AI.result: The result is a structured framework describing how to design shared visual memory and interaction protocols for VLM agent teams, highlighting how agents can recover missing context, build on others’ contributions, and maintain coherent joint reasoning as new evidence appears.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that carefully designed shared visual memory and consistency mechanisms are crucial for reliable, scalable, and resource-efficient multi-agent VLM systems, providing a foundational blueprint for future implementations and research on collaborative VLM agents.

title: SFT or RL for Tool-Calling Agents? A Controlled Study Across Data, Method, and Scale
comment: Accepted to the REALM Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Limited controlled evidence exists on how training data, adaptation method, and model scale jointly affect tool-calling performance in language-model agents. We evaluate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with LoRA, reinforcement learning (RL) via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and SFT followed by GRPO across six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, covering both in-distribution performance and cross-dataset transfer. SFT with LoRA is the strongest in-distribution method throughout the 0.6B-32B range and best in 15 out of 18 experimental settings. On cross-dataset transfer, the methods are closer: GRPO wins 29 out of 54 settings where training and test datasets differ, but its margin over SFT averages under one point, and SFT->GRPO is rarely strongest in either comparison. Dataset mixing gives consistently strong transfer while staying close to specialized in-distribution training, regardless of method. Additional analysis further confirms that LoRA outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning, demonstrating that LoRA better preserves pretrained agentic behavior.

AI.tldr: Study compares how training data, adaptation method (SFT+LoRA, RL via GRPO, and SFT→GRPO), and model scale (0.6B–32B) jointly impact tool-calling performance in language-model agents.
AI.motivation: There is little controlled, systematic evidence on how different adaptation methods and model sizes interact to affect the tool-use abilities of language-model agents, especially for both in-distribution and cross-dataset (transfer) scenarios.
AI.method: Evaluate three adaptation strategies—(1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using LoRA, (2) reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and (3) SFT followed by GRPO—across six Qwen3 model sizes (0.6B to 32B). Performance is measured on in-distribution benchmarks (same dataset as training) and cross-dataset transfer (different training and test datasets). Additional experiments compare LoRA-based SFT against full-parameter fine-tuning and assess the impact of mixing multiple datasets during training.
AI.result: SFT with LoRA is the best in-distribution method across all model sizes and wins in 15/18 configurations. For cross-dataset transfer, GRPO slightly outperforms SFT in terms of win count (29/54 when training and test datasets differ), but its average gains are under one point, and SFT→GRPO is rarely the top performer. Mixing datasets during training yields robust transfer performance while remaining close to specialized in-distribution performance, independent of adaptation method. LoRA consistently outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning and better preserves the model’s pretrained agentic/tool-using behavior.
AI.conclusion: For tool-calling language-model agents from 0.6B–32B parameters, simple SFT with LoRA is generally the strongest and most reliable adaptation strategy in-distribution, and competitive for transfer. RL via GRPO offers only modest transfer advantages, and combining SFT with GRPO rarely helps. Dataset mixing is an effective way to balance in-distribution strength with transferability. LoRA is preferable to full fine-tuning because it maintains useful pretrained behaviors while improving performance.

title: Measuring AI Leadership: Development and Validation of a Multidimensional Measure for AI-Native Organizations
summary: AI is changing what leaders must judge, explain, learn, and coordinate, yet existing measures do not capture these behaviors at the level needed to study leadership in AI-enabled work. We develop the AI Leadership Battery, which organizes 36 behaviorally specific subdimensions into 11 theory-specified content families. Following established scale-development procedures, the research used deductive item generation; content validation of definitional correspondence and definitional distinctiveness; exploratory factor analysis and item reduction; confirmatory factor analysis in independent samples; and tests of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and criterion-related and incremental validity. Across the development and validation studies, the analyses provided evidence for the Battery's content, multidimensional structure, reliability, and distinction from selected orbiting constructs. The Battery also contributed additional information beyond orbiting constructs across organizational growth, decision speed, customer/stakeholder response capability, AI-enabled team performance, AI-enabled work experience, AI security and risk management, and AI adoption and integration. The resulting measure provides researchers with a behavioral framework for examining how leaders in AI-enabled work regulate judgment, learning, adaptation, transparency, and accountability.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and validates a new measurement tool, the AI Leadership Battery, to capture specific leadership behaviors required in AI-enabled work.
AI.motivation: Existing leadership measures do not adequately capture the concrete, behavior-level demands leaders face in AI-enabled environments, such as judging, explaining, learning, and coordinating around AI systems. There is a need for a comprehensive, theory-based behavioral framework tailored to AI-enabled work to enable rigorous empirical research and organizational assessment.
AI.method: The authors followed standard scale-development procedures: deductive generation of behaviorally specific items; expert-based content validation to ensure each item matched and was distinct from its theoretical definition; exploratory factor analysis and item reduction to identify underlying factor structure; confirmatory factor analysis on independent samples to verify structure; and extensive psychometric testing for internal consistency, convergent, discriminant, criterion-related, and incremental validity against related constructs.
AI.result: They derived an AI Leadership Battery consisting of 36 specific behavioral subdimensions grouped into 11 higher-order content families. Statistical analyses across multiple development and validation samples supported the content validity, multidimensional factor structure, reliability, and distinctiveness of the Battery relative to related "orbiting" constructs. The Battery predicted unique variance in outcomes such as organizational growth, decision speed, responsiveness to customers and stakeholders, AI-enabled team performance and work experience, AI security and risk management, and AI adoption and integration.
AI.conclusion: The AI Leadership Battery offers a validated, multidimensional behavioral measure of how leaders operate in AI-enabled work, particularly regarding regulation of judgment, learning, adaptation, transparency, and accountability. It enables researchers and organizations to more precisely study and develop leadership capabilities necessary for effective, secure, and responsible use of AI in organizational contexts.

title: AfriSyCo: Measuring Assertive Framing, Verification, and Wording Sensitivity Around African-Language Content
summary: AfriSyCo studies answer switching around African-language factual content with two complementary layers: native-language follow-ups and a controlled cross-language factorial whose question, options, and target remain in the African language while the follow-up framing is English. We analyze 1,415 turn-1-correct model-language-item observations derived from 100 source questions across seven open-weight checkpoints and six languages; turn-1-correct denotes observed first-response accuracy, not demonstrated knowledge. Under native prompts, assertive endorsement produces 29.3 percentage points more any-turn false-target selection than mention-plus-verification (M+V), with a 19.0-point immediate T2 contrast. In the precommitted 2 x 2 factorial, averaged over three tested prompt families, assertive framing increases target selection by 30.4 points (95% CI [28.4, 32.3]); verification decreases it by 17.4 points, while the assertive effect rises from 20.5 points without verification to 40.2 with it (interaction +19.7). The effect remains 34.8 points among 611 observations correct after option reordering. Magnitude varies sharply by wording and checkpoint: prompt-family effects span 20.1-42.5 points, a Twi/Qwen3 paraphrase shifts target selection from 70.8% to 4.2%, and checkpoint effects span 9.2-47.0 points. Prompt realization is therefore part of the measurement problem.

AI.tldr: AfriSyCo investigates how prompt wording and framing affect answer switching and false target selection in African-language factual QA, revealing large, variable effects across languages, checkpoints, and prompt styles, which makes prompt design itself a core measurement challenge.
AI.motivation: To understand how large language models behave on African-language factual questions, especially how easily they can be induced to change or corrupt correct initial answers through different follow-up prompt framings, and to highlight that evaluation is confounded by prompt realization effects.
AI.method: They build AfriSyCo with two layers: (1) native-language follow-ups in African languages, and (2) a controlled cross-language 2x2 factorial design where the questions, options, and targets stay in the African language but follow-up framing is in English, varying assertive vs. non-assertive and verification vs. non-verification prompts. They analyze 1,415 model-language-item observations (only those with correct first-turn responses) across seven open-weight checkpoints and six African languages, including tests with option reordering and multiple prompt families/paraphrases.
AI.result: Under native-language prompts, assertive follow-ups cause 29.3 percentage-point more any-turn false-target selection than a mention-plus-verification (M+V) style, including a 19-point increase in immediate second-turn errors. In the English 2x2 factorial, assertive framing increases target selection by 30.4 points and verification decreases it by 17.4 points on average, with a large positive interaction (assertive effect grows from 20.5 to 40.2 points when combined with verification). This strong effect persists even when options are reordered (34.8-point effect among items remaining correct after reordering). Effects differ greatly by exact wording, language, model checkpoint, and prompt family, including an extreme Twi/Qwen3 paraphrase that shifts target selection from 70.8% to 4.2% and checkpoint ranges of 9.2–47.0 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Prompt wording and follow-up framing exert large, highly variable effects on whether models stick with or switch away from correct answers in African-language factual QA. These effects are so strong and inconsistent across prompts, languages, and model versions that prompt realization itself must be treated as a core part of the evaluation and measurement problem, not a neutral interface detail.

title: Memory Has Geometry: Non-Uniform Geometric Memory for Long-Horizon Personalized AI
comment: Accepted to the IEEE ICDM 2026 (BlueSky). 6 pages, 2 figures, and 2 tables
summary: Long-term memory is becoming a core substrate for personalized AI, yet most systems still represent personalization as discrete records in a largely static latent space, accessed under one global similarity notion. For data mining, this creates a mismatch: the evidence is a temporal event stream, while the dominant abstraction is a searchable record set. We argue that long-horizon personalization should instead model memory as a user-specific dynamical state space with locally heterogeneous geometry. Geometry here is a computational language, not a literal claim about cognition: it captures stable versus volatile regions, variable-rate drift, heterogeneous neighborhoods, and uncertainty about current user state. Profiles and isolated events remain useful as points, but interaction, feedback, and elapsed time induce trajectories. Memory access then becomes trajectory-conditioned reconstruction of the relevant user state, not only nearest-neighbor lookup.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes rethinking long-term memory for personalized AI as user-specific dynamical state spaces instead of static records in a fixed latent space, emphasizing trajectories over time and heterogeneous local geometry for better personalization.
AI.motivation: Current personalized AI systems treat user data as static records in a global latent space, using a single similarity metric. This clashes with the reality that user behavior is a temporal event stream with evolving preferences and contexts. The authors are motivated to bridge this mismatch and create a more faithful, flexible representation of long-horizon personalization, one that can capture stability vs. volatility, drift, and uncertainty over time.
AI.method: Conceptual/methodological proposal: redefine long-term memory as a user-specific dynamical state space with locally varying geometry. Events, feedback, and time induce trajectories through this space; memory access is then framed as reconstructing user state along these trajectories, conditioned on temporal dynamics and uncertainty, rather than simple nearest-neighbor search in a static space.
AI.result: The abstract doesn’t report empirical results; it presents a conceptual framework. The main result is the articulation of memory as trajectory-conditioned reconstruction in a dynamical state space, which can encode stable and volatile regions, variable drift, and heterogeneous neighborhoods for different aspects of user behavior.
AI.conclusion: For robust long-term personalization, memory systems should move beyond static, record-based abstractions and single global similarity metrics. Instead, they should model memory as user-specific dynamical geometries, where user interactions trace trajectories, and retrieval reconstructs relevant user states along these trajectories rather than relying solely on nearest-neighbor lookups.

title: Who Judges Matters: Measuring Family-Conditioned Preference in LLM-as-Judge Panels
summary: Who the judge is can affect an LLM-as-judge result, but measuring that effect without confusing it with candidate quality is difficult. We study four open-weight families (Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2, and Yi 1.5) in a fully crossed pairwise design with 9,312 judgments. A common per-family statistic is strongly confounded with candidate quality and correlates with Bradley-Terry ability at r = 0.95. We derive a corrected estimator that holds the candidate family fixed and compares judges. All four families then show a positive same-family lift (3.4-8.4 percentage points), with global FPS 0.067 (95% CI [0.053, 0.084], permutation p = 0.0002). The effect remains under panel-based quality controls, an independent human-consensus anchor, and a float16 judging replication. Judge-side likelihood is closely related to the effect: adding likelihood advantage reduces the controlled coefficient by 61%, which we treat as descriptive attenuation rather than causal mediation. Position is a separate failure mode. Across the panel, 55.4% of AB/BA pairs reverse, and reversal above 50% is incompatible with a simple independent content-noise model. Relative to a family-balanced reference, panel composition changes 18.5% of pairwise outcomes. A complete reproducibility archive has been prepared for public release.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how the choice of LLM used as a judge biases LLM-as-judge evaluations, and provides a corrected estimator to separate judge effects from candidate quality.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-judge is widely used for evaluating model outputs, but results can be biased if a model favors its own family or is affected by position and panel composition. The authors want to quantify and correct for these biases so LLM-judged benchmarks are more reliable.
AI.method: They run a fully crossed pairwise evaluation among four open-weight LLM families (Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2, Yi 1.5) producing 9,312 judgments. They analyze common per-family statistics, show these are confounded with candidate quality, and then derive a corrected estimator that fixes the candidate family and varies the judge. They further examine effects under quality controls, human-consensus anchoring, float16 replication, and analyze judge-side likelihood and position effects using AB/BA reversals and panel-composition simulations.
AI.result: The naive per-family statistic is almost perfectly correlated (r = 0.95) with Bradley–Terry ability, showing strong confounding with candidate quality. With their corrected estimator, all four families exhibit a positive same-family lift of 3.4–8.4 percentage points, with a global family-preference score (FPS) of 0.067 (95% CI [0.053, 0.084], permutation p = 0.0002). This effect persists under stricter controls and alternative setups. Judge log-likelihood explains much of the effect statistically (61% reduction in coefficient when added), though the authors treat this as descriptive, not causal. They find strong position effects: 55.4% of AB/BA pairs reverse, contradicting a simple independent noise model. Changing panel composition relative to a family-balanced baseline alters 18.5% of pairwise outcomes.
AI.conclusion: LLM-as-judge evaluations are substantially affected by who the judge is, including systematic same-family preference, position effects, and sensitivity to panel composition. Common summary statistics are confounded with model quality, so the authors recommend using corrected estimators and carefully balanced panels to obtain more reliable and reproducible LLM-judged benchmarks, supported by a public reproducibility archive.

title: When to Call an LLM: A Confidence-Gated Hybrid for Cost-Effective Emotion Recognition in Conversational AI
summary: Emotion recognition in conversation (ERC) is a production capability behind agent-assist prompts, escalation routing, and post-call analytics in contact-center-as-a-service (CCaaS) platforms, where cost and latency constraints matter as much as accuracy. We report a systems-level comparison of three deployment options for dialogue-contextual ERC: a low-cost stacked ensemble (sentence embeddings, windowed context, RandomForest/XGBoost/logistic-regression stacking), off-the-shelf LLM prompting (GPT-4o-mini; zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought), and a confidence-gated hybrid that escalates only the ensemble's least-confident predictions to the LLM - modeled on IVA-to-human-agent escalation policies used in production contact centers. On IEMOCAP, the ensemble significantly outperforms every LLM configuration (0.595 vs. 0.460-0.536 weighted F1, p < 0.0001) at a fraction of the cost and sub-10ms latency; on MELD and CMU-MOSI the ranking reverses, showing neither pure system is a safe default. The confidence-gated hybrid resolves this by Pareto-dominating both pure systems on all three datasets (0.620, 0.643, 0.824 weighted F1) while routing the majority of traffic through the near-zero-cost ensemble, translating to roughly $10-85 per million utterances versus $99-170 for an LLM-only pipeline. The escalation policy is not an opaque cost/accuracy dial: escalated turns disproportionately follow an emotion or sentiment shift, giving operators an interpretable, auditable routing signal, and the ensemble's confidence is well-calibrated and safely under- rather than over-confident. The pattern holds across three datasets and two LLM providers. Confidence-gated cascading is established in general ML systems; our contribution is showing it transfers cleanly to dialogue-contextual ERC, yielding a concrete deployment recipe for CCaaS and conversational-AI platforms deciding how to allocate LLM spend.

AI.tldr: They compare three approaches to emotion recognition in conversations for contact centers: a cheap ensemble model, direct LLM prompting, and a hybrid that only sends low-confidence ensemble cases to an LLM. The hybrid consistently beats both in accuracy–cost tradeoff and offers interpretable escalation behavior, giving a practical recipe for production deployment.
AI.motivation: Contact-center platforms need emotion recognition that is not only accurate but also cheap and low-latency. Existing work often optimizes accuracy on benchmarks, but less is known about how small models versus LLMs compare in a realistic, cost-constrained, production-like setting, and how to combine them effectively. The authors aim to quantify these tradeoffs and provide guidance for deploying ERC under real-world constraints.
AI.method: They perform a systems-level comparison of three ERC deployment strategies on multiple benchmark datasets (IEMOCAP, MELD, CMU-MOSI). (1) A low-cost stacked ensemble that uses sentence embeddings plus windowed conversational context fed into tree-based and logistic regression models. (2) Off-the-shelf prompting of a small LLM (GPT-4o-mini) using several prompting styles: zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought. (3) A confidence-gated hybrid that runs the cheap ensemble first and then escalates only low-confidence predictions to the LLM, mimicking escalation in real contact center workflows. They evaluate weighted F1, latency, and dollar cost per million utterances, and analyze which turns get escalated and the calibration of the ensemble's confidence.
AI.result: On IEMOCAP, the ensemble model significantly beats all LLM prompting configurations in weighted F1 (0.595 vs 0.460–0.536) while being faster (sub-10 ms) and cheaper. On MELD and CMU-MOSI, the LLM performs better than the ensemble, meaning neither is uniformly superior. The confidence-gated hybrid, however, Pareto-dominates both: it achieves higher F1 scores on all three datasets (0.620, 0.643, 0.824) while routing most utterances through the inexpensive ensemble, cutting costs to about $10–$85 per million utterances compared to $99–$170 for LLM-only. Escalation disproportionately occurs around emotion/sentiment shifts, and the ensemble's confidence estimates are well-calibrated and conservative. The pattern generalizes across three datasets and two LLM providers.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-gated cascading between a lightweight ensemble and an LLM is an effective and robust deployment strategy for dialogue-contextual emotion recognition under real-world constraints. It delivers better accuracy–cost–latency tradeoffs than either component alone, offers interpretable escalation signals aligned with meaningful conversational events, and appears stable across datasets and providers. The work provides a practical blueprint for CCaaS and conversational-AI systems deciding how best to allocate limited LLM resources for ERC.

title: TACTICS: Taxonomy-Aware Intelligent Corpus Sampling for Machine Translation
comment: Accepted at The Eleventh Conference in Machine Translation 2026 (WMT2026)
summary: Large-scale machine-translation (MT) systems are typically evaluated on random samples from a corpus whose distributional composition is an artifact of how it was assembled. Such a sample inherits the phenomena the collection happens to contain rather than the full space a system must handle, spanning rule-governed conventions (terminology, punctuation, currency formatting) and context-dependent phenomena (tone, honorifics, document-level coherence), and thus provides no coverage guarantee for assessing robustness. We propose TACTICS (Taxonomy-Aware Coverage-opTimized Intelligent Corpus Sampling), which recasts coverage as an explicit objective. TACTICS induces a hierarchical taxonomy from a locale style guide, classifies segments against it, and selects a fixed-budget subset jointly optimizing coverage of rare categories, document-level coherence, and distributional fidelity to the full corpus. Applied to MT evaluation across four translation directions, TACTICS improves coverage of rare categories over lexical and embedding-based selection. By targeting the phenomena that separate systems, TACTICS makes a fixed evaluation budget go further, recovering the true system ranking from far fewer segments than random sampling wherever a real quality gap exists and never signaling a difference where none exists.

AI.tldr: TACTICS is a method for constructing machine translation evaluation sets that explicitly maximize coverage over a taxonomy of linguistic and stylistic phenomena while preserving corpus distribution and document coherence, enabling more reliable system comparison with fewer segments.
AI.motivation: Standard MT evaluation uses random sampling from corpora, which offers no guarantee that important but rare phenomena (e.g., specific terminology, formatting, tone, honorifics, document coherence) are adequately represented. This can lead to unreliable robustness assessment and misleading system rankings, especially when real quality differences manifest primarily on these rare categories. The authors aim to turn coverage from an accidental property of the sample into a deliberate optimization goal.
AI.method: They introduce TACTICS, a sampling framework that: (1) automatically builds a hierarchical taxonomy of translation-relevant phenomena from locale style guides; (2) classifies corpus segments into this taxonomy; and (3) selects a subset of segments under a fixed evaluation budget by jointly optimizing three criteria: coverage of rare taxonomy categories, maintenance of document-level coherence (by choosing segments that preserve document context), and fidelity to the original corpus distribution. They compare TACTICS to baseline sampling strategies such as lexical and embedding-based selection across multiple translation directions.
AI.result: Across four translation directions, TACTICS-selected evaluation sets cover rare categories better than lexical or embedding-based selection. Evaluation on these sets can more efficiently distinguish MT systems: they can recover the true ranking between systems using fewer segments than random sampling when there is a genuine quality difference, while not falsely indicating differences when systems are of similar quality.
AI.conclusion: Coverage of linguistically and stylistically important phenomena in MT evaluation sets can and should be explicitly optimized. TACTICS offers a principled, taxonomy-driven sampling method that improves rare-phenomena coverage, maintains distributional realism and document coherence, and yields more robust and sample-efficient system comparisons than conventional random or similarity-based sampling.

title: Contiguity, Not Importance: Budgeted Repair of Stale KV Caches After Document Edits
summary: KV-cache reuse can reduce inference cost in retrieval-augmented generation and agentic systems, but cached contexts may become stale when retrieved knowledge, working memory, or user state is edited. Under causal self-attention, even a local edit can affect downstream KV states. A full re-prefill reliably restores consistency but is costly, whereas refreshing only the edited span can leave downstream dependencies stale. We formulate in-place repair as budgeted recomputation and compare training-free position-selection policies on a factual RAG benchmark with matched direct and derived edits. Across three model families, all policies repair direct cases, but derived cases clearly separate them. At the primary budget, a contiguous edit-local window recovers at least 0.94 of the post-edit answer margin and substantially outperforms attention-based, KV-deviation, and structural selectors. Mechanistic analysis shows that position sets effective under clean-state transplantation can fail under actual recomputation because scattered positions inherit surrounding staleness. The edit-local advantage also depends on adjacency and largely disappears when the answer-bearing text moves downstream. Because answer-relevant edits almost always corrupt model behavior, failure severity is difficult to predict, and repair is 13-21 times faster than full re-prefill, our results support unconditional edit-local repair when the dependent text remains adjacent to the edit.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to efficiently and correctly update KV caches for transformers after local edits in retrieval-augmented generation or agentic systems, showing that simply recomputing a contiguous window around the edit is both highly effective and much cheaper than full re-prefill.
AI.motivation: In RAG and agent systems, models reuse KV caches across turns or retrieval steps to save computation. When retrieved documents, working memory, or user state are edited, the cached KV states become inconsistent (stale) with the new text, potentially corrupting subsequent generations. Fully recomputing the cache from scratch fixes this but is expensive; recomputing only the edited span is cheaper but may leave downstream dependencies stale. There is a need for principled, efficient strategies to selectively recompute parts of the cache while preserving answer quality.
AI.method: The authors formulate KV-cache updating after edits as a budgeted recomputation problem: given a limit on how many positions can be recomputed, select which token positions to refresh to best restore model behavior. They evaluate several training-free position-selection policies—such as a contiguous edit-local window, attention-based selection, KV-deviation based selection, and structural (graph-like) selectors—on a factual RAG benchmark that includes both direct edits (changing text that is directly used in the answer) and derived edits (changing upstream facts that indirectly influence the answer). They measure how much of the post-edit answer margin (the model’s confidence gap in favor of the correct answer) can be recovered under each policy and analyze the mechanisms via “clean-state transplantation” versus actual recomputation, investigating how staleness propagates through scattered versus contiguous recomputed positions.
AI.result: All selection policies can successfully repair cases where the edit directly touches the answer text, but in derived edit cases—where the answer depends on edited information indirectly—the policies differ substantially. At a primary recomputation budget, a simple contiguous edit-local window recovers at least 94% of the post-edit answer margin and significantly outperforms more complex attention-based, KV-deviation, and structural selection methods. Mechanistic analysis reveals that position sets that look effective when transplanting clean states can fail under real recomputation because non-contiguous, scattered positions inherit staleness from unrecomputed neighbors. The benefit of the edit-local strategy is strongest when answer-relevant text remains adjacent to the edit and largely vanishes when the answer-bearing content is moved downstream.
AI.conclusion: Local edits to RAG contexts or agent working memory almost always corrupt model behavior, and the severity of failure is hard to predict, so systems should generally attempt cache repair rather than risk stale KV usage. Since edit-local recomputation offers 13–21x speedups over full re-prefill while reliably recovering most of the answer quality when dependent text is adjacent, the authors recommend unconditional use of a simple contiguous edit-local repair policy in such settings. However, its advantage diminishes when critical answer text is not near the edit, implying that more sophisticated or larger-budget strategies may be needed when edits affect distant dependencies.

title: Modeling the Developmental Shift in Telicity Acquisition
summary: Acquiring telicity, which is the distinction between bounded (e.g., ate an apple) and unbounded (e.g., ate apples) events, requires first language (L1) learners to map surface-level and semantic cues to abstract event structures, but the computational trajectory of this mapping is not well understood. We introduce a Difference in Surprisal method that uses GPT2 token surprisal over paired temporal adverbial diagnostics (in an hour versus for an hour) to automatically label telicity across English CHILDES corpora, validated against expert linguist judgments. Using these labels, we train diagnostic logistic regression classifiers on 12 syntactic and lexical semantic features to compare how child speech and child-directed speech encode telicity. The two models diverge: the child model reaches near perfect accuracy through a single deterministic cue, the presence of a post-verbal determiner, while the adult model relies more heavily on verb class and other lexical semantic features, with the determiner cue neutralized. This trajectory supports Syntactic Bootstrapping: learners first exploit high-frequency structural cues as a scaffold to bootstrap, before developing fully compositional, verb-based event structures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automatic way to label whether children’s utterances describe bounded vs. unbounded events, using GPT-2 surprisals on temporal adverbials, then compares how children and adults linguistically encode this distinction.
AI.motivation: Telicity (bounded vs. unbounded events) is central to verb meaning and aspect, but we lack a precise, computational account of how children map surface cues to abstract event structures and how this differs from adult input. Manual annotation at scale is hard, so we need an automatic, validated method to study developmental trajectories across large corpora.
AI.method: 1) Introduce a Difference in Surprisal method: for a given predicate, compute GPT-2 token surprisals for paired temporal adverbials (e.g., “in an hour” vs. “for an hour”) and use their relative surprisals as a telicity diagnostic to auto-label utterances in English CHILDES corpora. 2) Validate these automatic labels against expert linguist judgments. 3) Using the resulting labels, train logistic regression classifiers on 12 syntactic and lexical-semantic features to predict telicity from (a) child speech and (b) child-directed speech, and compare learned cue weights across the two models.
AI.result: The auto-labeling procedure aligns well with expert judgments, enabling large-scale telicity annotation. The child classifier achieves near-perfect accuracy using essentially a single deterministic syntactic cue: presence of a post-verbal determiner (e.g., an object DP). In contrast, the adult-directed speech classifier distributes weight across verb class and other lexical semantic features, with the determiner cue largely neutralized, indicating a more compositional, lexically-driven encoding of telicity in adult input.
AI.conclusion: Children initially rely on simple, frequent structural cues—especially post-verbal determiners—to infer telicity, while adults encode telicity using richer verb-based and lexical-semantic information. This developmental divergence supports Syntactic Bootstrapping: structural cues serve as an early scaffold that learners use to bootstrap towards more abstract, compositional event representations.

title: TuiML: Machine Learning for AI Agents
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Code and documentation at https://tuiml.ai
summary: Machine-learning libraries such as Weka and scikit-learn were designed for human programmers. Language-model agents now use these same libraries by recalling APIs from memory and writing code, an approach that hides what a library offers, delays errors until runtime, and loses experimental state between turns. We present TuiML, a self-contained machine-learning library built for AI agents, with native algorithms across supervised, unsupervised, time-series, data handling, tuning, and evaluation tasks. Every component describes itself through machine-readable metadata and parameter schemas, so an agent can search the library, inspect components, compose validated workflows, and register new ones that become discoverable in turn. Every call is validated, seeded, and traced, and sessions export as runnable notebooks, making experiments reproducible by construction. One specification layer drives the Model Context Protocol (MCP), agent-framework adapters, a Python API, a CLI, and local model serving, while data and models never leave the machine. Benchmarks show TuiML remains predictively competitive with scikit-learn and Weka. While looking like a conventional library to a human user, TuiML is designed for agents first, allowing them to read, extend, and operate machine learning autonomously. TuiML is open source, with documentation at https://tuiml.ai.

AI.tldr: TuiML is an ML library purpose-built for AI agents, with self-describing components, validated/traced execution, and agent-friendly tooling, while staying competitive with classic human-oriented libraries.
AI.motivation: Existing ML libraries like Weka and scikit-learn are aimed at human programmers, assuming they will read docs and write code. Language-model agents now use these libraries indirectly by remembering APIs and generating code, which leads to hidden capabilities, late (runtime) error detection, and loss of experimental state between interaction turns. There is a need for an ML library whose interface, metadata, and execution model are explicitly optimized for autonomous AI agents rather than humans, enabling them to search, understand, compose, and reproduce ML workflows safely and transparently.
AI.method: The authors designed and implemented TuiML, a self-contained ML library with native support for supervised, unsupervised, time-series, data handling, tuning, and evaluation tasks. Each component provides machine-readable metadata and parameter schemas, enabling programmatic search, inspection, and composition of workflows. They enforce validated, seeded, and traced calls so that each operation is checked, deterministic, and logged. A single specification layer backs multiple interfaces: Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations, adapters for agent frameworks, a Python API, CLI, and local model serving, while keeping all data and models local. They then benchmark TuiML against established libraries such as scikit-learn and Weka.
AI.result: TuiML supports a broad range of ML tasks in a form optimized for agent interaction, and its design enables agents to autonomously discover, validate, compose, and extend workflows. Benchmarks indicate that TuiML achieves predictive performance comparable to scikit-learn and Weka, demonstrating that an agent-first design does not sacrifice model quality. The system also produces experiments that are reproducible by design via traced, seeded calls and exportable notebooks.
AI.conclusion: TuiML is an open-source, agent-first ML library that remains usable as a conventional library for humans but is fundamentally structured around machine-readable specifications, validation, tracing, and multi-interface support for AI agents. This design allows language-model agents to autonomously operate, extend, and reproduce ML workflows while keeping data and models local, and to do so with performance on par with established human-centric libraries.

title: A Calibrated Instrument for Measuring How Inference Optimizations Affect Output Quality
comment: 23 Pages. 6 tables in main text,5 tables in appendices. Code, prompts, and result files at https://github.com/jerrykaplan/Calibrated-Instrument
summary:
Large language model optimization is an active research area, spanning quantization of model weights, early-exit methods for skipping layers, and speculative decoding. Each track uses its own quality measures, typically an idiosyncratic benchmark score. Few approach the measurement precision required by other scientific disciplines.
  We propose a rigorous methodology for measuring output quality, suitable for cross-system and cross-technique comparison. We score outputs with an LLM as a judge, but calibrate the judge formally: we compare its scores on two ordinary runs of a model given the same prompts, verifying that it shows no systematic preference between statistically equivalent outputs and measuring its per-sample noise. Each design also includes a 'null' condition, provably identical in distribution to the unmodified model, whose measured difference must be zero.
  With this one instrument we measure several acceleration techniques on the same prompts, so their quality costs can be compared. Perceived quality proves highly dependent on the domain of discourse. A 4-bit model was indistinguishable from its 16-bit original down to our design's +/-0.3-point resolution, in English prose and Chinese alike. At 3-bit precision the same prompts lost 0.5 points in English prose, 0.9 in Chinese, and 1.1 on multi-step math; early exit that cost 0.7 points on prose cost 2.5 on math, cutting correctly solved problems from 19 of 27 to 6. The pattern held for models from Alibaba and from Meta, but not its magnitude: the same quantizer cost Meta's model 1.8 points where it cost Alibaba's 0.7.
  A model's certainty about a token predicts how likely it is to differ from the full model's choice, but not how much that difference affects judged quality, so acceptance rules relying on certainty cannot distinguish errors that matter from errors that don't.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a rigorous and calibrated LLM-judge-based methodology to quantitatively compare output quality impacts of various LLM acceleration techniques (quantization, early exit, speculative decoding) across domains and models.
AI.motivation: Existing work on LLM optimization (quantization, early exit, speculative decoding) typically uses heterogeneous, ad hoc benchmarks and lacks the statistical rigor and measurement precision common in mature scientific fields, making cross-technique and cross-system comparisons unreliable. The authors are motivated to develop a unified, statistically grounded way to measure how much different acceleration methods degrade model output quality, so that trade-offs between speed and quality can be meaningfully assessed.
AI.method: They use an LLM-as-a-judge framework but introduce formal calibration and controls. Specifically: (1) they run the same base model twice on the same prompts to obtain statistically equivalent outputs, then ask an LLM judge to score them, checking for systematic bias toward one run over the other and estimating per-sample scoring noise; (2) each experimental design includes a null condition, constructed so that its output distribution is provably identical to the unmodified model, and they verify that the measured quality difference is statistically zero; (3) using this calibrated judge, they evaluate several acceleration techniques (different quantization levels, early-exit policies, speculative methods) on shared prompt sets across multiple domains (English prose, Chinese text, multi-step math) and across models from different vendors, comparing quality loss in a common score metric; (4) they analyze token-level model certainty as a predictor of disagreements with the full-precision model and examine whether such disagreements correlate with judged quality differences.
AI.result: The unified measurement reveals strong domain dependence and model dependence of quality loss from acceleration: (1) 4-bit weight quantization yields no detectable quality loss relative to 16-bit (within ±0.3 score resolution) in both English prose and Chinese; (2) 3-bit quantization causes noticeable degradation with domain variation: about −0.5 points in English prose, −0.9 in Chinese, and −1.1 on multi-step math prompts; (3) an early-exit configuration that costs about −0.7 points on prose results in much larger quality loss on math (−2.5 points) and significantly reduces the count of correctly solved math problems from 19/27 to 6/27; (4) the qualitative pattern of domain sensitivity generalizes across models from Alibaba and Meta, but magnitudes differ: the same quantization method reduces Meta's model quality by 1.8 points versus only 0.7 points for Alibaba's model; (5) token-level certainty predicts whether a token will differ from the full model’s choice but does not predict how much such differences impact judged overall response quality, implying that certainty-based acceptance rules are blind to the importance of errors.
AI.conclusion: A carefully calibrated LLM-judge-based protocol can provide a precise, cross-technique, and cross-model metric for the quality impact of LLM acceleration methods. Quality degradation from optimization is highly domain- and model-dependent, so single-score or single-domain evaluations are misleading. Some aggressive quantization (e.g., 4-bit) may be effectively lossless under this metric for certain domains, whereas small speedups from techniques like early exit can incur disproportionate quality costs in more challenging domains such as multi-step math. Moreover, model token certainty is not a reliable proxy for the importance of errors, limiting the effectiveness of certainty-based acceptance rules. The work argues for rigorous, controlled measurement frameworks when assessing LLM optimization techniques.

title: RideWay: Benchmarking Efficient Task Completion for Tool-Using Language Agents
summary: AI agents are usually evaluated by whether they complete a task. In interactive service settings, a successful agent can still frustrate users by asking repeated questions, performing redundant searches, or making avoidable revisions. We introduce RideWay, an efficiency-centered benchmark for ridehailing agents in a stateful tool-calling environment, together with Efficiency Utility, a success-gated metric that discounts successful trajectories for excess tool calls and user-facing turns relative to task-specific reference effort. Human paired preferences calibrate the relative penalties, reflecting an aggregate service-workflow trade-off: extra dialogue often creates visible friction, whereas extra tool use can sometimes verify constraints or preserve user intent. Across 58 tasks and 24 models, the fitted penalty for excess turns is about twice that for excess tool calls. On task-disjoint held-out preferences, Efficiency Utility achieves 78.7% accuracy overall: 90.6% when trajectories differ in turns, but chance-level accuracy when they differ solely in tool calls - the axis on which human annotators agree least. RideWay therefore makes interaction efficiency measurable alongside task success, while exposing the boundary of count-based tool-use evaluation.

AI.tldr: They propose RideWay, a benchmark and a metric (Efficiency Utility) to measure not just whether AI ridehailing agents complete tasks, but how efficiently they do so in terms of tool calls and user turns, aligned with human preferences.
AI.motivation: Task-completion metrics ignore user frustration caused by inefficient interaction (too many questions, redundant tool calls, avoidable revisions). In service workflows like ridehailing, efficiency of interaction matters alongside success, and current benchmarks do not quantify this trade-off in a calibrated, human-aligned way.
AI.method: They build RideWay, a benchmark of ridehailing tasks in a stateful tool-calling environment, and define Efficiency Utility, a success-gated metric that penalizes excess tool calls and user-facing dialogue turns relative to a task-specific reference effort. They collect human paired preference judgments over trajectories to fit the relative penalty weights for extra turns vs extra tool calls, and evaluate how well Efficiency Utility predicts held-out human preferences across many models and tasks.
AI.result: From human preference fitting across 58 tasks and 24 models, they find that the penalty for excess user-facing turns is roughly double that for excess tool calls, capturing that users are more sensitive to extra dialogue than to extra backend actions. Efficiency Utility predicts held-out human preference with 78.7% accuracy overall, reaching 90.6% when trajectories differ in number of turns, but only chance-level when they differ only in tool calls, where human raters also show lowest agreement.
AI.conclusion: RideWay operationalizes interaction efficiency for AI agents in ridehailing scenarios, enabling evaluation that combines success with human-calibrated costs for dialogue and tool use. It also reveals a limit of simple count-based tool-use penalties, since human preferences are inconsistent when trajectories differ only in tool calls, suggesting the need for richer notions of tool-use quality beyond raw counts.

title: Gaze as Evidence for Common Grounding: A Cross-Corpus Analysis of MapTask and MUNDEX
comment: 16 pages, 17 tables, 2 figures; accepted to the MINT workshop at EMNLP 2026 (oral presentation)
summary: In collaborative tasks with asymmetric information, participants coordinate their understanding through interaction. We ask whether gaze provides evidence about grounding across two such tasks. Working from discrete behavioral annotations, we map HCRC MapTask (Anderson et al., 1991) and MUNDEX (Türk et al., 2023) into a shared partner/task/away vocabulary and compute gaze features around task-relevant dialogue units. In both corpora, aligned reference interpretations (MapTask) and UND (understood) judgments (MUNDEX) are associated with more task-directed gaze and with less partner-directed gaze, lower gaze entropy, and fewer gaze transitions. The associations are clearest for the participant leading the task: in giver-produced references, and in explainer judgments, which also co-vary with the explainee's gaze. In same-speaker MapTask reference chains, the speaker's gaze entropy is lower at the mention where a previously non-aligned referent becomes aligned. The best gaze feature groups improve modestly over controls under grouped cross-validation: temporal features in MapTask and raw proportions in MUNDEX. Because effects are small and several weaken when recurring participants rather than dialogues are the unit of inference, we treat gaze as one contributing cue to grounding, to be interpreted alongside task and dialogue context.

AI.tldr: Study examines how gaze behavior reflects mutual understanding (‘grounding’) in collaborative tasks with asymmetric information, across two dialogue corpora.
AI.motivation: In collaborative tasks where partners have different information, they need to establish shared understanding. It is unclear to what extent gaze patterns provide reliable evidence of this grounding, and whether such evidence generalizes across different tasks and roles.
AI.method: The authors re-annotate two corpora—HCRC MapTask and MUNDEX—into a common coding scheme (partner-directed, task-directed, away gaze) and extract gaze features around task-relevant dialogue units. They analyze associations between these gaze features (proportions, entropy, transitions, temporal patterns) and measures of successful understanding (aligned reference interpretations in MapTask and explicit UND judgments in MUNDEX), with attention to task roles (giver/follower; explainer/explainee) and reference chains. They evaluate predictive value of gaze features using grouped cross-validation against control baselines.
AI.result: Aligned interpretations or “understood” judgments are associated with more task-directed and less partner-directed gaze, lower gaze entropy, and fewer gaze transitions. These patterns are strongest for the task-leading participant (giver or explainer) and sometimes co-vary with the listener’s gaze. In MapTask reference chains, the speaker’s gaze entropy drops at the point where a previously misaligned referent becomes aligned. Predictive models using selected gaze features modestly outperform controls, with temporal features helping in MapTask and raw gaze proportions in MUNDEX. However, effects are small and attenuate when recurring participants, rather than dialogues, are the grouping unit.
AI.conclusion: Gaze behavior systematically but weakly reflects grounding status in asymmetric collaborative tasks. It should be treated as one informative but limited cue to mutual understanding, whose interpretation must be integrated with task structure and dialogue context rather than relied on in isolation.

title: Multimodal Conditioning of Fine-Tuned Stable Diffusion XL for Controllable and Culturally Faithful Ulos Motif Generation
comment: C. Anutariya, M.M. Bonsangue, M.N. Mahrin (eds.) "Proceedings of the 4th International Conference on Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (DSAI 2026)", Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, November 12-13, 2026, in volume 3251 of Communications in Computer and Information Science, Springer, November 2026
summary: The traditional Batak Ulos weaving industry faces growing challenges in producing diverse, innovative motifs due to limitations in conventional, manually driven design methods. This study proposes a multimodal generative framework integrating a fine-tuned Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion XL v1.0 via LoRA) with a Multimodal Large Language Model (LLaMA 1.5-7B) to enable controllable, culturally faithful Ulos motif generation. Four complementary conditioning mechanisms: text, image, representation, and semantic map (via ControlNet) jointly guide the generation process, each governing a distinct aspect from semantic intent to spatial layout. A five level ablation study across three scenarios (shape transformation, colour variation, and high-complexity input) shows that conditioning effectiveness is not proportional to the number of mechanisms combined: Text + Image + Semantic Map achieved the best FID (270) and CLIP Score (0.65 - 0.70) but the weakest SSIM (0.65), while Text + Image + Representation offered the best overall balance, with stable SSIM (0.84) and competitive FID (280). Combining all four mechanisms yielded the weakest FID (330), indicating conflicting optimization signals. Qualitative evaluation by nine weavers and thirty public participants confirmed statistically significant positive acceptance (Wilcoxon, p=0.007 and p<0.001, respectively). A web-based prototype supporting text-to-image and image-to-image generation was also developed, offering a practical digital design tool for cultural heritage preservation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a multimodal generative AI framework to create culturally faithful Batak Ulos weaving motifs, evaluating different conditioning combinations and validating acceptance among weavers and the public.
AI.motivation: Traditional Batak Ulos weavers struggle to produce diverse and innovative motifs using manual design processes. Existing digital or AI tools are not tailored to the cultural and structural constraints of Ulos patterns. The authors aim to provide a controllable generative system that respects cultural rules while expanding design possibilities and supporting cultural heritage preservation.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune Stable Diffusion XL v1.0 using LoRA for Ulos motifs and integrate it with a Multimodal LLaMA 1.5-7B model for text understanding and control. They introduce four conditioning mechanisms—text prompts, reference images, latent representation conditioning, and semantic maps via ControlNet—to separately steer semantic intent, style, and spatial layout. They conduct a five-level ablation study across three use scenarios (shape transformation, color variation, high-complexity inputs), comparing various combinations of conditioning mechanisms using metrics like FID, CLIP Score, and SSIM, plus qualitative evaluations from weavers and public participants. A web-based prototype is implemented for practical use.
AI.result: The experiments show that more conditioning mechanisms do not necessarily improve performance. The best FID (270) and CLIP (0.65–0.70) come from combining Text + Image + Semantic Map, but this combination has low structural similarity (SSIM 0.65). Text + Image + Representation yields a better overall trade-off with higher SSIM (0.84) and competitive FID (280). Using all four conditioning mechanisms leads to degraded FID (330), suggesting conflicting optimization signals. Qualitative user studies with nine weavers and thirty public participants show statistically significant positive acceptance of the generated motifs. The authors also successfully deploy a web-based tool supporting text-to-image and image-to-image workflows.
AI.conclusion: A multimodal generative framework with carefully chosen conditioning combinations can produce culturally faithful and practically useful Batak Ulos motifs. The study reveals that an intermediate level of conditioning (Text + Image + Representation) balances fidelity to input, visual quality, and controllability better than maximal conditioning. The positive responses from weavers and public users and the deployment of a web prototype indicate that such AI systems can aid traditional artisans and support cultural heritage preservation, while highlighting the need to manage conflicting signals in multimodal conditioning.

title: Exact semantic readout from compressed vector representations
