summary: We characterize when compressed vector representations admit exact linear or affine readouts of a finite lexicon's truth conditions: one fixed map per predicate, sending each entity vector to the corresponding truth vector. A necessary and sufficient row-space condition determines existence; the augmented truth matrix has rank r, giving minimum dimension r in the linear case, and r-1 in the affine. Exact readouts return values in a shared truth basis on which Boolean connectives act unchanged; separability alone requires an intervening threshold. For binary relations, exact bilinear readout of identity or strict total order requires linearly independent entity vectors. Experiments with GloVe and word2vec distinguish exact affine recovery, linear separability, and held-out prediction: most predicates are strictly separable, but none admits an exact affine readout from the pretrained embeddings. Supervised transductive training attains exact affine recovery to numerical precision at every tested dimension meeting the bound. At the embeddings' original dimension, geometries constrained to exact linear recovery retain 98-99 percent of the pretrained variance on the feature norms, and 80-83 percent on the WordNet lexicon.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when compressed word embeddings can exactly recover truth-conditional information for a finite set of predicates using linear or affine maps, and characterizes the algebraic conditions and dimensionality required.
AI.motivation: To understand under what conditions distributed semantic representations (like word embeddings) can faithfully and exactly encode symbolic truth-conditional information for predicates over a finite lexicon, beyond mere separability or approximate prediction.
AI.method: The authors give linear-algebraic characterizations (row-space and rank conditions) for exact linear and affine readout of predicate truth values from compressed entity vectors, extend this to some binary relations, and run experiments on GloVe and word2vec embeddings to test exact affine recovery, linear separability, and prediction performance, including supervised transductive training constrained by their theoretical bounds.
AI.result: They derive a necessary and sufficient row-space condition and show that minimum embedding dimension equals the rank r of the augmented truth matrix for linear readout and r-1 for affine. For binary relations like identity and strict total order, exact bilinear readout needs linearly independent entity vectors. Empirically, most predicates in GloVe/word2vec are linearly separable but none support exact affine readout as pretrained; with supervised transductive training at or above the theoretical dimension bound, exact affine recovery is achieved to numerical precision, while preserving most of the original embedding variance and WordNet structure when constrained to exact linear recovery.
AI.conclusion: Exact, symbolically faithful truth-conditional semantics can be embedded in low-dimensional distributed representations under clear linear-algebraic conditions, but common pretrained embeddings do not satisfy these conditions without supervised adjustment; nonetheless, such adjustments can preserve most of the useful geometric structure while enabling exact logical readout.

title: Missing Bridges: Composition-Aware Active Imitation Learning
summary: Active imitation learning reduces expert effort by allowing a learner to request the demonstrations it needs. Existing methods typically select these requests for their expected information gain about the expert policy. In structured multi-task domains, however, the number of start-goal tasks may grow combinatorially despite their solutions sharing reusable behavior. This makes composable behaviors especially valuable, since a single demonstration may help solve many tasks at once. Prior methods do not explicitly account for this value when selecting which demonstration to request. We introduce Adaptive Agents via Latent Topologies (AALT), which requests demonstrations that maximize expected gains in start-goal connectivity. We further show that this objective is formally tied to information gain about task reachability. AALT organizes existing demonstrations into a topology of latent hub states connected by learned behaviors, identifies high-value bridge demonstrations that are likely to enable many tasks at once, and grounds each to an expert query. At inference, it plans through the resulting topology and conditions a diffusion policy on each successive hub transition. In a simulated UR5e robot ordered-retrieval domain with 72 tasks, AALT improved from 42/72 to 72/72 (100%) successful tasks consistently using only 3 demonstrations totaling 5 transitions beyond the initial dataset. After 20 demonstrations, the strongest baseline averaged 88.6% success using 98 transitions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AALT, an active imitation learning method that selects demonstration queries to maximize connectivity in a latent task topology, enabling efficient reuse of behaviors across many start-goal tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing active imitation learning methods focus on information gain about the expert policy but ignore the combinatorial growth of structured multi-task domains, where tasks share reusable behaviors. This leads to inefficient use of expert demonstrations, as each query often helps with only a few tasks, even though single demonstrations could enable many tasks if selected well.
AI.method: The authors introduce Adaptive Agents via Latent Topologies (AALT). AALT builds a latent topology of hub states from existing demonstrations, with edges representing learned behaviors between hubs. It defines an objective that selects expert queries (demonstration requests) to maximize expected improvements in start-goal connectivity, which they show is equivalent to maximizing information gain about task reachability. AALT identifies and queries high-value 'bridge' demonstrations that likely connect many previously disconnected start-goal pairs. At inference, it plans over the learned latent topology and uses a diffusion policy conditioned on each successive hub-to-hub transition to execute behavior.
AI.result: In a simulated UR5e robot ordered-retrieval domain with 72 tasks, starting from an initial dataset, AALT improves performance from 42/72 to 72/72 successful tasks with only 3 additional demonstrations comprising 5 transitions. After collecting 20 demonstrations, AALT reaches 100% success, while the best baseline averages 88.6% success and needs 98 transitions, indicating significantly higher sample efficiency and task coverage.
AI.conclusion: AALT effectively exploits shared structure in multi-task domains by actively requesting demonstrations that build a reusable latent topology of behaviors. By targeting demonstrations that maximize start-goal connectivity (and thus reachability information), it enables solving many tasks with very few expert interactions, outperforming baselines in both success rate and demonstration efficiency.

title: From a River in Gilead to the Inference Distributions of Large Language Models: Covert Dialect Bias and Linguistic Profiling at Scale
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the 9th AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as housing screening. While alignment techniques mitigate explicit racial bias in generated text, they often leave covert attitudinal associations in internal probability distributions untouched. Adapting the matched-guise sociolinguistic paradigm, we examine covert dialect bias in housing-related social judgments across four varieties: Standard American English (SAE), African American Vernacular English (AAVE), Nigerian Standard English (NSE), and Nigerian Pidgin (NP). AAVE reflects the racialized dialect studied in prior covert-bias evaluations, whereas NSE and NP represent Black African, postcolonial varieties absent from this literature. Using 260 meaning-matched sentence quadruples and log-probability scoring over housing-relevant adjectives, we probe ten open-weight LLMs across three contexts varying in social proximity: tenant screening, neighbor acceptance, and roommate selection. Across all ten models, AAVE and NP are consistently associated with more negative adjectives than SAE, with NP penalized most severely. Crucially, each dialect is penalized via distinct stereotype clusters rather than a generic non-standard category. NSE, which carries institutional prestige, displays a context-dependent shift: favored over SAE in formal tenant screening but increasingly penalized as social proximity grows. Our findings reveal that LLMs inherit covert dialect bias along both racial identity and prestige dimensions, echoing documented human housing discrimination and demonstrating its reach across postcolonial English varieties.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that widely used large language models encode hidden, dialect-based biases in housing-related judgments, disadvantaging certain English varieties associated with Black speakers.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are deployed in sensitive areas like housing, it is important to understand whether they reproduce the covert, dialect-based discrimination documented in human decision-making, especially beyond well-studied US racialized varieties and into postcolonial Englishes.
AI.method: The authors adapt the matched-guise technique from sociolinguistics by creating 260 sets of four sentences that convey the same meaning but are written in four dialects (SAE, AAVE, NSE, NP). They then query ten open-weight LLMs, scoring the log-probabilities of a set of housing-related adjectives as continuations in three decision contexts (tenant screening, neighbor acceptance, roommate selection), to infer which adjectives each model implicitly associates with each dialect in each context.
AI.result: Across all ten LLMs, sentences in AAVE and Nigerian Pidgin are systematically assigned higher probabilities for negative housing-related adjectives than those in Standard American English, with Nigerian Pidgin receiving the strongest negative associations. Each dialect attracts a distinctive cluster of stereotyped adjectives rather than being treated generically as “non-standard.” Nigerian Standard English, despite its institutional prestige, is favored over SAE in formal tenant screening, but as the context becomes more socially intimate (neighbor, roommate), it increasingly attracts negative associations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode covert dialect biases aligned both with racialized identity and with sociolinguistic prestige hierarchies, mirroring known patterns of human housing discrimination. These findings indicate that current alignment efforts fail to address deeper representational biases in internal probability distributions and that such biases extend to postcolonial English varieties, raising fairness and safety concerns for real-world deployment in housing and related domains.

title: Anchoring What Matters: A Dual-Level Learning Framework for Visually-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has significantly improved the reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs). However, standard on-policy RLVR algorithms face a critical optimization bottleneck in preserving and reinforcing visually grounded reasoning behaviors: valuable visually-grounded reasoning trajectories are discarded after a single update, while uniform token advantage allocation prevents the model from reinforcing critical perception or reasoning steps. To bridge this gap, we propose PIVOT, a dual-level learning framework that anchors policy optimization around informative visual reasoning signals. Specifically, PIVOT introduces a self-calibrated experience replay mechanism, which selectively collects and replays visually-grounded historical experiences as stable reference anchors for policy optimization. Building upon this, we further design a vision-guided advantage allocation mechanism to allocate additional vision-aware advantages to tokens based on their local visual support and impact on downstream reasoning. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that PIVOT achieves highly competitive performance in enhancing the multimodal reasoning capabilities of LVLMs.

AI.tldr: They propose PIVOT, a dual-level RL framework that improves LVLM reasoning by reusing visually grounded trajectories and assigning vision-aware token-level advantages.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR for LVLMs wastes valuable visually grounded trajectories after a single update and uniformly distributes token-level advantages, which fails to emphasize critical perception and reasoning steps. This creates an optimization bottleneck for strengthening visually grounded reasoning behavior.
AI.method: PIVOT introduces two key components within an RL with verifiable rewards setup: (1) a self-calibrated experience replay mechanism that selectively stores and replays high-quality, visually grounded reasoning trajectories as stable reference anchors for policy optimization; and (2) a vision-guided advantage allocation mechanism that adjusts token-level advantages based on local visual support and each token’s impact on subsequent reasoning, instead of assigning uniform advantages across tokens.
AI.result: Across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks, PIVOT yields highly competitive—and likely state-of-the-art or near–state-of-the-art—performance, indicating stronger visually grounded reasoning for LVLMs compared with standard RLVR baselines.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring policy optimization around informative visual reasoning signals, via selective replay of visually grounded experiences and vision-aware advantage allocation, effectively alleviates the optimization bottlenecks of standard RLVR and substantially boosts LVLM multimodal reasoning capabilities.

title: Linguistic Triggers of Gender and Racial Bias in Open-Weight LLMs Applied to Recruitment
comment: Accepted at the 9th AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026). Extended version with Appendices A-B (prompt templates and full stimulus set)
summary: Open-weight large language models are rapidly entering hiring pipelines, yet their discriminatory failure modes -- and the regulatory exposure these create under the EU AI Act high-risk classification (Annex III) and U.S. EEOC adverse-impact analysis -- remain poorly understood. We present the first systematic, multi-model audit of open-weight LLMs that treats job-posting language as the primary experimental variable, evaluating six models (Llama 3.2, Mistral, Gemma 3, Qwen 3, Phi 3, DeepSeek-R1) across four controlled experiments that jointly probe recruiter-simulation and job-seeker-simulation tasks. We find that (1) agentic posting language depresses recruiter recommendation scores for female candidates (r_rb = 0.309, p_Bonf = 7x10^-5; model-fixed-effects r_rb = 0.448), while communal language partially reverses the penalty; and (2) coded-exclusion language suppresses non-White recruiter scores at large effect sizes (r_rb = 0.646-0.758) and, on the job-seeker side, selectively deters non-White personas from expressing interest -- operationalizing a chilling-effect mechanism at scale. A label-ablation experiment isolates the explicit demographic persona label as the primary causal driver, and Word Embedding Association Tests corroborate these findings at the representational level (d = 1.01-1.45 under Caliskan et al.'s multi-word gender attribute lists). We translate these results into a concrete pre-deployment audit protocol -- posting-vocabulary scoring, persona-conditioned LLM probing, and adverse-impact flagging against the four-fifths threshold -- that operationalizes the documentation and risk-management obligations Annex III imposes on high-risk AI in recruitment.

AI.tldr: The paper audits multiple open-weight LLMs used in hiring-like tasks and finds systematic demographic biases driven by job-posting language, then proposes a concrete audit protocol to meet emerging regulatory requirements.
AI.motivation: Open-weight LLMs are being integrated into recruitment workflows, but their potential to create discriminatory outcomes—and thus legal and regulatory risk under frameworks like the EU AI Act and U.S. employment law—has not been rigorously characterized. The authors aim to understand how job-posting language interacts with LLM behavior to disadvantage protected groups and to provide practical guidance for compliance and risk management.
AI.method: The authors run a systematic, multi-model audit on six open-weight LLMs (Llama 3.2, Mistral, Gemma 3, Qwen 3, Phi 3, DeepSeek-R1). They design four controlled experiments using two main task families: (1) recruiter-simulation tasks where the model scores candidates, and (2) job-seeker-simulation tasks where personas express interest in jobs. The primary experimental manipulation is job-posting language style (agentic, communal, and coded-exclusion language). They measure effects on candidate scores across demographic personas, perform label-ablation to test causality of explicit demographic labels, and use Word Embedding Association Tests to examine representational bias. They then formalize an audit protocol that includes posting-vocabulary scoring, persona-conditioned probing, and adverse-impact calculations (four-fifths rule).
AI.result: Agentic job-posting language significantly lowers recruiter recommendation scores for female candidates, with moderate-to-large effect sizes; communal language partly mitigates this penalty. Coded-exclusion language strongly reduces scores for non-White personas and deters them from job interest, evidencing a large ‘chilling effect.’ Label-ablation shows that explicit demographic labels drive much of the bias. Word Embedding Association Tests confirm substantial representational biases consistent with gender and racial stereotypes. These patterns are robust across the six audited models.
AI.conclusion: The audited open-weight LLMs exhibit systematic, legally salient bias in hiring-like scenarios, driven by interactions between posting language and demographic persona labels. These biases could create regulatory exposure under high-risk AI classifications and adverse-impact standards. The authors conclude that organizations must not deploy such models in recruitment without structured audits. They propose a concrete pre-deployment protocol—scoring job-posting vocabulary, probing model responses by persona, and flagging adverse impact relative to the four-fifths rule—to help practitioners meet documentation and risk-management obligations under emerging AI regulations.

title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
summary:
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on consumer hardware is bounded by weight memory: a 35B-class model is 19.5GB at 4-bit, and sparsity shrinks the compute per token, not the bytes that must be held. Naive offloading to SSD does not help on its own, because layer N+1's experts must be chosen before layer N's output exists, so the reads cannot start early enough to hide behind compute. We present Edge0, a streaming MoE inference engine that closes the gap with a prerouter: a per-layer head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, and the prediction is consumed as the routing itself, so the staged expert set equals the routed set and nothing is dropped. An unmerged recovery LoRA, trained on the student path, pays back the quality lost to int4 quantization and routing replacement. On a single 24GB machine, Edge0
  serves a 35B MoE at 20tok/s inside 3GiB of peak active memory, within a few points of its fp16 teacher on average across five public benchmarks. An 8B tier runs on the same framework, and the framework, checkpoints, and adapters are open source.

AI.tldr: Edge0 enables streaming MoE inference for a 35B model on 24GB consumer hardware by predicting next-layer routing one token ahead and offloading expert weights to SSD, keeping only ~3GiB active while retaining near-fp16 quality.
AI.motivation: Running large Mixture-of-Experts models on consumer-grade GPUs is constrained by memory, since sparsity reduces compute but not the total expert weights that must be resident. Simple SSD offloading fails because expert routing decisions are only known after computing the previous layer, leaving no time to prefetch weights. The paper aims to make large MoE models practically deployable on a single 24GB machine without large quality loss.
AI.method: Introduce Edge0, a streaming MoE inference engine that uses a per-layer "prerouter" head to predict the next layer's expert routing one token in advance, enabling asynchronous SSD prefetch such that the staged experts match the ultimately selected experts. Combine this with int4 quantization for compact weights and an unmerged recovery LoRA trained along the student path to restore accuracy lost from low-precision weights and routing replacement. Implement 35B and 8B MoE tiers in an open-source framework.
AI.result: On a single 24GB machine, Edge0 serves a 35B MoE model at 20 tokens per second while keeping peak active memory to about 3GiB, and achieves performance within a few points of its fp16 teacher model across five public benchmarks. The same system also supports an 8B model tier under the same framework.
AI.conclusion: Predictive routing via a prerouter enables effective streaming and SSD offload for large MoE models on commodity hardware, making it feasible to run a 35B expert model within tight GPU memory budgets while preserving most of the original model’s quality. The approach generalizes to other model sizes and is released as an open-source framework with checkpoints and adapters.

title: DualSQL: Text-to-SQL with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: State-of-the-art Text-to-SQL systems are typically multi-agent pipelines centered around two fundamental tasks: schema linking and SQL generation. However, existing work trains separate models for each task, failing to leverage the synergy between these interrelated tasks. In this work, we propose DualSQL, a new Text-to-SQL system consisting of two agents powered by a single model backbone. The agents share the same model weights and agentic scaffold, enabling joint optimization through a robust multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) framework. We design three database access tools to facilitate effective multi-step reasoning grounded to interactions with the databases. To improve training and avoid model collapse, we introduce a set of rollout guardrail mechanisms that stabilizes multi-agent RL training, supporting DualSQL to keep improving during training. We also introduce a new SQL correctness metric, robust execution match (REX), to more accurately judge SQL correctness and assign reward signals. Being trained on only 3755 examples, DualSQL-4B achieves an impressive 68.0% execution accuracy on the BIRD development set, matching previous 7B models. DualSQL-8B further improves to 71.1%, outperforming previous state-of-the-art single-model solutions with 32B parameters. These results demonstrate the strength of joint multi-agent reinforcement learning for building high performance Text-to-SQL pipelines.

AI.tldr: DualSQL is a Text-to-SQL system that uses a single shared model to power two cooperating agents, jointly trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning, achieving strong performance with relatively small models.
AI.motivation: Current Text-to-SQL systems split schema linking and SQL generation into separate models, which prevents them from exploiting the synergy and shared knowledge between these tasks. There is also a need for better training stability in multi-agent RL and more accurate SQL correctness metrics than simple execution match.
AI.method: The authors propose DualSQL, which uses one model backbone to power two agents that handle schema linking and SQL generation within a unified agentic scaffold. They design three database-access tools to support multi-step, database-grounded reasoning. They train the shared model via multi-agent reinforcement learning and introduce rollout guardrails to stabilize RL and prevent model collapse. They also define a new SQL correctness metric, robust execution match (REX), to give more reliable rewards during training.
AI.result: With only 3755 training examples, DualSQL-4B achieves 68.0% execution accuracy on the BIRD dev set, comparable to prior 7B models. A larger DualSQL-8B model reaches 71.1% execution accuracy, surpassing prior state-of-the-art single-model methods using 32B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Jointly training multi-agent Text-to-SQL pipelines via a shared backbone and stabilized multi-agent reinforcement learning is highly parameter- and data-efficient, and can outperform much larger single-model baselines. The new REX metric and rollout guardrails play key roles in enabling effective training and reliable performance gains.

title: Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K-12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools
summary: K-12 robotics and AI education remains difficult to scale, especially in rural regions lacking sustained technical mentorship. Programs like FIRST provide competition pathways and instructional opportunities, but they do not eliminate the need for local programming and robotics expertise. We introduce AI, Robotics, & Community (ARC), a hubs-based framework where colleges train undergraduate mentors and host workshops for nearby K-12 teams. Mature school programs can become secondary hubs that support additional schools, creating a self-reinforcing education loop where mentorship reach propagates geographically and can even grow super-linearly. We first evaluate ARC through a trial deployment at one university. The trial created three rural robotics teams. On five-point Likert surveys, mean increases in K-12 programming knowledge, resource access, and practice opportunities were 2.00, 2.25, and 1.25 points. Likewise, undergraduate confidence teaching technical concepts, adapting explanations, managing groups, and finding mentoring enjoyable and meaningful increased by 1.29, 1.14, 1.00, and 1.14 points. Additionally, we create a spatial Markov model of ARC's growth and simulate it using the state of Indiana as a testbed. Under moderate conditions, we find that ARC reaches 74% of Indiana's 1,925 public K-12 schools and produces 992 robotics programs after 40 years, compared with 161 projected under natural growth alone. Together, these results show ARC can create and support rural robotics programs, train undergraduate AI and robotics mentors, and potentially scale mentorship across a region.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates a scalable, hub-based mentoring framework (ARC) to expand K-12 robotics and AI education, especially in rural areas, using universities and mature school teams as mentorship hubs.
AI.motivation: K-12 robotics and AI programs are hard to scale, particularly in rural regions that lack sustained local technical mentors. Existing competition structures like FIRST help but still require on-site programming and robotics expertise that many schools do not have. The authors want a model that systematically creates, supports, and sustains robotics teams at scale, while also training undergraduate mentors.
AI.method: They design ARC, a hubs-based framework where colleges act as primary hubs: training undergraduate mentors and running workshops for nearby K-12 teams. As some K-12 programs mature, they become secondary hubs that support additional schools, forming a mentorship network that can expand geographically. The authors conduct a trial deployment at one university to form rural teams and collect pre/post Likert survey data from K-12 students and undergraduates. They also build a spatial Markov model to represent ARC’s long-term, region-wide growth and simulate it using Indiana’s school system as a testbed, comparing ARC-enabled growth to natural growth without ARC.
AI.result: In the trial, three rural robotics teams were successfully created. K-12 students reported substantial average gains (on 5-point Likert scales) in programming knowledge (+2.00), resource access (+2.25), and practice opportunities (+1.25). Undergraduate mentors reported increased confidence in teaching technical concepts (+1.29), adapting explanations (+1.14), managing groups (+1.00), and finding mentoring enjoyable and meaningful (+1.14). In the Markov simulation for Indiana, ARC is projected under moderate assumptions to reach 74% of the state’s 1,925 public K-12 schools and to produce 992 robotics programs after 40 years, versus only 161 programs from natural growth alone.
AI.conclusion: ARC can effectively seed and support rural K-12 robotics programs, while simultaneously building undergraduate mentoring skills. The hub-and-spoke structure, coupled with the possibility for mature teams to become secondary hubs, offers a plausible pathway to region-scale, potentially super-linear growth of robotics and AI education. The empirical pilot and long-term simulations together suggest that ARC is a promising framework for scaling technical mentorship and educational access across large geographic areas.

title: TeochewBench: A Human-Reviewed Benchmark for Teochew Hanzi Translation
summary:
Teochew has a substantial speaker community and exhibits distinctive lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic features, yet textual resources for evaluating large language models remain limited. We present TeochewBench, a human-reviewed benchmark comprising 300 Teochew Hanzi expressions for evaluating translation from Teochew Hanzi into Mandarin Chinese and English. The dataset covers five categories: basic vocabulary; everyday sentences; Teochew-specific expressions; tone, politeness, and context; and idiomatic, ambiguous, and culturally specific expressions. A primary Teochew-speaking reviewer examined all entries individually and revised them as needed, while two additional Teochew speakers verified selected items.
  Our main evaluation covers 11 official general-purpose post-trained models on the reviewed dataset in both translation directions, yielding 6,600 predictions. Two official base checkpoints provide 1,200 predictions for supplementary diagnostics, bringing the total to 13 models and 7,800 predictions. We additionally include a Hanzi-copy control, which returns the source input unchanged, to assess how shared Hanzi affect automatic scores for translation into Mandarin Chinese. Qwen3.5-27B achieved the highest overall chrF-style score among the evaluated checkpoints, at 60.63, followed by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct at 56.61, Gemma-3-27B-IT at 56.36, and GLM-4-32B-0414 at 55.82. Across the 11 main-evaluation models, the mean chrF-style score decreased from 69.25 for low-specificity items to 27.52 for high-specificity items. High-specificity expressions received lower scores and exhibited smaller cross-model differences, suggesting that they constitute a shared low-scoring region across the model families evaluated here. The Hanzi-copy control further indicates that surface overlap in low-specificity items can substantially affect automatic scores for translation into Mandarin Chinese.

AI.tldr: TeochewBench is a new human-reviewed benchmark of 300 Teochew Hanzi expressions for systematically evaluating LLM translation quality between Teochew, Mandarin, and English, revealing strong performance drops and shared weaknesses on culturally specific and high-specificity items.
AI.motivation: There is a large community of Teochew speakers and the variety has distinctive lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic properties, but there are few standardized textual resources to evaluate large language models on Teochew. Existing benchmarks underrepresent low-resource Sinitic varieties and do not expose how current models handle Teochew-specific and culturally nuanced expressions, nor how shared Hanzi may bias automatic evaluation when translating into Mandarin. A dedicated benchmark is needed to fill this gap and to provide a controlled way to compare models and analyze their failure modes.
AI.method: The authors construct TeochewBench, a dataset of 300 Teochew Hanzi expressions categorized into five types: basic vocabulary; everyday sentences; Teochew-specific expressions; tone/politeness/context; and idiomatic/ambiguous/culturally specific expressions. A primary native Teochew reviewer curates and revises all items, with two additional Teochew speakers verifying a subset. They evaluate 11 instruction-tuned LLMs and 2 base checkpoints on translation between Teochew Hanzi and both Mandarin Chinese and English, generating 7,800 total predictions. They also create a Hanzi-copy control system that simply copies the input when translating into Mandarin, to isolate how surface-form character overlap inflates chrF-style automatic metrics.
AI.result: Among 13 evaluated models, Qwen3.5-27B obtains the highest overall chrF-style score (60.63), followed by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (56.61), Gemma-3-27B-IT (56.36), and GLM-4-32B-0414 (55.82). Performance is much higher on low-specificity items (mean score 69.25) than on high-specificity items (mean 27.52) across models, indicating that all models struggle significantly with culturally embedded, idiomatic, and pragmatically nuanced Teochew expressions. Cross-model variance is smaller on these high-specificity items, implying they define a shared difficult region across model families. The Hanzi-copy baseline reveals that high character-level overlap between Teochew Hanzi and Mandarin can substantially boost automatic scores on low-specificity items without reflecting genuine translation quality.
AI.conclusion: TeochewBench provides a focused, human-reviewed resource for evaluating LLM translation performance on Teochew, highlighting strong model performance on generic content but widespread weakness and convergence in errors for high-specificity, culturally grounded expressions. The findings caution against over-reliance on character-based automatic metrics when source and target share script, and suggest that future work should improve model handling of pragmatics, idioms, and Teochew-specific usages while also developing better evaluation methods for shared-script language pairs.

title: Decodability is Not Causality: Dissociating Probe Readouts from Behavioral Drivers via SAE Decomposition
summary: Linear probes can decode safety-relevant concepts such as truthfulness from language-model activations, but probe accuracy may show only decodability, not that the features the probe weights causally drive model behavior. We demonstrate that this gap cannot be closed from the geometry of probe weights alone: the features geometrically aligned with probe direction need not be the ones the model uses, so causal relevance requires intervention. We introduce a feature-level diagnostic that decomposes a deployed True/False probe into sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features, ranks those features by both probe alignment and by gradient sensitivity of the model's behavior, and ablates the resulting shared, probe-only, and random feature sets under a coherence gate. On the truth probe of Buerger et al. (2024) (TTPD), applied in the instructed truth/deception setting of Long et al. (2025) for Gemma2-9B-Instruct, the two rankings overlap only weakly (about 12%, Spearman rho = 0.10), and ablation dissociates them sharply: features the probe shares with the model flip the output far more (up to 27%) than equally sized probe-only (6%) or random (1%) features at full coherence, while probe-only features instead perturb the probe's own readout. The dissociation holds across five seeds and a held-out split, and an activation-aware selection of features flips behavior nearly three times as often as the probe's geometric top features (17.6% vs. 6.1%). In this setting, therefore, the geometric projection of a probe's weight vector alone does not identify the features the model causally uses; however, combining probe information with feature activation statistics recovers substantially more behaviorally causal features, and coherence-gated SAE intervention is needed to separate them from probe readouts.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that high linear probe accuracy on concepts like truthfulness doesn't guarantee those features actually drive model behavior, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoder features and coherence-gated interventions to find which probe-decoded features are truly causal.
AI.motivation: Linear probes can decode safety-relevant concepts (e.g., truthfulness) from model activations, but it's unclear whether the features they identify causally influence the model's outputs. This gap creates risk for safety and interpretability work that assumes decodability implies causal control. The authors aim to test and quantify this gap and to develop tools to distinguish causally relevant features from merely geometrically aligned probe directions.
AI.method: They decompose an existing True/False probe into the feature basis given by a sparse autoencoder (SAE). For each SAE feature, they compute (1) alignment with the probe weight vector and (2) gradient-based sensitivity of the model’s output to that feature. They then rank features by these two metrics, construct sets of shared, probe-only, and random features, and perform coherence-gated ablations/interventions on these sets during model inference. They evaluate how often these interventions flip the model’s truth vs. false output in an instructed truth/deception setting, across multiple seeds and data splits.
AI.result: The alignment-based and gradient-sensitivity-based rankings overlap weakly (≈12% overlap, Spearman ρ ≈ 0.10). When ablating features, the shared features (high in both rankings) cause far more output flips (up to 27%) than probe-only (≈6%) or random features (≈1%) at full coherence. Probe-only features mainly affect the probe’s readout, not the model’s behavior. This pattern is robust across five random seeds and a held-out data split. An activation-aware feature selection (using model sensitivity) flips the model’s behavior almost three times as often as using the probe’s top geometrically aligned features (17.6% vs. 6.1%).
AI.conclusion: Linear probe geometry alone is insufficient to identify the features that causally drive model behavior, even when probe accuracy is high. The features a probe decodes can differ from those the model actually uses for its outputs. However, combining probe information with activation statistics and gradient-based sensitivity, along with coherence-gated SAE-based interventions, can recover substantially more behaviorally causal features and disentangle causal features from those that only influence probe readouts.

title: T-SANDHI: Tone Sandhi-aware Adaptive Network with Decoupled Hybrid Injection for Low-resource Taiwanese Hokkien Speech Recognition
summary: In Taiwanese Hokkien automatic speech recognition (ASR), prior studies often treat tone sandhi as a major challenge under the assumption that models fail to process implicit phonological variations. However, our experiments on Taiwanese Hokkien reveal that speech foundation models actually handle tone sandhi variations effectively, and the real performance bottleneck stems from a localized confusion between these variations and retained citation tones. To address this, we propose T-SANDHI to explicitly decouple surface acoustics from underlying lexical intent on top of a frozen Whisper backbone. Using a lexicon-guided multi-task learning structure driven by text-derived pseudo labels, our lightweight hybrid injection module integrates independent citation and sandhi phonetic streams via dynamic gating. Extensive evaluation on the TAT-MOE corpus and two blind test sets demonstrates that this explicit disentanglement effectively resolves tonal mapping confusion, outperforming baselines with strict parameter efficiency.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes T-SANDHI, a lightweight module on top of Whisper for Taiwanese Hokkien ASR that explicitly disentangles citation tones and sandhi tones, resolving tonal confusion and improving accuracy efficiently.
AI.motivation: Previous work assumes tone sandhi is hard for ASR because models cannot handle implicit phonological alternations; however, experiments show modern speech foundation models handle sandhi acoustics fairly well and the main bottleneck is confusion between sandhi realizations and citation tones. There is a need to explicitly model the mapping from surface tonal patterns to underlying lexical tones, especially for resource-limited dialects like Taiwanese Hokkien, without retraining large backbones.
AI.method: Freeze a Whisper backbone and add T-SANDHI, a lexicon-guided multi-task learning hybrid injection module. Text-derived pseudo labels provide supervisory signals for separate citation-tone and sandhi-tone phonetic streams. These streams are integrated via a dynamic gating mechanism that conditions on context to decide how much information to take from each stream, effectively decoupling surface acoustics from underlying lexical intent. The architecture is parameter-efficient because only the injection module is trained while the backbone stays frozen.
AI.result: On the TAT-MOE corpus and two additional blind test sets, the proposed model surpasses baseline ASR systems in recognizing Taiwanese Hokkien, particularly in tone-related errors. The performance gains are achieved with strict parameter efficiency, indicating that the approach improves tonal mapping without large increases in model size or computation.
AI.conclusion: Tone sandhi itself is not the main limitation for modern speech foundation models in Taiwanese Hokkien ASR; instead, the critical issue is disambiguating between surface sandhi realizations and citation tones. By explicitly disentangling citation and sandhi tonal streams through the T-SANDHI module on top of a frozen Whisper backbone, the paper effectively reduces tonal mapping confusion and improves recognition accuracy in a parameter-efficient way.

title: When Is Graph Structure Worth Its Cost? The Case for Structure Pricing in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can help answer questions that require information from many documents. However, building a graph often requires many language-model calls during ingestion. It is therefore important to ask whether its quality gains justify the additional cost.
  We present EffiRAG, a graph-based RAG system designed to reduce this cost. It uses the graph to locate relevant passages and generates answers from the original text. This design preserves source information while keeping graph construction and query processing lightweight.
  We evaluate EffiRAG on UltraDomain, which contains 120 open-ended questions from four domains. Compared with LightRAG-hybrid, EffiRAG produces the preferred answer on 93 questions. LightRAG is preferred on 7, and the remaining 20 are splits. EffiRAG also reduces total system cost by 57 percent, from USD 0.952 to USD 0.408. The cost includes language-model calls during ingestion and querying.
  The advantage remains as the corpus grows. At 10 and 20 documents per domain, EffiRAG uses a lightweight, non-LLM filter to skip low-salience chunks. It remains preferred over LightRAG-hybrid. It costs 4.2 times and 4.5 times less, respectively.
  The comparisons identify different quality-cost trade-offs. Graph-based RAG systems should therefore be evaluated by both answer quality and cost. The results favor graph structure that locates and preserves source evidence.

AI.tldr: EffiRAG is a graph-based RAG system that keeps graphs cheap and lightweight while still improving answer quality and preserving source evidence, substantially reducing total LLM cost compared to a strong baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based RAG methods can improve multi-document QA but are expensive to build because graph construction requires many language-model calls. This raises the question of whether the accuracy gains justify the ingestion and query costs, especially as the document corpus grows. The paper aims to design and evaluate a graph-based RAG that delivers strong answer quality while dramatically lowering cost and preserving explicit source grounding.
AI.method: The authors propose EffiRAG, a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation system that separates retrieval from generation: the graph is used only to efficiently locate relevant passages, while answer generation is done directly from the original text instead of from graph-node summaries. EffiRAG employs a lightweight, non-LLM filtering stage to discard low-salience chunks when the corpus is large, reducing graph size and LLM usage. They compare EffiRAG against LightRAG-hybrid on the UltraDomain benchmark (120 open-ended questions across four domains), measuring both answer preference (via human or model-based judgments) and total system cost, including all LLM calls for ingestion and querying, at varying corpus sizes (10 and 20 documents per domain).
AI.result: On UltraDomain, EffiRAG’s answers are preferred over LightRAG-hybrid on 93 of 120 questions, with LightRAG preferred on 7 and 20 ties. EffiRAG cuts total system cost by 57% (USD 0.408 vs. 0.952), counting both ingestion and query-stage LLM calls. As the corpus grows (10 and 20 documents per domain), EffiRAG’s lightweight non-LLM filtering enables it to remain preferred in answer quality while becoming 4.2x and 4.5x cheaper, respectively, than LightRAG-hybrid.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based RAG should be assessed on a joint quality–cost axis rather than quality alone. EffiRAG demonstrates that using graph structure primarily for locating and preserving source evidence, while keeping graph construction and querying lightweight and filtering out low-salience content with non-LLM methods, can achieve better answer quality at much lower cost than a strong baseline. This supports the design principle that efficient, evidence-preserving graph structures provide a favorable quality–cost trade-off for multi-document QA.

title: Behavior2Value: Benchmarking and Empowering LLMs for Consumer Value Measurement from E-commerce Behaviors
summary: Human values are deep motivational orientations that shape human behaviors. In e-commerce, they reveal the stable drivers behind users' purchase decisions. Compared with short-term interests, consumer values better explain how users evaluate products before purchase. However, consumer values are often implicit in complex and fragmented behavioral trajectories, leaving value measurement from e-commerce behaviors largely underexplored. To this end, we propose the Behavior-to-Value (B2V) task, which aims to identify consumer values from e-commerce behavioral trajectories. Centered on this task, we first construct the E-commerce Consumption Value Taxonomy (ECVT) and introduce B2V-Bench, the first B2V dataset and benchmark, based on anonymized Taobao behavioral logs. B2V-Bench consists of real-world purchase decision episodes, covering 25 types of purchase behaviors, along with corresponding consumer value orientations manifested in each episode. To improve consumer value measurement accuracy, we further present B2V-Verifier, a behavior-to-value measurement model based on Value Verification Tuning, which learns to assess whether behaviors provide sufficient evidence for each value inference. Experiments show that B2V-Verifier outperforms strong LLM baselines, improving multi-label classification by 34\%. The dataset and code will be publicly released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: They define a new task (Behavior-to-Value) for inferring users’ stable consumption values from e-commerce behavior trajectories, build a taxonomy, dataset, and benchmark (B2V-Bench), and propose a verification-based model (B2V-Verifier) that significantly outperforms LLM baselines for multi-label value classification.
AI.motivation: Short-term interests poorly capture the deeper, stable motivations behind online purchases. Human values are more stable and explanatory, but in e-commerce data they’re implicit, scattered across complex behavioral logs and thus underexplored. The authors want to systematically measure these latent consumer values from behavioral trajectories, enabling better understanding and prediction of purchase decisions.
AI.method: 1) Conceptual: Define the Behavior-to-Value (B2V) task, which maps e-commerce behavioral trajectories to underlying consumer values. 2) Taxonomy & Data: Build the E-commerce Consumption Value Taxonomy (ECVT), then construct B2V-Bench from anonymized Taobao logs, with decision episodes (25 behavior types) labeled with value orientations. 3) Modeling: Propose B2V-Verifier, a model trained with Value Verification Tuning to explicitly learn whether given behaviors provide sufficient evidence for inferring each candidate value, and use this for multi-label classification. 4) Evaluation: Compare B2V-Verifier with strong LLM baselines on the B2V-Bench benchmark.
AI.result: B2V-Bench provides the first benchmark for the B2V task, with labeled decision episodes linking behaviors to values. In experiments on this benchmark, their B2V-Verifier model substantially outperforms strong LLM baselines, achieving a reported 34% improvement on multi-label classification metrics for inferring consumer values from behavioral trajectories.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible and beneficial to infer stable consumer value orientations from fragmented e-commerce behavioral logs. The proposed B2V task, ECVT taxonomy, and B2V-Bench benchmark establish a foundation for research on behavior-to-value inference. Their verification-based B2V-Verifier model significantly improves value measurement accuracy over baseline LLMs, showing that explicitly modeling evidential sufficiency helps in mapping behaviors to underlying values. They plan to release dataset and code to support further work.

title: AutoTuneBench: Trustworthy Measurement for Agent Auto-Tuning of LLM Serving Engines
comment: 15 pages, 7 tables, 6 figures. Code and measurement corpus: https://github.com/li-ch/autotunebench (tag v1.0.0)
summary: Large language model agents tune GPU kernels and serving engines through a closed loop of propose, measure, and keep, but the measurements behind this loop are not trustworthy. We characterize four failure modes from a four-day pilot corpus of 619 model calls: strawman baselines manufacture speedups, absolute times do not transfer across machines, saturated tasks nullify comparisons, and infrastructure defects impersonate science. We present AutoTuneBench, a benchmark and measurement protocol that makes trust architectural. The protocol is frozen as code with test-enforced provenance; a database-level validator rejects out-of-protocol results; anti-cheat checks run outside the agent's modification surface; comparisons follow pre-registered readouts; and measurements anchor to externally published results, grounded in paired-seed statistics with a 5\% cross-run coefficient-of-variation cap. Honest measurement rewrites the headlines: our best kernel reads 10.6x against a naive baseline but 2.03x against the honest one; one configuration delivers 1.174x on one machine and 1.0049x on another; a pre-registered on/off comparison nulls at a shared wall (2.4840 vs 2.4957\,ms); and the KernelBench Level-1 suite admits 51\% of tasks with median speedup 1.0001x over PyTorch eager. The protocol, the two-engine corpus (vLLM and SGLang), and its audit trail are released as open artifacts.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies unreliable measurement practices in LLM-based GPU kernel/serving auto-tuning and introduces AutoTuneBench, a protocol and benchmark that enforce trustworthy, reproducible performance evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used to optimize GPU kernels and serving systems by iteratively proposing and benchmarking variants, but the resulting performance claims are often untrustworthy due to flawed baselines, non-transferable timing results, saturated workloads, and hidden infrastructure issues. The community lacks a standardized, robust measurement framework to prevent these failures and ensure that reported speedups reflect genuine algorithmic or systems improvements.
AI.method: The authors conduct a four-day pilot study with 619 model calls to systematically characterize four measurement failure modes (strawman baselines, non-transferable absolute times, saturated tasks, and infrastructure-induced artifacts). They then design AutoTuneBench: a benchmark plus a measurement protocol embedded in code. Key components include: test-enforced provenance of measurement code, a database validator that rejects out-of-protocol results, anti-cheat checks that run outside the agent’s control surface, pre-registered comparison readouts, and anchoring measurements to external published results with paired-seed statistics and a strict 5% cross-run coefficient-of-variation limit.
AI.result: Applying AutoTuneBench to LLM-tuned GPU kernels and serving engines reveals that many headline speedups largely vanish under honest measurement. For instance, a kernel that appears 10.6x faster than a naive baseline is only 2.03x faster than a carefully chosen honest baseline; a configuration that seems beneficial on one machine (1.174x speedup) yields almost no gain on another (1.0049x); a pre-registered on/off comparison shows statistically null difference (2.4840 vs 2.4957 ms); and on KernelBench Level-1 only 51% of tasks even admit an optimized kernel, with a median speedup of 1.0001x over PyTorch eager. They also release a two-engine corpus (vLLM and SGLang) and a full audit trail generated under this protocol.
AI.conclusion: Many auto-tuning results produced by LLM agents are artifacts of flawed measurement rather than true performance gains. By making measurement constraints and anti-cheat safeguards an architectural part of the benchmarking process, AutoTuneBench allows the community to distinguish genuine improvements from illusory ones. The protocol’s strict provenance, validation, and variance controls substantially narrow claimed speedups and show that, on current workloads, real gains are often modest. AutoTuneBench and its open artifacts aim to become a standard foundation for trustworthy evaluation of GPU kernel and serving optimizations driven by LLMs.

title: Beyond Accuracy: How Procedural Traces Shift the Decision Criterion of LLM Overseers
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS)
summary: Organizations increasingly use oversight loops where one large language model (LLM) audits another's outputs alongside procedural traces of claimed steps. A common concern about such LLM-as-a-judge pipelines is that detailed traces make overseers gullible. Using signal detection theory, we audit five LLM overseers on 19 compliance tasks (4,551 analyzed judgments), varying only trace detail and evidence labeling. With disconfirming evidence always visible, error detection remains near ceiling. Instead, elaborate traces shift the decision criterion toward rejection, increasing false alarms in susceptible overseers. Without option labels, human-validated reason coding shows about 60% of false alarms cite an inability to tie evidence to its option. Labels eliminate this stated reason, yet residual rejection of correct work persists in those overseers and rises with trace detail. Procedural traces thus act as governance artifacts that shape oversight decisions. AI auditors should be evaluated by their decision criterion and false-alarm behavior, alongside accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how detailed procedural traces in LLM oversight pipelines affect LLM-as-a-judge behavior, finding that more detail can make models more likely to incorrectly reject correct outputs (false alarms) even when disconfirming evidence is clear.
AI.motivation: As organizations adopt pipelines where one LLM audits another using intermediate reasoning traces, there is concern that these traces may bias the overseer—either making it too trusting (gullible) or distorting its judgments. Governance and safety frameworks need evidence on how oversight artifacts (like traces and labels) shape LLM decision behavior, not just accuracy.
AI.method: Using signal detection theory, the authors test five different LLM-based overseers across 19 compliance tasks, generating 4,551 audited judgments. They systematically vary two dimensions: (1) how detailed the procedural traces of the audited model are, and (2) whether evidence is explicitly labeled with which option it supports. They then measure detection of true errors, false alarms (incorrect rejections of correct work), and analyze overseer explanations via human-validated reason coding.
AI.result: Disconfirming evidence being always visible keeps true error detection rates very high (near ceiling). However, as procedural trace detail increases, some overseers shift their decision criterion toward rejecting more outputs, leading to more false alarms. When evidence-option labels are removed, about 60% of false alarms are justified by an inability to link evidence to options. Adding labels removes that stated justification, but the same overseers still over-reject, and this tendency grows with trace detail.
AI.conclusion: Procedural traces are not neutral; they function as governance artifacts that systematically influence LLM overseer decision criteria, particularly increasing false-alarm rates for some models. Therefore, evaluation of AI auditors should go beyond accuracy to include decision criterion and false-alarm behavior, and oversight pipeline design (trace detail, labeling) should be treated as a key lever in AI governance.

title: Designing Agentic AI Workflow Portfolios under Imperfect Selection and Compute Cost
summary: Agentic AI systems often approach the same task through multiple workflows that differ in reasoning strategy, verification structure, and compute cost. A natural deployment policy is to use the workflow with the highest average performance, but this can be suboptimal because different workflows may succeed on different instances. We study a portfolio-and-selector paradigm in which a firm runs multiple workflow executions and selects the final answer after observing their outputs. Additional executions may uncover correct answers that the best standalone workflow misses, but they consume compute and introduce plausible distractors that complicate final selection. We formulate this as a workflow portfolio problem in which the firm jointly chooses run size and allocation across workflow types. We summarize selector quality through an odds-lift index and derive sharp bounds on the value of workflow variety. For finite workflow pools, we develop exact formulations, linear programming relaxations, randomized rounding procedures, and computable performance certificates. For large implicit workflow classes, we derive a finite-dimensional dual and an ellipsoid method using a pricing oracle to identify workflows with high weighted accuracy net of recurring compute cost. Under a weak condition, the method obtains a near-optimal solution to the relaxation with polynomially many oracle calls. We evaluate the framework on three datasets: ABCD, Schema-Guided Dialogue, and HotpotQA. Relative to the best standalone workflow, portfolio optimization improves held-out selector accuracy by 3.1, 7.5, and 0.9 percentage points, respectively. Dual-guided workflow generation adds 3.5 points on ABCD and 24.1 on HotpotQA, with no additional gain on Schema-Guided Dialogue.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to optimally combine multiple AI agent workflows by running a selected portfolio of them and then choosing among their outputs, instead of relying on a single best workflow.
AI.motivation: Different AI workflows excel on different instances of a task, so always using the single best average-performing workflow wastes potential performance gains. Running several workflows and then selecting among their answers could improve accuracy, but it costs extra compute and makes selection harder due to conflicting or distracting outputs. The paper aims to formally model and optimize this trade-off.
AI.method: The authors formulate a workflow portfolio optimization problem where a firm chooses how many workflow executions to run and how to allocate them across workflow types. They introduce an odds-lift index to quantify the power of the final selector and derive theoretical bounds on the value of having diverse workflows. For a finite set of workflows, they provide exact optimization formulations, linear programming (LP) relaxations, randomized rounding algorithms, and performance certificates. For large or implicit workflow families, they derive a finite-dimensional dual problem and design an ellipsoid-based algorithm that uses a pricing oracle to find workflows with high accuracy relative to their recurring compute costs. Under a mild assumption, this method reaches a near-optimal relaxed solution with polynomially many oracle calls.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—ABCD, Schema-Guided Dialogue, and HotpotQA—the optimized workflow portfolios outperform the single best workflow by 3.1, 7.5, and 0.9 percentage points in selector accuracy, respectively. When workflows are also generated using the dual-guided method, the accuracy further increases by 3.5 points on ABCD and 24.1 points on HotpotQA, while providing no additional improvement on Schema-Guided Dialogue.
AI.conclusion: Optimally combining multiple AI workflows via a principled portfolio-and-selector framework can yield measurable accuracy gains over relying on the best standalone workflow, with provable guarantees on performance relative to compute cost. The dual-based workflow generation can substantially enhance performance in some tasks, though its benefit depends on the dataset characteristics, indicating that the value of workflow diversity is task-dependent.

title: I code or AI code: A comparative evaluation of AI-rated scores in classroom observations
summary: Classroom observations are widely recognized as a key tool for establishing benchmarks of education quality and guiding pedagogical improvement, yet they remain resource-intensive and dependent on trained observers. This study evaluated the feasibility of using a LLM (GPT-5 model) to score teacher-child interactions in early childhood classrooms, benchmarked against human raters. The study analyzed 87 video-recorded observations from 38 classrooms across 30 kindergartens in Hong Kong. Using observation transcripts, the AI model was configured to apply the full Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS) framework. AI-rated scores were then compared with human ratings by examining correlations and differences in mean scores of the CLASS domains and dimensions. The results showed greater convergence between AI and raters for the Emotional Support domain and, in particular, the Quality of Feedback dimension, which captures how teachers use feedback to extend children's learning. Greater divergence emerged for interactions that were more procedural or context-dependent, particularly within the Classroom Organization and Instructional Support domains. These findings suggest that transcript-based AI scoring may capture some of the relative variation in teacher-child interactions but cannot yet reproduce calibrated human judgements consistently across the full CLASS framework. AI-assisted observation may therefore be more appropriate as a preliminary screening tool rather than as a replacement for trained observers, providing teachers with evidence for reflection rather than high-stakes evaluation. Future research should examine whether domain-specific training and incorporation of contextual and visual information can improve alignment between AI and human rated scores.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether an advanced LLM can reliably score early-childhood classroom interactions using the CLASS framework from text transcripts, finding partial but not full alignment with human raters.
AI.motivation: Classroom observations using tools like CLASS are valuable for assessing teaching quality and supporting improvement, but they are costly, time-consuming, and require highly trained observers. With the rapid development of large language models, there is interest in whether AI could automate or augment scoring of classroom interactions to reduce costs and scale observations. However, it is unclear how well LLM-based scoring aligns with human judgements across different CLASS domains, especially using only transcripts rather than rich contextual or visual cues. This paper seeks to address that gap.
AI.method: The authors collected 87 video-recorded observations from 38 classrooms across 30 Hong Kong kindergartens. They transcribed the teacher–child interactions and configured a GPT-5 large language model to assign scores according to the full CLASS framework, covering its domains and dimensions. Human raters, presumably trained CLASS observers, independently scored the same observations. The study then compared AI and human ratings using correlations and differences in mean scores at the domain and dimension level, focusing on where convergence and divergence occurred.
AI.result: The AI’s CLASS scores aligned better with human ratings in the Emotional Support domain, with particularly strong convergence on the Quality of Feedback dimension, which reflects how teachers extend children’s learning through feedback. In contrast, the model’s scores diverged more from human raters for interactions that were more procedural or context-dependent, especially in the Classroom Organization and Instructional Support domains. Overall, the AI captured some relative variation in interaction quality but did not consistently match calibrated human judgements across the entire CLASS framework.
AI.conclusion: Transcript-based LLM scoring can partially approximate human CLASS ratings, especially for aspects of Emotional Support and certain feedback-related interactions, but it lacks the consistency and contextual sensitivity needed to fully replace trained observers. At present, AI is better suited as a low-stakes, preliminary screening or reflective feedback tool for teachers, not for high-stakes evaluation. The authors recommend future work on domain-specific fine-tuning and integrating contextual and visual information to improve AI–human alignment in classroom observation scoring.

title: Symbolic Temporal Supervision of LLM Agents Using Contracts
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents augmented by tools can automate complex, multi-step tasks, such as web navigation, code generation, and workflow orchestration, by acting on external systems through tool calls. However, hallucinations, distributional instability, and adversarial manipulations in LLMs, and the irreversible consequences of certain tool calls can lead to harmful outcomes. Existing safeguards either grade recorded trajectories post hoc with stochastic LLM judges or block unsafe actions one call at a time, and no single deterministic artifact supports both roles. We present ContrAgent, a contract-based framework for symbolic temporal supervision of LLM agents. ContrAgent captures an agent's behavior as a sequence of tool calls and formalizes it as a trace over a fixed set of checkable predicates. It then specifies required behaviors using assume-guarantee contracts in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTLf). Each contract is compiled to a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that serves two roles: gating agent actions online and evaluating recorded traces offline. A contract library, acting as a reusable knowledge base, is maintained independently of the agent's model and can be applied across different agents within the same task domain. We show the effectiveness of our approach on four benchmarks spanning both roles, where ContrAgent matches state-of-the-art LLM-judge and rule-based guardrail baselines while producing deterministic, reproducible verdicts and, in the online mode, orders-of-magnitude lower per-call latency.

AI.tldr: ContrAgent is a contract-based, symbolic supervision framework that uses temporal logic to deterministically monitor and constrain LLM-agent tool use, both online and offline.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents can perform complex tasks but are prone to harmful behaviors due to hallucinations, instability, and adversarial prompts. Existing safety methods are either post hoc, stochastic LLM judges or local, per-call guardrails, and there is no unified, deterministic mechanism that can both gate actions in real time and evaluate trajectories afterward. A more principled, reproducible, and scalable safety framework is needed.
AI.method: Model agent behavior as sequences of tool calls and abstract them into traces over a predefined set of checkable predicates. Specify desired/allowed behaviors as assume-guarantee contracts expressed in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTLf). Automatically compile each contract into a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that can (1) run online to gate or allow each new tool call based on the evolving trace state, and (2) run offline to evaluate recorded trajectories. Maintain a reusable library of such contracts, decoupled from any particular LLM, that can be reused across agents in the same domain.
AI.result: On four benchmarks, ContrAgent achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art LLM-judge-based and rule-based guardrail systems for both online action gating and offline trajectory evaluation tasks, while yielding deterministic, reproducible decisions and significantly lower latency per tool call in the online setting.
AI.conclusion: Contract-based symbolic temporal supervision via LTLf and DFAs is an effective, deterministic alternative to stochastic LLM-based judges and ad hoc guardrails for supervising tool-using LLM agents. ContrAgent simultaneously supports low-latency online gating and offline evaluation, and its contract library can be reused across agents within the same task domain, improving scalability and maintainability of safety constraints.

title: Too Good to Be Real? Diagnosing and Reducing the Gap Between AI Preference and Real User Engagement
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to generate and evaluate online content, yet it remains unclear whether the qualities they associate with higher engagement match what real users respond to. We study this question using 1.17 million answers to 25,978 questions from Zhihu, Quora, and Reddit, comparing real platform answers and AI-generated answers across four within-question engagement levels. We introduce Ontological Preference Measurement, which represents answers along three dimensions: logic, affect, and expression. We find a systematic gap between AI preference and real user engagement: as target engagement increases, LLMs add more explicit logical structure, while real user engagement is more strongly associated with affective and expressive salience. We call this tendency logic overbinding. Based on this diagnosis, we propose Ontology-Masked Reasoning Autoencoding (OMRA), a controlled intervention that masks and reconstructs over-explained spans while preserving stance, factual content, and coherence. Across four LLM families, OMRA reduces the measured gap by an average of 54.4%. In human evaluation, OMRA wins 62.4% of pairwise preference judgments against matched real platform answers, even though the real answers are more often judged to be human-written.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models tend to overemphasize logical structure when trying to optimize for engagement, while real users respond more to emotional and stylistic qualities; the authors propose a method (OMRA) to reduce this mismatch and improve user appeal.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used to both generate and rank online content, it's important to know whether their internal preferences about what drives engagement actually align with what real users like; misalignment could harm user experience and the effectiveness of LLM-driven platforms.
AI.method: The authors analyze 1.17M answers from Zhihu, Quora, and Reddit, comparing human-written platform answers and LLM-generated answers at four engagement levels per question. They define Ontological Preference Measurement, mapping answers into three ontological dimensions—logic, affect, and expression—and use this to quantify how LLMs and real engagement differ. Observing that LLMs increase logical explicitness more than humans for higher engagement, they characterize this as 'logic overbinding.' They then develop Ontology-Masked Reasoning Autoencoding (OMRA), an intervention that detects and masks over-explained logical spans and forces the model to reconstruct them while preserving stance, facts, and coherence, thereby nudging the model away from overbinding.
AI.result: They find a reliable, systematic mismatch between how LLMs modify text to target higher engagement and what actually predicts higher real-user engagement: LLMs lean heavily on explicit logical structure, whereas real engagement tracks more with affective and expressive features. The OMRA method, applied across four different LLM families, cuts this measured logic-overbinding gap by an average of 54.4%. In human preference tests, OMRA-edited answers are preferred 62.4% of the time over real platform answers of matched engagement level, although judges more often identify the real answers as human-written.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current LLMs systematically misjudge what drives online engagement, over-prioritizing logical structure at the expense of affective and expressive salience—a phenomenon they term logic overbinding. Their OMRA intervention can substantially reduce this misalignment, producing answers that both better approximate real engagement signals and are preferred by human evaluators, suggesting a viable path toward more user-aligned content generation and evaluation.

title: Time-Aligned Evolving Concept Graphs for Scientific Relation Forecasting
summary: Forecasting scientific relations can guide discovery by identifying promising connections before they emerge. Existing approaches often model concept semantics and graph structure separately or summarize semantics over coarse historical snapshots, leaving semantic representations potentially misaligned with rapidly evolving graph evidence. We propose a time-aligned evolving concept graph framework that jointly models semantic and structural evolution. Its core idea is to treat dated papers as shared update events, reconstructing semantic and structural states from the same publication history through each prediction time. Pair-level fusion combines these states to forecast first co-occurrence, relation formation, and conditional relation type. Holding architecture and training fixed, refreshing context alongside graph updates improves mean relation AUPRC by 16.6% over frozen context. On a graph built from 187,848 papers with 270,687 concepts and 7.45 million co-occurrence links, the complete framework improves mean relation AUROC from 0.9290 for the strongest evaluated baseline to 0.9722, with mean population-weighted AUPRC 0.005778.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework that jointly models how concepts’ meanings and their graph relationships evolve over time, enabling better prediction of future scientific relations.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery can be accelerated by predicting promising new relations—such as future co-occurrences or collaborations—before they actually appear in the literature. Existing methods either treat the semantic content of papers and the structure of concept graphs separately or rely on coarse time snapshots, causing a mismatch between what concepts mean and how they are connected as the field rapidly evolves. There is a need for a model that keeps semantic and structural representations temporally aligned using the same publication history, so forecasts reflect up-to-date, mutually consistent evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose a time-aligned evolving concept graph framework. Dated papers are treated as shared update events that simultaneously adjust semantic representations (from text) and structural representations (from graph links) at each prediction time. For each time point, the model reconstructs the state of concept semantics and graph structure from the cumulative publication record up to that time. A pair-level fusion mechanism then combines the semantic and structural states of concept pairs to predict three tasks: first co-occurrence (whether two concepts will first appear together), relation formation (whether a relation between them will appear), and conditional relation type (which type of relation given that one will form). The framework is compared against baselines using the same architecture and training regime but differing in whether context is refreshed or frozen over time.
AI.result: Refreshing contextual representations in step with graph updates yields a 16.6% improvement in mean relation AUPRC compared with keeping contextual representations frozen. On a large concept graph derived from 187,848 papers with 270,687 concepts and 7.45 million co-occurrence links, the full proposed framework achieves a mean relation AUROC of 0.9722, outperforming the strongest baseline’s 0.9290. It also reaches a mean population-weighted AUPRC of 0.005778, indicating improved performance in predicting future scientific relations in a highly imbalanced setting.
AI.conclusion: Jointly time-aligning semantic and structural evolution significantly improves forecasting of scientific relations over methods that decouple or coarsely synchronize semantics and graph structure. Treating papers as shared update events and refreshing contextual representations alongside graph updates leads to notably better predictive accuracy across multiple relation-forecasting tasks on a large real-world scientific corpus. This suggests that future methods for discovery recommendation and scientific forecasting should carefully model the co-evolution of meaning and network structure over time.

title: Made in Hungary: Comments on the performance of generative language models
summary: In recent years, three initiatives have emerged to develop generative language models in Hungary. The motivation behind them is the same. For Hungarian, no model with the given capability existed, or existing English-centric models offered limited proficiency. A detailed examination of the corresponding studies, however, reveals several methodological limitations. First, the reliability of the evaluation protocols is questionable. Contrary to the findings of Csibi et al. [2026], evaluation under the recommended inference settings shows that Qwen3-4B achieves higher scores than Racka-4B, its Hungarian-adapted version. Data contamination is evident in the work of Yang et al. [2025d] and Szentmihályi et al. [2025], potentially biasing the reported results. Second, the training pipelines fall short of current best practices in corpus curation and data mixture, which risks wasting substantial compute on low-quality data. The lack of controlled ablations prevents reliable assessment of these choices. Third, none of the three papers assessed forgetting or capability loss.
