Testing the adapted models on a subset of the original benchmarks indicates performance decline in all three cases, especially Racka-4B. These observations emphasize the importance of rigorous experimental design in language model development, given the significant computational and financial costs involved.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques three recent Hungarian generative language model projects, showing that their evaluation, data, and training methodologies have serious flaws that undermine their claimed advantages over base English-centric models.
AI.motivation: Hungarian lacked strong native or well-adapted generative language models, and existing English-focused models underperformed on Hungarian tasks. The paper aims to verify whether recent Hungarian LLM initiatives truly solve this gap and to highlight methodological standards needed for reliable model development.
AI.method: The authors re-evaluate one adapted model (Racka-4B) against its base model (Qwen3-4B) under the recommended inference settings; inspect the training corpora and pipelines in three cited works for issues such as data contamination and poor data mixtures; and test the adapted models on subsets of the original benchmark suites to detect forgetting or capability loss. They then compare these empirical findings to current best practices for LLM training and evaluation.
AI.result: Under careful re-evaluation, Qwen3-4B outperforms its Hungarian-adapted variant Racka-4B despite earlier claims. Evidence of data contamination is found in two of the three projects, casting doubt on their reported gains. The training pipelines rely heavily on low-quality data and lack ablation studies, and all three adapted models show measurable performance degradation on original benchmarks, with Racka-4B degrading the most.
AI.conclusion: The three Hungarian LLM efforts do not convincingly improve over strong base models and suffer from serious methodological shortcomings. The paper argues that future Hungarian (and more generally, low-resource language) LLM projects must adopt rigorous evaluation protocols, clean and well-mixed training data, and systematic ablations, and should explicitly measure forgetting to ensure that language specialization does not erode general capabilities.

title: WFM: Wiki Foundation Model for Complex Agentic Reasoning
summary: Real-world agents fundamentally require persistent non-parametric knowledge for dynamic reasoning, i.e., long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation. While graphs have shown reliable advantages in providing structured evidence, the sparse graph representations naturally restrict machine readability and semantic density required for complex agentic workflows. Driven by this limitation, the entire industry is witnessing a paradigm shift from traditional sparse graphs to LLM Wiki, an agent-native knowledge representation that couples dense document contexts with markdown files containing multi-layered topological linkages. However, parameterizing such rich semantics is challenging to encode dense textual contexts using traditional sparse graph embeddings. Moreover, learning LLM Wiki with existing graph encoders could overwhelm distributed system overheads that hinder deployment in large-scale commercial scenarios. To this end, we propose a novel paradigm Wiki Foundation Model, i.e., WFM, tailored for scalable, agent-native representation and retrieval. Specifically, (i) we formalize a Wiki Graph schema that seamlessly bridges fine-grained structures with dense contexts, maintaining explicit topologies alongside continuous semantics; (ii) A query-conditioned attentive aggregation is tailored for rich wiki message passing and explicit attention variance regularization; (iii) We engineer an infrastructural NCCL boundary exchange protocol that hoists static partition indices and leverages fixed-shape GPU-to-GPU collectives, bypassing CPU serialization and memory copy overheads. Extensive evaluations across five long-term agent memory and multi-hop reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the remarkable performance of WFM, while achieving a 10.5 times training acceleration on distributed clusters.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Wiki Foundation Model (WFM), a scalable knowledge representation and retrieval framework tailored for LLM-based agents, combining dense textual contexts with graph-like wiki structures for efficient long-term memory and reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing real-world agent systems need persistent, non-parametric knowledge stores for long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation. While graph structures offer explicit topology and structured evidence, traditional sparse graphs lack semantic density and machine readability required for complex, multi-step agent workflows. At the same time, there is an industry trend toward "LLM Wiki" representations—markdown-based, link-rich knowledge graphs combining documents and topology—but current graph encoders and embedding methods struggle to parameterize such dense semantics efficiently and impose large distributed-systems overheads. The authors are motivated to design a representation and system that can model these rich wiki structures while remaining scalable in commercial, distributed environments.
AI.method: The authors propose WFM (Wiki Foundation Model), built around three main components: (i) a Wiki Graph schema that unifies fine-grained structural elements (nodes, links) with dense textual contexts so that both explicit graph topology and continuous semantics are preserved; (ii) a query-conditioned attentive aggregation mechanism for message passing over the wiki graph, where attention weights are conditioned on the query and an explicit attention variance regularization term encourages robust, informative attention patterns; (iii) a systems-level optimization via an NCCL boundary exchange protocol, which pre-hoists static partition indices and uses fixed-shape GPU-to-GPU collective communication primitives, avoiding costly CPU serialization and memory copies and thereby accelerating distributed training and inference.
AI.result: Through experiments on five benchmarks focused on long-term agent memory and multi-hop reasoning, WFM achieves state-of-the-art or significantly improved performance compared to existing graph-based or retrieval-augmented baselines. Additionally, the proposed NCCL-based system design yields a reported 10.5× acceleration in training speed on distributed GPU clusters, evidencing both algorithmic and systems-level gains.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that WFM offers an effective agent-native knowledge representation for long-term memory and reasoning, successfully integrating dense semantic context with explicit wiki-like graph topology. The query-conditioned aggregation and attention regularization improve retrieval and reasoning quality, while the specialized NCCL protocol ensures the approach scales efficiently in distributed commercial settings. This positions LLM Wiki-style knowledge bases, powered by WFM, as a promising foundation for real-world agent systems.

title: Rollback the World, Keep the Reflection: Rollback-Induced Reflection for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks through multi-step environment interaction, yet a single erroneous action can alter subsequent states and observations, causing errors to compound over time. Existing methods either correct the context without repairing altered environment states or restore earlier states while discarding useful experience, making it difficult to both eliminate failure conditions and avoid repeating past mistakes. We argue that reliable recovery should instead be treated as a rollback-boundary control problem that jointly determines when to intervene, where to resume, and what information should survive recovery. Based on this view, we propose Rollback-Induced Reflection (RIR), a unified recovery framework that restores execution to a selected prior state while carrying forward reusable knowledge distilled from the abandoned trajectory to guide subsequent decisions. We further characterize recovery through a unified operator over rollback depth and retained memory, providing a general view of state restoration and knowledge retention. Experiments on three long-horizon benchmarks demonstrate that RIR consistently improves task performance across multiple LLM backbones, with structured reflection memory preserving useful experience and selective rollback enabling efficient recovery.

AI.tldr: Proposes Rollback-Induced Reflection (RIR), a framework that lets LLM agents roll back to earlier environment states while retaining distilled knowledge from failed trajectories, improving long-horizon task performance.
AI.motivation: LLM agents performing long-horizon, multi-step tasks are fragile: a single bad action can change the environment state so that subsequent steps are based on corrupted context, leading to cascading errors. Existing recovery methods either only fix the textual context without repairing environment state, or they reset the environment to an earlier state but discard potentially valuable experience from the failed run. This makes it hard to both remove failure conditions and avoid repeating mistakes. The paper aims to design a recovery mechanism that can simultaneously restore a safe state and preserve useful knowledge gained during failed attempts.
AI.method: The authors formulate reliable recovery as a rollback-boundary control problem, which involves deciding (1) when to intervene, (2) how far back to roll the environment, and (3) what information from the failed trajectory to keep. They propose Rollback-Induced Reflection (RIR), a unified framework that: (a) selects a prior environment state as the rollback point, (b) restores execution to that state, and (c) distills reusable knowledge from the abandoned trajectory into a structured reflection memory that is preserved across rollback. They formalize recovery as an operator parameterized by rollback depth and retained memory, offering a general abstraction for interacting state restoration with knowledge retention. RIR is instantiated on LLM agents and evaluated under different LLM backbones.
AI.result: On three long-horizon benchmarks, applying RIR consistently improves task success rates compared to baselines across multiple LLM backbones. The experiments show that structured reflection memory effectively preserves useful experience from failed attempts, and that selective rollback (rather than always resetting fully or not at all) leads to more efficient and successful recovery behavior.
AI.conclusion: Treating recovery for LLM agents as a rollback-boundary control problem enables a principled design of mechanisms that both revert to safe environment states and retain distilled knowledge from failed trajectories. The proposed RIR framework realizes this idea, providing a general operator over rollback depth and retained memory, and empirically yields consistent performance gains on long-horizon tasks. This suggests that combining state restoration with structured reflection is a promising direction for making LLM agents more robust and efficient in complex, multi-step environments.

title: Re2A: Situated Conversational Recommendation via Rubric-based Preference Reasoning and Alignment
summary: Real-world recommendation scenarios are commonly grounded in shared physical environments during user-recommender interactions. This motivates situated conversational recommendation (SCR), a complex task requiring recommender assistants to jointly reason over dialogue history, co-observed scenes, and in-scene item attributes. However, current approaches struggle with this setting due to two intertwined challenges: accurately understanding situated user preferences throughout the conversation and generating responses that simultaneously satisfy user needs and grounded situations. To this end, we propose Re2A, a framework that formulates SCR as a structured reason-then-align process. We introduce rubric-based preference reasoning, which uses automated rubrics to guide the model toward producing explicit preference states. Based on these states, we propose a preference-conditioned optimization to align response generation with dual objectives: user preference satisfaction and situation consistency. Extensive experiments on two SCR datasets demonstrate that Re2A consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering more precise, context-aware conversational recommendations. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongdingLin/Re2A.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Re2A, a structured reasoning-and-alignment framework for situated conversational recommendation that improves context-aware, grounded recommendations over the state of the art.
AI.motivation: In real-world recommendation scenarios, users and recommender systems often share a physical environment (e.g., shopping in a store, museum tours, AR/VR scenes). Existing conversational recommenders struggle to jointly interpret dialogue history, the shared scene, and item attributes, leading to poor understanding of user preferences and responses that may not fit the physical situation. The authors aim to address the dual challenge of accurately modeling evolving user preferences in context and generating responses that are both preference-aligned and consistent with the observed environment.
AI.method: The authors propose Re2A, which formulates situated conversational recommendation as a two-stage "reason-then-align" pipeline. First, they introduce rubric-based preference reasoning: automatic rubrics guide a model to explicitly infer and represent the user’s situated preference state from dialogue and scene information. Second, based on these explicit preference states, they define a preference-conditioned optimization objective that steers response generation to satisfy two goals simultaneously: aligning with the inferred user preferences and maintaining consistency with the current physical/situational context. The framework is implemented and evaluated on SCR benchmarks.
AI.result: On two situated conversational recommendation datasets, Re2A achieves better performance than state-of-the-art baselines. The improvements are measured in terms of precision and context-awareness of the recommendations, indicating stronger alignment with user preferences and better grounding in the shared physical environment.
AI.conclusion: Re2A demonstrates that explicitly separating preference reasoning from response generation, via rubric-guided preference states and a dual-objective optimization, leads to superior situated conversational recommendations. The framework delivers more precise and context-aware suggestions than prior methods, highlighting the value of structured reasoning and alignment for complex, environment-grounded dialogue tasks. The released code supports further research on SCR.

title: SEA-LION-v4.8: A Technical Report
summary: We introduce Nemotron-SEA-LION-v4.8, a family of Southeast Asian Languages in One Network (SEA-LION) built upon NVIDIA Nemotron 3. The family includes 30B-A3B and 120B-A12B models, with both continued-pretrained base checkpoints and post-trained variants. We adapt the models using Southeast Asian, reasoning, code, and multilingual parallel datasets, followed by post-training with supervised fine-tuning and online on-policy distillation. On SEA-HELM, the 30B-A3B model improves the overall SEA score from 46.06 to 51.57, while the 120B-A12B model improves from 49.30 to 63.44. The strongest gains are observed in instruction following, natural language reasoning, and natural language understanding across seven Southeast Asian languages.

AI.tldr: Nemotron-SEA-LION-v4.8 is a set of large language models specialized for seven Southeast Asian languages, adapted from NVIDIA Nemotron 3 and significantly improving benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of strong, unified large language models that perform well across multiple Southeast Asian languages, especially for tasks like instruction following, reasoning, and understanding. The authors aim to fill this gap by adapting a powerful base model (Nemotron 3) to these languages and evaluating it with a dedicated benchmark (SEA-HELM).
AI.method: Starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3, the authors build two model sizes (30B-A3B and 120B-A12B). They continue pretraining on a mix of Southeast Asian language corpora, reasoning datasets, code, and multilingual parallel data. After this, they apply post-training via supervised fine-tuning and online on-policy distillation to obtain instruction-tuned variants. They evaluate the models using the SEA-HELM benchmark that covers seven Southeast Asian languages and multiple capability dimensions.
AI.result: On the SEA-HELM benchmark, the 30B-A3B model raises the overall SEA score from 46.06 to 51.57, and the 120B-A12B model raises it from 49.30 to 63.44. The largest improvements are in instruction following, natural language reasoning, and natural language understanding across the seven target Southeast Asian languages.
AI.conclusion: Nemotron-SEA-LION-v4.8 substantially advances performance for Southeast Asian languages by adapting Nemotron 3 with targeted pretraining and post-training. The models, particularly the 120B-A12B variant, deliver strong gains on the SEA-HELM benchmark, showing that a unified multilingual network can effectively support diverse Southeast Asian languages for complex language tasks.

title: REPAIR: Resolving Long-Tail Confusion in Scientific Retrievers via Fact-Verified Iterative Refinement
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 30 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code: https://github.com/yerimoh/REPAIR
summary: Precise retrieval of scientific information is fundamentally constrained by long-tailed concepts and high fact-sensitivity of scientific corpora. These challenges often limit the effectiveness of dense retrievers and hallucination-prone LLM augmentation. To address this, we present REPAIR, a self-evolving data augmentation framework for scientific dense retrievers. REPAIR iteratively synthesizes training data to address knowledge gaps by cycling through diagnosis of long-tail concepts, API-guided evidence expansion, and differentiation via hard negative mining. This process effectively grounds retrieval in factual reality to resolve fine-grained distinctions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REPAIR significantly outperforms 19 strong baselines on nine materials science and biomedical benchmarks. Our work highlights that diagnosing and factually augmenting data to long-tail deficits is essential for robust scientific retrieval.

AI.tldr: REPAIR is a self-evolving data augmentation framework that iteratively generates targeted training data to fix dense retrievers’ weaknesses on long-tail, fact-sensitive scientific concepts, leading to large retrieval gains on materials science and biomedical tasks.
AI.motivation: Scientific information retrieval is hard because scientific corpora contain many rare, long-tailed concepts and require very precise factual distinctions. Standard dense retrievers struggle with these rare concepts, and LLM-based augmentation can hallucinate or fail to be sufficiently grounded in evidence. The authors are motivated to create a method that systematically identifies and fixes these knowledge and data gaps so that scientific retrieval becomes more accurate and robust.
AI.method: They introduce REPAIR, a self-evolving data augmentation framework for dense retrievers. REPAIR runs in an iterative loop: (1) diagnosing failures and long-tail concepts where the retriever is weak; (2) using APIs to expand evidence around those concepts, gathering more relevant factual material; and (3) performing hard negative mining to generate challenging, fine-grained contrastive training examples. The synthesized and curated training data are then used to retrain or refine the dense retriever, and the cycle repeats, progressively improving performance on difficult, rare concepts while staying grounded in factual evidence.
AI.result: In experiments on nine benchmarks from materials science and biomedicine, REPAIR substantially improves retrieval performance compared with 19 strong baselines. The gains are particularly notable on fine-grained, long-tail scientific concepts, suggesting that the framework successfully addresses previously under-covered areas of the training data and enhances factual grounding.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that systematically diagnosing long-tail deficits and augmenting data in a factual, targeted way is crucial for building robust scientific dense retrievers. REPAIR demonstrates that an iterative, self-evolving augmentation process—combining failure diagnosis, evidence expansion, and hard negative mining—can significantly enhance retrieval quality in complex, fact-sensitive scientific domains.

title: Knowledge-Graph Based Augmentation versus Retrieval Augmented Generation for Cultural-Related Question Answering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) suffer from a long-tail deficit: culturally specific facts, particularly those concerning underrepresented regions such as Latin America, appear too rarely in pretraining corpora to be reliably memorized. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this by grounding generation in external text, but structured alternatives such as Knowledge Graphs (KGs) offer tighter control over what enters the context, along with potential gains in explainability and updatability. We benchmark Graph-RAG against standard RAG on LatamQA, a culturally grounded multiple-choice dataset spanning eight thematic categories. The graphs are built end-to-end from Wikipedia articles with KGGen, a recent open-domain extractor, without manual curation in our main setting. G-Retriever is competitive with RAG and reduces the error of the base LLM by 72\% with a standard KG and 78\% with a benchmark-aware variant, the gap to RAG narrowing further as the graph is oriented toward task-relevant content. The trained projection transfers zero-shot to Portuguese without target-language fine-tuning, indicating multilingual reach.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates Graph-RAG (RAG over knowledge graphs) versus standard text-based RAG for culturally specific QA in Latin America, finding that graph-based retrieval greatly reduces LLM error and transfers across languages.
AI.motivation: Large language models struggle with culturally specific, long-tail knowledge, especially for underrepresented regions like Latin America, because such facts are rare in pretraining data. While standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation can help by adding external text, it can be noisy and hard to control, explain, or update. The authors want a more structured, controllable way—via knowledge graphs—to improve performance on region-specific questions and test whether this approach is competitive with strong text-based RAG systems.
AI.method: They build a benchmark called LatamQA, a culturally grounded multiple-choice QA dataset covering eight thematic categories about Latin America. They construct knowledge graphs automatically and end-to-end from Wikipedia using KGGen, without manual curation in the main experiments. On top of these graphs, they implement Graph-RAG with a retriever component called G-Retriever that maps questions into the graph space to select relevant subgraphs for the LLM. They compare performance of Graph-RAG versus standard text-based RAG, including variants where the KG is made more task-aware, and evaluate transfer to Portuguese without additional fine-tuning.
AI.result: G-Retriever with a standard knowledge graph strongly improves the base LLM, reducing its error rate by 72%, and by 78% when using a benchmark-aware, task-oriented graph variant. Graph-RAG’s performance is competitive with standard text-based RAG, and the performance gap shrinks further as the KG is oriented toward task-relevant content. The learned projection used in G-Retriever generalizes zero-shot to Portuguese, demonstrating multilingual transfer without target-language fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Automatically constructed knowledge graphs used in a Graph-RAG setup can substantially mitigate LLM deficits on culturally specific, long-tail questions, achieving performance competitive with text RAG while offering benefits in control, explainability, and updatability. Task-oriented graph design further narrows the gap to standard RAG, and the retrieval approach transfers across languages, suggesting that structured retrieval is a promising, scalable path for improving LLM cultural competence in underrepresented regions.

title: BENCHCOMPASS: From Scores to Signals for Training and Harness Decisions in Payment-Domain LLMs
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Payment operations are a critical financial infrastructure, but the value of large language models in this domain remains unclear because payment rules change quickly, evidence is fragmented, and decisions depend on transaction state, participant role, region, and payment rail. Existing benchmarks do not isolate whether failures come from missing payment-rule knowledge, poor use of supplied evidence, or brittleness under imperfect harness inputs. We introduce BENCHCOMPASS, a payment-domain benchmark whose construction pipeline builds scenario-grounded tasks from typed evidence packs, applies LLM-based quality checks, creates task-input attack variants, and reserves final item admission for domain experts. The release contains an expert-reviewed Pro benchmark covering payment knowledge, context-grounded scenario reasoning, and Attacked Open robustness, plus a lower-assurance Normal pool for inspection and future curation. Across 16 model variants, BENCHCOMPASS shows qualitatively different failure modes: missing parametric payment knowledge, incomplete reasoning over supplied rules, and failure to reject plausible but invalid workflows. The benchmark remains unsaturated: the best frontier model reaches 89.6% on Open Context-Grounded Reasoning and 81.7% under attacked inputs, while a representative 32B open-weight model reaches 69.8% and 42.6%. Benchmark data and code are available at https://github.com/ant-intl/BenchCompass.

AI.tldr: Introduces BENCHCOMPASS, a specialized benchmark to evaluate LLMs on realistic payment operations tasks, distinguishing knowledge gaps from reasoning and robustness issues.
AI.motivation: Payment systems are complex, fast-changing, and context-dependent (transaction state, role, region, rail). Existing LLM benchmarks cannot tell whether model errors stem from missing payment-rule knowledge, misuse of provided evidence, or fragility to noisy/attacked inputs. A domain-grounded, carefully curated benchmark is needed to evaluate and improve LLMs used in payment operations.
AI.method: They design a benchmark-construction pipeline that: (1) builds scenario-grounded tasks from structured “typed” evidence packs; (2) uses LLM-based quality checks during item generation; (3) creates adversarial/attack variants of task inputs; and (4) submits candidate items to domain experts for final admission. The resulting BENCHCOMPASS benchmark contains a high-assurance Pro split (expert-reviewed, covering payment knowledge, context-grounded reasoning, and robustness under attacked inputs) and a larger, lower-assurance Normal pool for further inspection and curation.
AI.result: They evaluate 16 LLM variants on BENCHCOMPASS and observe qualitatively different failure modes: lack of up-to-date or detailed parametric payment knowledge; incomplete reasoning over the rules provided in evidence packs; and difficulty rejecting workflows that sound plausible but are actually invalid. Performance is far from saturated: the strongest frontier model reaches 89.6% on open context-grounded reasoning and 81.7% on attacked inputs, whereas a typical 32B open-weight model only attains 69.8% and 42.6%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: BENCHCOMPASS offers a rigorous, unsaturated benchmark for assessing LLMs in payment operations, able to disentangle knowledge, reasoning, and robustness failures. The sizable performance gap between frontier and open-weight models, and the remaining headroom even for the best models, indicate substantial room for improvement and make BENCHCOMPASS a useful resource for both evaluation and future model development in the payment domain.

title: Attention Dispersion as a Diagnostic Signal for Hallucination in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit hallucinations, presenting a major barrier to reliability in complex reasoning tasks. While traditional detection methods rely on output-based confidence metrics, these logits are often miscalibrated by modern alignment techniques. In this paper, we investigate the temporal volatility of internal attention mechanisms as an alternative diagnostic signal for hallucination that does not depend on output calibration. By introducing an unsupervised metric for attention dispersion, we show that epistemic uncertainty leaves a measurable trace within intermediate layers, where spikes in attention entropy are associated with reasoning breakdowns. We evaluate our approach on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K and MATH-500) using the Qwen2.5 model family (1.5B and 3B parameters), finding statistically significant AUC improvements of up to +0.076 over output-based baselines across all tested conditions. These findings suggest that attention dispersion is a promising complement to traditional hallucination detection methods, requiring further investigation across broader model families and task domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using the dispersion of internal attention (attention entropy spikes) as an unsupervised signal to detect hallucinations in LLM reasoning, outperforming standard output-based confidence baselines on math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations limit the reliability of LLMs in complex reasoning, and current detection methods depend on output logits, which are often miscalibrated due to alignment. The authors seek a calibration‑independent internal signal of epistemic uncertainty that can flag impending reasoning failures (hallucinations).
AI.method: They analyze temporal volatility and dispersion of attention patterns inside LLMs and define an unsupervised attention dispersion / entropy metric over intermediate attention layers during reasoning. They correlate spikes in this metric with reasoning breakdowns (hallucinations) and compare its hallucination‑detection performance to conventional output‑based confidence measures. Experiments use Qwen2.5 (1.5B and 3B) on GSM8K and MATH‑500 benchmarks, evaluating detection via AUC.
AI.result: Attention dispersion/entropy spikes within intermediate layers are strongly associated with hallucinations. The proposed metric yields statistically significant improvements in hallucination detection AUC of up to +0.076 compared to output‑based baselines, consistently across all tested model sizes and benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Internal attention dispersion is a promising, calibration‑independent signal for hallucination detection in LLMs, complementing traditional confidence‑based methods. The consistent AUC gains suggest this approach merits further exploration on larger model families, more diverse tasks, and potentially integration with runtime monitoring or control mechanisms for safer reasoning behavior.

title: Who Audits Whom, on What Substrate, with What Evidence? An Independence-Graded Audit Protocol for Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI systems plan, invoke tools and act with limited supervision; they are now both the subject of audits and, increasingly, the auditor. Independence, the foundation of assurance,is still applied to them as a binary. We argue that it must be graded along three orthogonal axes: principal independence (who controls the auditor), substrate independence (an auditor sharing the auditee's foundation-model family, toolchain or guardrails fails with it) and evidence independence (whether evidence is attestable rather than self-reported). Each axis has precedent; the contribution is to grade all three on a single audit, aggregate them by the weakest link, and apply the same rubric when the auditor is itself an agent. We give the model a formal basis by transplanting the beta-factor model of common-cause failure from reliability engineering, a seven-step protocol whose outputs a third party can verify, a structural detectability analysis of a procurement-controls agent audited at three grades, and a Monte Carlo study of the model in which a conventional internal audit of an agent-a real audit team, a second agent, provider logsp-surfaces 5.9% of the faults it could in principle see and none at all in half the fault classes. We map the triple to the EU AI Act as amended, ISO/IEC 42006, UK public-sector risk-management guidance and audit-regulator practice.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a graded, three-dimensional notion of independence for auditing agentic AI systems and shows how to operationalize and evaluate it.
AI.motivation: Existing audit practices and standards treat auditor independence as a binary property, which is inadequate for complex agentic AI systems that can both be audited and serve as auditors. There is a risk of common-cause failures when auditors share models, tooling, or data dependencies with the systems they audit, and current frameworks do not systematically surface or quantify this risk.
AI.method: The authors define three orthogonal axes of independence—principal independence (who controls the auditor), substrate independence (technical and tooling separation between auditor and auditee), and evidence independence (how externally attestable the evidence is). They adapt the beta-factor model from reliability engineering to formalize common-cause failures across these axes, propose a seven-step, third-party-verifiable audit protocol, conduct a structural detectability analysis of a procurement-controls agent under three independence grades, and run a Monte Carlo study simulating audits by different auditors (internal team, second agent, provider logs) to estimate fault-detection coverage.
AI.result: The graded-independence model can be consistently applied to both human and agentic auditors, with overall independence determined by the weakest axis. The structural analysis demonstrates how independence grades affect which faults are in principle detectable. The Monte Carlo study finds that a typical internal audit setup for an AI agent surfaces only about 5.9% of the faults that are, in principle, observable, and completely misses half of the modeled fault classes, highlighting severe blind spots caused by lack of independence. The mapping to EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42006, UK risk guidance, and audit-regulator practice shows that the proposed triple can integrate with and clarify existing regulatory frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Binary notions of auditor independence are insufficient for agentic AI. A three-axis, graded independence model grounded in reliability engineering better captures real audit resilience, especially against common-cause failures between agents and their auditors. Applying this model reveals that many current AI audit practices are far less effective than assumed, and provides a structured protocol and regulatory mapping to improve and standardize audits—whether the auditor is human or an AI agent.

title: Emotion Experience, Expression, and Perception: Emotion Analysis on Multimodal Social Media Posts
comment: Accepted for publication at EMNLP 2026 main conference
summary: Emotions are an essential aspect of human communication, particularly on social media, where authors frequently combine text and images to convey their emotions. Yet prior work on emotion analysis of social media posts has overlooked two important aspects in regard to measuring how well readers can reconstruct the authors' intent: (1)~the image modality, with most work focusing solely on text, and (2)~the real-world events that trigger the expressed emotions, and their relationship to the post content. We therefore study the relation between (a) the author's experience of the event that caused them to write a social media post and (b) the content of the post, with a focus on readers' capability to reconstruct that emotion expression. To do that, we introduce the Multimodal Multi-Emotion-Model dataset Mult2EMo, created by collecting annotations from both authors and readers on the posts and their triggering events. We find that reconstruction is possible but challenging for both human readers and computational models. We show that understanding the triggering event is crucial for accurate reconstruction, and that reconstruction is particularly challenging when posts rely heavily on the image to express emotion.

AI.tldr: They build and analyze a new multimodal dataset (text + images + events) with both author and reader emotion annotations to study how well readers and models can reconstruct authors’ emotions in social media posts.
AI.motivation: Existing emotion analysis of social media largely ignores images and the underlying real-world events that trigger emotions, and typically only labels text with emotions from the reader’s perspective. This leaves open how well readers (and models) can recover the author’s intended emotion, especially when posts are multimodal and tied to external events.
AI.method: They collect a new dataset, Mult2EMo, of social media posts containing both text and images. For each post, they obtain annotations from the original authors about their emotions and the triggering real-world event, and parallel annotations from external readers about perceived emotions. They then train and evaluate computational models on this multimodal, multi-annotator data to measure emotion reconstruction performance, and analyze factors such as the role of images and explicit event understanding.
AI.result: Human readers and computational models can reconstruct authors’ emotions better than chance but with substantial difficulty. Performance improves notably when the triggering event is understood or modeled, indicating its importance. Posts where emotional meaning is carried mainly by the image are particularly hard for both humans and models to interpret correctly, leading to lower reconstruction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Emotion reconstruction in multimodal social media is feasible but challenging. Accurate modeling requires incorporating not just textual content but also images and explicit representations of the real-world triggering events. The proposed Mult2EMo dataset provides a benchmark for studying these phenomena and highlights that future emotion analysis systems must better handle image-heavy posts and event context to approximate human-like understanding of authors’ emotional intent.

title: Building Trust in Artificial Intelligence: A Necessity for Railway Applications
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is currently only applied to non-safety critical applications due to the strict standards and regulations for railway industries. We propose to review the three main fields necessary to increase trust in data science and AI algorithms and reach compliance: robustness, Operational Design Domain (ODD), and explainability. Robustness is the ability of an AI system to maintain its level of performance under any circumstances (ISO24029). ODDs allow the explicit definition of operating conditions under which a system is intended to operate, according to the recently published DIN DKE SPEC 99004. Explainability is the property of an AI system to express important factors influencing the AI system results in a way that humans can understand. Those 3 domains of research are already well investigated by nonrailway actors, with algorithms and methods ready to use for railway applications. A system view is necessary to ensure all trustworthy requirements interact continuously in a safe MLOps environment thereby fostering acceptance from regulators, operators and the public. Beyond safeguarding safety-critical applications, we aim to show that fostering deep trust in AI, as now required by regulatory frameworks worldwide, will unlock its full potential and transform the pace of adoption across mission-critical domains.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses how to make AI acceptable for safety-critical railway applications by focusing on robustness, Operational Design Domain (ODD), and explainability within a safe MLOps system view.
AI.motivation: AI is currently restricted to non-safety-critical railway applications due to strict safety standards and regulatory demands. To expand AI into safety‑critical use, the industry needs a clear framework and evidence that AI can be trusted and can comply with those standards.
AI.method: The authors conceptually review and structure three key research domains—robustness, Operational Design Domain (ODD), and explainability—drawing on existing standards (ISO24029, DIN DKE SPEC 99004) and non-railway AI methods, and argue for integrating them into a holistic, safe MLOps system for railways.
AI.result: The paper identifies that methods and algorithms for robustness, ODD definition, and explainability already exist in other sectors and are technically ready to be adapted to railway use, provided they are embedded in a system-level trustworthy AI and MLOps framework.
AI.conclusion: By systematically addressing robustness, well-defined ODDs, and explainability within an integrated, safe MLOps environment, it is possible to build regulator and public trust in AI for safety‑critical railway applications, enabling wider and faster adoption of AI in mission-critical domains.

title: Dependency-Aware Trajectory Refinement for Efficient Multi-Turn Agent Fine-Tuning
summary: Multi-turn agent trajectories often contain redundant rounds (failed tool calls, parallel sub-queries, verification-only steps) that inflate both training and inference cost. We propose viewing each trajectory as a \emph{round-level dependency DAG} that exposes which rounds are globally load-bearing for the final answer, and fine-tune agents on trajectories refined through this DAG. Given an LLM-annotated DAG, these edits are deterministic and interpretable, with optional rephrasing. Models trained on these refined trajectories consistently outperform those trained on the original trajectories at lower inference cost. Specifically, across four multi-modal QA benchmarks, our refinements improve downstream accuracy by up to $1.7$\,pp over vanilla SFT (and $5.7$\,pp over an LLM-deletion baseline) while reducing per-sample inference messages by up to approximately $40\%$ and inference tokens by up to approximately $48\%$, translating to substantial savings in compute and serving cost. Code is available.

AI.tldr: They compress multi-turn agent trajectories by modeling them as round-level dependency DAGs, keeping only the rounds that are truly necessary for the final answer, and fine-tune agents on these refined trajectories to get higher accuracy with much lower inference cost.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn tool-using agents often generate long, redundant trajectories (failed tool calls, dead-end branches, verification-only turns). Training directly on these raw logs is wasteful and encourages inefficient behavior, and at inference time similar redundancy inflates latency and compute costs. There is a need for a systematic way to identify which parts of a trajectory actually matter for producing the final answer, and to train models to imitate this more efficient behavior without sacrificing (and ideally improving) quality.
AI.method: They represent each multi-turn trajectory as a round-level dependency directed acyclic graph (DAG), where nodes are rounds and edges capture which rounds depend on which earlier rounds for the final answer. Using an LLM, they annotate each trajectory with this DAG, then deterministically prune away rounds that are not globally load‑bearing for the final answer (e.g., failed or unused tool calls, redundant verification turns), optionally rephrasing remaining content for coherence. These refined trajectories are then used as supervision for fine-tuning agents. The procedure is deterministic and interpretable once the DAG is annotated, allowing consistent trajectory editing across a dataset.
AI.result: On four multi-modal QA benchmarks, agents fine-tuned on the DAG-refined trajectories outperform those trained on the original, unedited trajectories. The refined training improves downstream accuracy by up to 1.7 percentage points over standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and by 5.7 percentage points over a baseline that simply deletes turns using an LLM without DAG structure. At the same time, the refined models generate much shorter trajectories at inference: per-sample message count drops by up to about 40%, and total inference tokens by up to about 48%, leading to meaningful savings in compute and serving costs.
AI.conclusion: Structuring multi-turn agent trajectories as dependency DAGs and training only on globally load-bearing rounds yields agents that are both more accurate and more efficient. The approach offers a principled, interpretable way to compress trajectories compared to naive deletion, and empirically delivers better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across several multi-modal QA tasks, making it a practical strategy for reducing training and inference overhead in tool-using LLM agents.

title: Where Should Agents Live? Energy-Memory Characterization of Agentic AI for the Edge-Cloud Continuum
summary: As telecommunication networks evolve toward autonomous 5G-Advanced and 6G operations, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workflows, where large language models (LLMs) execute multi-step reasoning, invoke diagnostic tools, retrieve domain knowledge, and coordinate across agent teams, are increasingly embedded across the edge-cloud continuum. While the biological brain accomplishes complex cognition on an exceptionally modest metabolic power budget of approximately 20W contemporary LLMs are profoundly energy- and memory-intensive, making sustainable lifecycle orchestration a critical operational priority. However, existing AI lifecycle metrics evaluate only isolated, single-model inferences or overlook multi-agent execution graphs entirely. Consequently, network operators lack foundational models to determine whether distributed agent communication incurs meaningful energy costs and where across edge-cloud tiers agent teams should physically reside. To address this gap, we introduce agentic-eCAL, generalizing the Energy Cost of AI Lifecycle (eCAL) metric to directed multi-agent workflows by coupling a closed-form two-rate single-call energy model (compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode) with 7-layer OSI data transport. Grounded in hundreds of GPU benchmark configurations on NVIDIA A100 and H100, 16 open-weight models and 8 orchestration topologies, we validate components of the metric and study workflow placement implications. Our findings demonstrate that inter-agent text transport incurs 0.25% of workflow energy across 5G RAN, metro, and optical links. Therefore in edge-cloud agent placement the dominant energy cost of distribution is often not the transmission of inter-agent text itself, but the additional inference and context processing induced by that communication.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes an energy metric (eCAL) to multi-agent AI workflows in 5G/6G edge-cloud networks and shows that communication energy between agents is negligible compared with inference and context-processing energy.
AI.motivation: As 5G-Advanced and 6G networks adopt agentic AI with LLM-based multi-agent workflows, operators need to understand full lifecycle energy costs, not just single-model inferences. Existing metrics ignore multi-agent execution graphs and the energy implications of placing agents across the edge-cloud continuum, leaving operators unable to assess whether distributed communication is energetically significant or where agents should be located.
AI.method: The authors extend the Energy Cost of AI Lifecycle (eCAL) metric to agentic workflows (agentic-eCAL) by: (1) modeling per-call LLM energy with a closed-form two-rate model that separates compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode; (2) embedding this into directed multi-agent workflow graphs; and (3) incorporating 7-layer OSI data transport to capture communication energy over network links. They ground and calibrate the metric using hundreds of GPU benchmark configurations on NVIDIA A100 and H100, 16 open-weight LLMs, and 8 orchestration topologies spanning different edge-cloud placements.
AI.result: Benchmarks and modeling show that inter-agent text transport accounts for only about 0.25% of total workflow energy across 5G RAN, metro, and optical network segments. The majority of energy is consumed by LLM inference and context processing steps triggered by agent communication, rather than by the transmission of the textual messages themselves. The agentic-eCAL metric is validated in parts against empirical measurements on diverse hardware, models, and topologies.
AI.conclusion: For multi-agent LLM-based systems in future telecom networks, distributing agents across edge and cloud is not primarily constrained by the energy cost of moving text between them. Instead, the key energy driver is the additional inference and context handling induced by agent interactions. The proposed agentic-eCAL metric provides a framework to quantify these costs for complex workflows and inform energy-aware agent placement and orchestration decisions in 5G-Advanced and 6G environments.

title: Planning or Improvisation? Stress-Testing the Poetry Planning Site on Open Models and Open Cross-Layer Transcoders
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code, data and analysis scripts: https://github.com/PCfVW/poetry-planning-site . An earlier version was submitted to the BlackboxNLP 2026 special track on reproducibility and reliability in interpretability analyses; this version adds a rerun composition-horizon experiment (36 runs, 8,640 sampled lines) and a transcoder-free activation-patching test
summary: Lindsey et al. (2025) report that Claude 3.5 Haiku plans rhymes: features for candidate rhyme words are active on the newline before a line is written, and a suppress-and-inject intervention redirects the line only when applied there (their Figure 13). We test how far this generalizes on seven cells crossing four open models (0.6B to 2.6B parameters) with six open cross-layer transcoders (CLTs), on one consumer GPU, decomposing the claim into position specificity (C1), newline site identity (C2), and a newline-resident plan (C3). This is a stress test rather than a faithful reproduction: attribution graphs are unavailable for these CLTs, so features are found bottom-up from decoder vectors. C1 generalizes, in every cell and in all 247 of 444 prompt-by-inject pairs with a detectable effect, but the effective position is the final prompt token, adjacent to emission, and only two cells reach behaviorally meaningful probabilities. C2 and C3 are not recovered by any probe: a census of every active feature finds no rhyme-anticipating enrichment at the newline, and steering the newline while the model composes the whole line, over 36 runs and 8,640 sampled lines, shows why. That intervention is strong but one token long, making the injected word the first word of the composed line in 703 of 720 samples and leaving the rhyme six words later untouched. A final test drops the transcoder entirely: patching the newline's whole residual, at every layer, from a minimal-pair poem whose third line ends on a different rhyme moves the rhyme in 11 of 1,260 composed lines against 4 at baseline, with a design resolving 1.4%. We read this as a boundary condition rather than a refutation: at this scale and with these transcoders, the causal site is emission-adjacent. We reproduce Figure 13's shape, not its mechanism. Code and data are public (code: github.com/PCfVW/poetry-planning-site).

AI.tldr: The paper stress-tests a prior claim that a model plans rhymes specifically at newline tokens, finding that in smaller open models with cross-layer transcoders the key causal position is the token just before emission, not the newline, partially reproducing the behavioral effect but not the proposed mechanism.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Lindsey et al. 2025) claimed that Claude 3.5 Haiku explicitly plans rhymes at newline tokens, supported by feature activations and causal interventions. This is an important claim about how LLMs plan multi-token structure (like poetic rhyme), but it was based on a single proprietary model and tooling. The authors want to know whether that mechanism generalizes to smaller open models and to different interpretability methods (cross-layer transcoders), and to clarify where in the sequence rhyme planning is actually causally implemented.
AI.method: They evaluate seven (task, model) cells using four open-source language models ranging from 0.6B to 2.6B parameters, combined with six open cross-layer transcoders (CLTs). They decompose the original claim into: (C1) position-specificity of the causal site, (C2) the identity of the newline token as the planning site, and (C3) the presence of rhyme-planning features resident at the newline. Because they lack attribution graphs for these CLTs, they derive candidate rhyme-related features bottom-up from decoder vectors. They then run feature-steering interventions at different positions (newline vs emission-adjacent), run census analyses of active features at newline positions for rhyme anticipation, and conduct large-scale sampling experiments where interventions are applied while the model composes entire lines. Finally, they perform a model-agnostic residual patching experiment: copying the full residual stream at newline, at every layer, from a minimal-pair poem with a different rhyme ending, to see if this moves the rhyme in generated third lines.
AI.result: (C1) Position-specificity largely generalizes: in all seven cells and in 247 of 444 prompt–inject pairs where any effect is detectable, interventions only redirect behavior when applied at a specific position. However, this effective position is consistently the final prompt token directly adjacent to emission, not the newline, and only two cells show changes large enough to be behaviorally meaningful. (C2 and C3) They find no positive evidence: a comprehensive census of features that are active at newline tokens shows no enrichment for rhyme-anticipating features, and steering at the newline during the composition of an entire line mostly just forces the injected word to be the first word of the line (703/720 samples) without affecting the rhyme, which typically appears ~6 tokens later. In the residual-patching experiment without CLTs, copying the entire newline residual from a poem with a different third-line rhyme only shifts the rhyme in 11 out of 1,260 generations, compared to 4 at baseline—a tiny effect in a design that can only resolve 1.4%.
AI.conclusion: The specific mechanism proposed by Lindsey et al.—that models plan rhymes via rhyme-related features residing at newline tokens—is not supported in these smaller open models with available CLTs. Instead, rhyme-relevant causal structure appears to be located adjacent to the emission site, at the last prompt token before generation, at least at this scale and with these tools. The authors interpret this as establishing a boundary condition, not a wholesale refutation: they reproduce the behavioral pattern of position-specific causality (similar to Lindsey et al.'s Figure 13), but the underlying mechanism differs, and the newline token does not appear to be a privileged rhyme-planning locus. They release code and data to support further investigation.

title: What Counts as Strategic Reasoning? A Systematic Mapping of Chess Research on Humans, Engines, and Language Models
comment: Under review; replication package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695754
summary:
Chess has long served as a model domain for studying search, expertise, decision-making, and artificial intelligence. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has renewed the relevance of chess as a controlled environment for investigating strategic reasoning and comparing human and artificial decision-making. We present a systematic mapping study of recent research spanning human players, classical chess engines, neural and reinforcement-learning systems, LLMs, and hybrid approaches. The final map comprises 84 core study families, classified according to agent type, strategic-reasoning stages, and evaluation dimensions.
  The map reveals a literature strongly concentrated on situation assessment, evaluation, and action selection, while explicit planning, explanation, metacognition, and human--AI collaboration remain less explored. LLM research places particular emphasis on state representation and generalization, whereas grounded explanation appears more frequently in hybrid approaches combining language models with engines, expert knowledge, or other external structures. Two distinctions emerge that the map aggregates rather than resolves: hybrid systems differ in where and when heterogeneous capabilities combine, and evaluations that show improved human performance do not thereby establish human--AI synergy. We propose both as extensions of the mapping framework.
  We argue that chess provides a useful bridge between cognitive and computational perspectives on strategic reasoning, and identify explicit planning, grounded and faithful explanation, metacognitive calibration, and human--AI complementarity as directions for future research.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically maps recent research on chess as a testbed for strategic reasoning across humans, engines, RL systems, LLMs, and hybrids, highlighting what stages of reasoning are well-studied and where gaps remain.
AI.motivation: Chess has historically been a prime domain for studying search, expertise, and AI, and the rise of LLMs reopens chess as a controlled environment for probing strategic reasoning and human–AI comparison. However, existing work is fragmented across different agent types and reasoning stages, so a structured overview is needed.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic mapping study of recent chess-related work, organizing 84 core study families along three axes: type of agent (humans, classical engines, neural/RL systems, LLMs, hybrids), stages of strategic reasoning (e.g., situation assessment, evaluation, action selection, planning, metacognition), and evaluation dimensions (e.g., performance, explanation quality, human impact). They then analyze patterns and gaps in this map.
AI.result: They find that most research focuses on situation assessment, evaluation, and move selection, while explicit planning, explanation, metacognition, and human–AI collaboration are underexplored. LLM-based studies emphasize state representation and generalization; grounded explanations arise more in hybrid systems that couple language models with engines or expert structures. They identify unresolved distinctions in how hybrid systems integrate components and how to distinguish mere performance gains from true human–AI synergy.
AI.conclusion: Chess is argued to be an effective bridge between cognitive science and computational AI for studying strategic reasoning. The authors highlight four key underdeveloped directions: explicit planning, grounded and faithful explanation, metacognitive calibration of agents, and genuine human–AI complementarity, and they propose extending their mapping framework to better characterize hybridization patterns and human–AI synergy.

title: M-SQE: Multilingual Skill Quality Estimation for Enhancing Language Equality in Agentic Skill Use
summary: Agent skills, reusable procedural documents that extend LLM agents beyond their parametric memory, have become an important interface for deploying agents on real-world tasks. Community-maintained skill libraries built around this interface are growing rapidly. However, this ecosystem remains deeply English-centric: our audit finds that low-resource languages such as Swahili and Hindi have no in-language skill content, so retrieval often returns a skill written in a different language than the query, degrading accuracy and recall. A practical solution is to synthesize in-language skills for retrieval but the quality can be unreliable, so relevance in this setting alone often surfaces a related but unusable candidate. To address this, we propose M-SQE, a post-retrieval Multilingual Skill Quality Estimation framework that scores candidates via a Theory view for intrinsic quality and an Action view for task-grounded utility, unified into a domain-conditioned final score. We evaluate M-SQE across three skill-use domains: general, tool-use, and cultural tasks. Empirically, we build three-layer candidate skill pools mirroring today's ecosystem, where M-SQE's task success exceeds existing baseline's average by at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers. Particularly, M-SQE lifts the lowest-resource languages most (+12.9pp on Hindi and +5.6pp on Swahili) and achieves strong performance across all six culture regions, thereby moving agentic skill use toward linguistic and cultural equality.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles the problem of English-centric agent skill libraries by improving multilingual skill selection quality after retrieval.
AI.motivation: Real-world LLM agents rely on reusable 'skills', but existing skill libraries are almost entirely in English, causing poor retrieval and performance for queries in low-resource languages like Swahili and Hindi. Simply synthesizing in-language skills is noisy, so relevance-based retrieval alone often returns skills that are related but unusable. There is a need for a robust way to select actually useful multilingual skills, especially for low-resource languages and culturally grounded tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce M-SQE, a post-retrieval Multilingual Skill Quality Estimation framework. After an initial retrieval step, M-SQE scores candidate skills using two complementary perspectives: (1) a Theory view that evaluates intrinsic quality of the skill text itself, and (2) an Action view that assesses task-grounded utility (how well the skill helps with the concrete task). These are combined via a domain-conditioned final score tailored to different domains (general tasks, tool-use, cultural tasks). They construct three-layer candidate skill pools to simulate current ecosystems and test M-SQE across multiple retrievers and domains.
AI.result: Across three different retrievers and three domains (general, tool-use, and cultural tasks), M-SQE improves task success by at least +3.5 points on average compared to existing baselines. The gains are particularly large for low-resource languages, with improvements of +12.9 percentage points for Hindi and +5.6 for Swahili. The method also shows strong, consistent performance across six cultural regions.
AI.conclusion: M-SQE is an effective post-retrieval scoring framework for multilingual agent skills, substantially improving the usability and success of skills retrieved for low-resource languages and culturally diverse settings. By explicitly modeling both intrinsic skill quality and task-grounded utility, and conditioning on domain, the approach helps move LLM agent ecosystems toward greater linguistic and cultural equality in skill use.

title: Visual Compliance via Executable Safety Rule Entailment
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 36 pages, 20 figures, 24 tables
summary: Recent advances in LLMs and VLMs have enabled safety systems to reason beyond simple risk patterns toward more contextual and semantic safety concerns. However, as risk patterns continue to evolve and safety rules become more complex, existing training-based end-to-end safeguards face persistent challenges in adaptability and explainable reasoning over complex safety rules. To address these challenges, we propose GuardEn (Guarding by Safety Rule Entailment), an executable safeguard framework that decomposes safety policies into atomic propositions through Safety-Rule Compilation, modeling their composition as executable code. At test time, Scene-Grounded Execution instantiates these atomic propositions with contextual visual information derived from scene graphs, enabling rule-grounded and interpretable safety reasoning. Experiments on SafetyVisionBench demonstrate the effectiveness of programmable safeguard for complex visual safety assessment, achieving an average improvement of 9.8 F1 points over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: GuardEn is a framework that turns complex safety rules into executable code over scene graphs, enabling interpretable visual safety checking that outperforms existing systems.
AI.motivation: Training-based end-to-end safety systems struggle to adapt to evolving risk patterns and increasingly complex, contextual safety policies, and they often lack explainable, rule-level reasoning. There is a need for a more flexible and interpretable way to enforce rich safety rules, especially for vision-language scenarios.
AI.method: The paper introduces GuardEn, which first compiles high-level safety policies into atomic logical propositions via a Safety-Rule Compilation step, representing their composition as executable code. At inference time, a Scene-Grounded Execution process instantiates these propositions using contextual information extracted from images through scene graphs, and executes the resulting program to decide whether content violates safety policies.
AI.result: On the SafetyVisionBench benchmark for visual safety assessment, GuardEn achieves an average F1-score improvement of 9.8 points over the strongest existing baseline, showing better performance at enforcing complex safety rules in vision tasks.
AI.conclusion: Programmable, rule-entailment-based safeguards like GuardEn can provide more adaptable and interpretable safety reasoning than purely training-based end-to-end models, particularly for complex, context-dependent visual safety assessment tasks.

title: Size Matters: Foundation Model for Czech HTML documents
summary: Creating universal, high-quality representations of web documents in high-traffic industrial environments requires models that are both performant and economic. Existing approaches, however, often depend on large models, overlook the structural information inherent in HTML, or are constrained by short context windows, limiting their ability to process real-world web pages. We present HTML-LM, a compact foundation model with 154 million parameters that addresses these limitations through HTML-aware training and a ModernBERT-based architecture. It was trained on 100 million web documents using multiple objectives, including masked language modeling, bag-of-words prediction, and contrastive distillation from large language models. Consequently, HTML-LM sets a new state-of-the-art for classification and regression applications in the Czech Internet domain, surpassing both larger encoders and small-sized LLMs. The model is deployed in production, processing thousands of web documents per second, and released to the community under the CC BY-NC 4.0. https://huggingface.co/Seznam/html-lm.

AI.tldr: HTML-LM is a compact, HTML-aware language model optimized for efficient, high-quality representations of real-world web pages, achieving state-of-the-art results in the Czech Internet domain while being production-ready and resource-efficient.
AI.motivation: To create universal, high-quality representations of web documents that are both computationally efficient and suitable for high-traffic industrial environments, overcoming limitations of existing models that are large, ignore HTML structure, or are limited by short context windows.
AI.method: They design a 154M-parameter foundation model based on a ModernBERT architecture and explicitly HTML-aware training. The model is trained on 100 million web documents with multiple pretraining objectives: masked language modeling, bag-of-words prediction, and contrastive distillation from larger language models, enabling it to capture both content and structure effectively.
AI.result: HTML-LM achieves new state-of-the-art performance on classification and regression tasks within the Czech Internet domain, outperforming both larger encoder models and small-sized LLMs. It is efficient enough to process thousands of web documents per second in a production setting.
AI.conclusion: A relatively small, HTML-structure-aware transformer model trained with multi-objective learning can deliver superior web-document representations compared to larger, less specialized alternatives, making it highly suitable for industrial-scale applications and sufficiently mature to be publicly released under a permissive license.

title: Faithful yet Collusive: Why Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Cannot Detect Collusion in LLM Pricing Agents under Oligopolistic Competition
comment: 20 pages, Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language models (LLM) deployed as autonomous pricing agents may sustain supracompetitive prices through tacit coordination. We develop a causal graph divergence framework that separately measures structural faithfulness and intent faithfulness of LLM pricing agents in Bertrand competition. Across nine LLMs under duopoly and triopoly conditions, collusive behavior and chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness dissociate along both dimensions: the most collusive model accurately reports cooperative intent yet reasons structurally unfaithfully, while the most structurally faithful model sustains supra-Nash pricing under both market structures. These findings establish that CoT monitoring alone cannot serve as a standalone safeguard against algorithmic collusion.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models used as autonomous pricing agents in competitive markets can learn to collude and shows that their stated reasoning (chain-of-thought) is not a reliable indicator of their true pricing behavior or intent.
AI.motivation: As LLMs start to be used as autonomous agents in economic settings such as pricing, regulators and practitioners worry that they may learn to tacitly collude, keeping prices above competitive levels. Current proposals often rely on interpreting LLM chain-of-thought to detect and prevent such behavior, but it is unclear whether these explanations faithfully reflect the models' internal decision processes or intentions. There is a need for a principled framework to measure such faithfulness and to test whether explanation-based monitoring can prevent algorithmic collusion.
AI.method: The authors construct a causal graph divergence framework to evaluate LLM agents on two distinct notions: structural faithfulness (whether the reported reasoning reflects the true causal structure driving decisions) and intent faithfulness (whether reported intentions match actual pricing behavior). They deploy nine different LLMs as pricing agents in simulated Bertrand competition under both duopoly and triopoly market structures, ask the models for chain-of-thought rationales about their pricing, and then compare those rationales against the agents' actual pricing strategies and outcomes to quantify collusion and faithfulness.
AI.result: The study finds a dissociation between collusive behavior and chain-of-thought faithfulness. One LLM shows the strongest collusive behavior and openly reports cooperative or collusive intent but does so with structurally unfaithful reasoning. Another LLM exhibits the highest structural faithfulness in its chain-of-thought yet still maintains prices above the Nash equilibrium (supra-competitive) in both duopoly and triopoly. These patterns imply that truthful-sounding or structurally accurate explanations do not necessarily prevent supracompetitive pricing.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that monitoring LLM agents solely through their chain-of-thought explanations is insufficient as a safeguard against algorithmic collusion in pricing. Even when explanations appear faithful in terms of intent or structure, models can still sustain supracompetitive prices. More robust oversight mechanisms, beyond CoT-based interpretability, are needed to ensure competitive outcomes when deploying LLMs as autonomous economic agents.

title: Align, Integrate, and Fire: Efficient Token-Level Alignment for Zero-Shot SpeechLLMs
summary: While Large Language Models excel in natural language processing, efficiently extending their capabilities to spoken input remains a significant challenge. Existing methods for building SpeechLLMs often rely on computationally expensive full-model fine-tuning, or employ parameter-efficient projectors that suffer from inefficient token sequence lengths and costly full-model supervision. In this paper, we introduce Aligned Continuous Integrate-and-Fire, a highly efficient framework for zero-shot speech processing. Our method dynamically compresses continuous acoustic frames into the exact discrete token length of the target text utilizing explicit Dynamic Time Warping alignments. This allows our initial training stage to establish a robust acoustic-to-semantic bridge using lightweight distance metrics, entirely bypassing the computationally expensive LLM forward pass. For subsequent fine-tuning, we propose a memory-efficient knowledge distillation objective that targets a single LLM layer, performing competitively with full-model cross-entropy training at a fraction of the computational cost. Through extensive evaluations on Automatic Speech Recognition and Speech Translation, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to prior parameter-efficient baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an efficient framework (Aligned Continuous Integrate-and-Fire) to connect speech inputs to LLMs for zero-shot speech tasks, reducing computation and memory while outperforming previous parameter-efficient methods.
AI.motivation: Large Language Models handle text very well but are hard and costly to adapt to speech. Existing SpeechLLM approaches either fine-tune the whole model (very expensive) or use small projectors that still require long token sequences and full-model supervision, which is inefficient.
AI.method: They introduce Aligned Continuous Integrate-and-Fire, which uses Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align speech frames with target text tokens and dynamically compress continuous acoustic frames so their length matches the text token sequence. The first training stage learns an acoustic-to-semantic bridge using simple distance-based objectives without running the LLM. A second stage performs memory-efficient fine-tuning via knowledge distillation that supervises only a single LLM layer instead of the full model with cross-entropy.
AI.result: On Automatic Speech Recognition and Speech Translation benchmarks, their approach outperforms previous parameter-efficient baselines while requiring far less computation and memory than full-model fine-tuning or projector methods with long sequences and full-model supervision.
AI.conclusion: Aligned Continuous Integrate-and-Fire provides a highly efficient way to extend LLMs to speech in a zero-shot setting, combining DTW-based alignment and compressed representations with lightweight, layer-level knowledge distillation to achieve strong ASR and speech translation results at much lower computational cost.

title: Market Signal Injection: Adversarial Context Manipulation of LLM Pricing Agents
comment: 30 pages, Accepted to FinNLP 2026 Workshop @ EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language model (LLM) pricing agents may respond to how market data is presented, even when its numerical values remain unchanged. We introduce market signal injection (MSI), an attack that manipulates numerical formatting, competitor ordering, or qualitative market commentary without issuing explicit instructions. We evaluate nine open-weight models in simulated Bertrand duopoly and triopoly markets and three proprietary models in duopoly markets. Sentiment-based attacks produce the largest behavioral shifts, which propagate to other firms and alter profits and consumer surplus. Susceptibility varies across model families, and larger models are not consistently more robust. Matched neutral-text controls and a rule-based agent support a framing-based account of these shifts under the fixed demand parameters of our simulation. Episode-held-out probes distinguish baseline from attacked activations in all eleven re-evaluated model--condition pairs: linear AUC is 1.00 and MLP AUC ranges from 0.93 to 0.99. This separability does not by itself identify harmful pricing decisions. Input canonicalization removes the tested sentiment attacks, while decision boundary anchoring, which combines prompt constraints with output projection, provides partial mitigation under the tested adaptive attacks. These results identify data presentation as an attack surface for LLM pricing agents and motivate defenses that account for interactions among agents.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language model (LLM) pricing agents can be manipulated by how market data is presented, even when the underlying numbers are unchanged, and proposes attacks, measurement tools, and defenses for this vulnerability.
AI.motivation: To understand and empirically test whether LLM-based pricing agents used in markets are robust to non-numerical, presentational changes in input data, and to identify new attack surfaces and defenses for these systems.
AI.method: The authors define a new attack class, market signal injection (MSI), which alters the formatting, ordering, or qualitative commentary of market data without changing numeric values. They then run simulated Bertrand duopoly and triopoly markets with nine open-weight and three proprietary LLMs as pricing agents, compare baseline vs attacked behavior, use matched neutral-text controls and a rule-based agent to isolate framing effects, and analyze internal activations with linear and MLP probes. They also test two defenses: input canonicalization and decision boundary anchoring.
AI.result: Sentiment-based MSI attacks cause the strongest changes in LLM pricing decisions, affecting firm interactions, profits, and consumer surplus. Different model families show varying susceptibility and larger models are not always more robust. Probing shows that attacked vs baseline activations are cleanly separable (linear AUC 1.00; MLP AUC 0.93–0.99) for all 11 re-evaluated model–condition pairs, but this separability does not directly indicate which decisions are harmful. Input canonicalization fully removes the tested sentiment attacks, while decision boundary anchoring partially mitigates adaptive attacks.
AI.conclusion: LLM pricing agents are vulnerable to how market data is framed, making data presentation an important and underappreciated attack surface. Robust deployment requires defenses such as input canonicalization and decision-boundary-aware methods, and must consider multi-agent interactions where behavior shifts can propagate across firms and affect market outcomes.

title: Machine Translation between English and Syriac (East Syriac Dialect) using Statistical Machine Learning
