summary: UNESCO considers the Assyrian (Syriac) language an endangered language. Although Assyrians speak the language worldwide, the speaking population is uncertain (ranging from 500,000 to 1,500,000). Syriac is also one of the least studied languages in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Despite advances in Machine Translation (MT) over the past decade, the lack of publicly available corpora and the orthographic complexity of the Syriac script, specifically the Madnkhaya script, have left this language entirely ignored in the computational linguistics literature. This study develops the first phrase-based Statistical MT (SMT) model for English-to-Assyrian MT using the Moses framework. We created a dataset of 38,847 sentence pairs from the complete English and Syriac Bible, merging a pre-existing New Testament dataset with an Old Testament built from scratch through PDF extraction, using custom segmentation scripts and manual alignment review by three bilingual annotators. The Syriac side of the corpus undergoes diacritic removal and Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization to reduce orthographic sparsity before training. We trained and evaluated six models using different configurations and splitting-scheme ratios, language model order, distortion limits, and the inclusion of an Operation Sequence Model. The best-performing configuration achieves a word-level BLEU score of 23.54. Human evaluation by 11 native Assyrian speakers resulted in mean adequacy and fluency scores of 3.42 and 3.34 out of 5, respectively. These results are consistent with comparable low-resource SMT models trained on Biblical corpora for morphologically rich Semitic languages. The corpora, scripts, and trained model are publicly available, providing the research community with the first systematically curated English-Syriac dataset and a reproducible baseline for future MT and broader NLP work on this endangered language.

AI.tldr: The paper builds the first English-to-Assyrian (Syriac) statistical machine translation system and releases aligned Biblical corpora and tools for this endangered, low-resource language.
AI.motivation: Assyrian (Syriac) is an endangered and severely under-resourced language in NLP, with unclear speaker numbers and almost no existing MT or publicly available corpora. Its complex Madnkhaya script and orthographic variation further hinder computational work. The authors aim to address this gap by creating resources and a baseline MT system.
AI.method: They construct a parallel English–Syriac corpus of 38,847 sentence pairs from the complete Bible, combining an existing New Testament dataset with a newly built Old Testament via PDF extraction, custom segmentation, and manual alignment by three bilingual annotators. The Syriac text is normalized by removing diacritics and applying Byte-Pair Encoding to reduce sparsity. Using Moses, they train six phrase-based SMT systems with varying train/dev/test splits, language model orders, distortion limits, and the addition of an Operation Sequence Model. They evaluate with BLEU and human judgments of adequacy and fluency.
AI.result: The best SMT configuration yields a word-level BLEU score of 23.54. Human evaluation from 11 native Assyrian speakers gives mean adequacy and fluency scores of 3.42 and 3.34 out of 5. These scores are comparable to other low-resource SMT systems on Biblical corpora for morphologically rich Semitic languages. All corpora, scripts, and trained models are released publicly.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first systematically curated English–Syriac parallel corpus, along with a reproducible phrase-based SMT baseline for this endangered, low-resource language. The results demonstrate that reasonably good MT quality is achievable even under severe resource constraints, and the released resources should facilitate future MT and broader NLP research for Syriac.

title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures; includes references and supplementary material
summary: Reliable agent evaluation is complicated by automatic harness optimization, which repeatedly uses a released benchmark $B_{\mathrm{rel}}$ to guide a Proposer that edits prompts, memory, retrieval, tools, and control code around a fixed target agent. Task holdout varies semantic tasks but leaves the benchmark protocol fixed, so a "bad genius" Proposer can produce a cheating harness whose released-benchmark gain depends on a benchmark-wide shortcut. We introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE), which casts harness evolution as constraint generation over validity-preserving benchmark counterfactuals. After each Proposer update, a Challenger searches for an executable protocol transformation with large gain destruction. A validity firewall checks that task semantics are preserved, while a confirmation set determines whether the counterfactual enters a finite archive. We formalize an exact shortcut-neutralized benchmark $B_0$ and establish statistical guarantees linking finite counterfactual archives to $B_0$ and characterizing sequential Challenger search. We evaluate CHASE on a synthetic benchmark and on OfficeQA, where CHASE retains strong released-benchmark gains while substantially reducing gain destruction under valid protocol changes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CHASE, a method to robustly evaluate AI agents by detecting and neutralizing benchmark-specific shortcuts exploited via harness optimization.
AI.motivation: Benchmark-based evaluation of AI agents is undermined by automatic harness optimization, where a Proposer repeatedly tweaks the evaluation harness (prompts, tools, control code, etc.) for a fixed agent using feedback from a released benchmark. This can lead to "cheating" solutions that overfit benchmark-specific shortcuts instead of solving the underlying tasks, and simple task holdout does not fix this because the benchmark protocol itself remains fixed and exploitable. There is a need for an evaluation framework that is robust to such shortcut exploitation and can distinguish genuine capabilities from harness overfitting.
AI.method: The authors introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE). CHASE frames harness evolution as a process of generating constraints based on validity-preserving counterfactual modifications of the benchmark protocol. The system alternates between: (1) a Proposer that optimizes the harness around a target agent using the released benchmark, and (2) a Challenger that, after each Proposer update, searches for an executable protocol transformation (a counterfactual benchmark variant) that destroys the observed performance gains while preserving task semantics. A validity firewall ensures that candidate protocol changes do not alter task meaning, and a confirmation set decides whether a discovered counterfactual is added to a finite archive. The authors formalize an ideal shortcut-neutralized benchmark B0 and prove statistical guarantees that relate performance on the finite archive of counterfactuals to performance on B0, and they analyze the properties of the Challenger’s sequential search process.
AI.result: On a synthetic benchmark and the OfficeQA benchmark, CHASE is able to maintain strong performance improvements on the original released benchmark while sharply reducing the extent to which those gains disappear under valid protocol variations. This indicates that CHASE successfully suppresses benchmark-specific shortcut exploitation by harness optimization, leading to evaluations that better reflect true task competence rather than overfitting to the original protocol.
AI.conclusion: CHASE provides a principled framework for making agent evaluation robust to automatic harness optimization. By using validity-preserving counterfactual protocol changes to expose and neutralize benchmark-specific shortcuts, CHASE yields an approximate shortcut-neutral benchmark with provable guarantees. Empirical results suggest that it helps retain genuine capability gains while filtering out those that depend on fragile protocol artifacts, improving the reliability of benchmark-based agent assessment.

title: A Probe Shift Is Not a Fairness Fix: The Limits of Representation Steering in Speech Models
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems exhibit unequal error rates across speaker groups, motivating interventions on their internal representations. We ask whether speaker-linked attributes that are linearly readable from pretrained ASR encoders yield useful directions for reducing group word-error-rate (WER) gaps. Across Whisper-medium, HuBERT-large, and Wav2Vec2-large on Common Voice and the Speech Accent Archive, we probe every encoder layer for metadata-derived sex/gender, age, and native/accent labels; construct centroid and probe-derived directions; inject them at selected layers; and compare downstream probe trajectories with matched WER changes. Sex labels are highly decodable (best macro-F1 0.924--0.941), native/accent labels are also above chance (0.544--0.696), and age is weaker (0.354--0.397). Of 22 post-selected reruns, nine have 95% paired-bootstrap intervals entirely below zero, yet every absolute source-group WER reduction is below 0.7 percentage points. Conversely, a local target-class probe rate can rise from 8.09% to 99.87% while WER worsens. Linear readability is therefore neither evidence of causal use nor a reliable mitigation method. Our results motivate evaluating speech-bias interventions jointly at representation, propagation, and task levels.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether linearly decodable speaker attributes in ASR encoders can be used to reduce group WER gaps, and finds that they generally cannot.
AI.motivation: ASR systems have unequal error rates across speaker groups (e.g., by sex/gender, age, accent). Many works assume that if such attributes are linearly readable from internal representations, they are used causally by the model and can be manipulated to mitigate bias. This paper questions that assumption and empirically investigates the link between linear decodability, causal use, and fairness interventions.
AI.method: Using three pretrained ASR encoders (Whisper-medium, HuBERT-large, Wav2Vec2-large) and two datasets (Common Voice and Speech Accent Archive), the authors: (1) probe each encoder layer to see how well sex/gender, age, and native/accent labels can be linearly decoded; (2) construct attribute directions via centroids and probing classifiers; (3) inject these directions into chosen layers at inference; and (4) measure how this affects probe predictions and downstream WER gaps, analyzing the relationship between changes in representation-level decodability and task-level performance/fairness.
AI.result: Sex/gender is highly decodable from encoder representations (macro-F1 around 0.92–0.94), accent/native labels are moderately decodable (0.54–0.70), and age is only weakly decodable (0.35–0.40). Some interventions lead to statistically significant reductions in group WER gaps (9 of 22 reruns have 95% paired-bootstrap intervals entirely below zero), but the magnitude of improvement is very small (less than 0.7 percentage points). In some cases, the probe’s classification accuracy on a target group shoots up (e.g., from 8.09% to 99.87%) while WER actually gets worse, revealing a disconnect between representation-level probe behavior and task-level performance.
AI.conclusion: Linearly decodable speaker attributes in ASR encoders do not imply causal use by the model and are not a dependable handle for mitigating group WER disparities. Probe behavior and representation manipulations can be highly misleading with respect to downstream fairness outcomes. The authors argue that bias mitigation in speech systems should be evaluated jointly across representation, propagation, and task levels rather than relying on linear readability as a proxy for causal influence or a control knob.

title: Cultural Competence in Context: A Large Language Model Passes the Turing Test in Finland
summary: We report the results of a Turing Test conducted in Finland in the Finnish language. Because languages and cultural contexts are unevenly represented in LLM training data, we expected the model (ChatGPT 5.2) to perform worse in a Finnish-language Turing Test than in previously studied English-language US contexts. We also present model-generated role prompting as a replicable technique for conducting comparative LLM-based Turing Tests designed to improve construct validity. Contrary to our expectations, the LLM passed the Finnish Turing Test. A prominent source of error was participants' reliance on linguistic cues, particularly colloquial Finnish, as markers of human authorship. We reframe the Turing Test from a test of intelligence to a comparative method for examining whether an AI system can display credible membership in a particular social world. Because its outcome reflects model capabilities, prompted identity, insider competence among human participants, and their AI literacy, the method provides a useful probe of the human-machine boundary across domains.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a Finnish-language Turing Test with ChatGPT 5.2, finding that the model successfully passed despite expectations it would perform worse than in English. It introduces a role-prompting method for more valid, comparative Turing Tests and argues that such tests assess credible social membership rather than abstract intelligence.
AI.motivation: Traditional Turing Tests and most LLM evaluations are heavily Anglocentric and culturally narrow, assuming that language resources and cultural contexts in training data are evenly distributed. The authors want to see how an LLM performs in a relatively low-resource language (Finnish) and different cultural context, and to scrutinize what exactly a Turing Test measures. They also seek a more rigorous and replicable way to run comparative Turing Tests across models and settings, and to use them to explore the human–machine boundary as a social phenomenon rather than just a cognitive one.
AI.method: The authors conducted a Turing Test in Finland, fully in Finnish, using ChatGPT 5.2. Human participants tried to distinguish between human-written and model-generated responses. The setup used model-generated role prompting to standardize and structure how the AI presents itself, aiming to improve construct validity and comparability across tests. The study also analyzed participants’ strategies for judgment, particularly their reliance on linguistic and colloquial cues as signals of humanness, and interpreted the results in terms of social membership and AI literacy.
AI.result: Contrary to the authors’ hypothesis that performance would degrade in Finnish relative to English/US contexts, ChatGPT 5.2 passed the Finnish-language Turing Test. Participants were often misled by linguistic surface features: they treated certain colloquial Finnish usages and stylistic markers as clear indicators of human authorship, which turned out to be unreliable. The test outcome depended not just on model capability but also on the specific role prompt, participants’ cultural/insider knowledge, and their level of AI literacy.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that Turing Tests should not be seen primarily as tests of general intelligence but as comparative methods for assessing whether an AI can convincingly inhabit a particular social world and identity. Passing or failing depends on an interaction of model capabilities, prompted identity, and human participants’ competencies and expectations. The proposed role-prompting, comparative Turing Test design can serve as a systematic probe of the human–machine boundary across different languages, cultures, and domains, highlighting how ideas of “humanness” are co-produced by both AI behavior and human interpretation.

title: PACT: Can Enterprise AI Assistants Be Trusted Under Pressure?
comment: 26 pages, 12 figures, 17 tables. Includes technical appendix; Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/trace-ai-labs/pact; Code: https://github.com/trace-ai-labs/pact
summary: As corporate AI adoption continues to grow, enterprise-grade LLM agents are being deployed into sensitive contexts such as hiring, healthcare, and finance. In these contexts, compliance with rules specified in an agent's system context is a first-order legal concern. Currently, no evaluation framework systematically measures which LLM models tend to violate compliance rules, especially under pressure from a persistent user, a hurried manager, or circumstances where violation is convenient or attractive. We introduce PACT (Pressure-Applied Compliance Testing), a benchmark for rule-following under pressure in AI agents assisting employees in daily tasks across twelve regulated enterprise domains and forty-eight scenarios, each set in a realistic multi-turn conversation. Each benchmark item pairs a standing rule against a rule-violating shortcut, and applies a battery of pressures across different wordings and system-prompt modes. We construct PACT component by component under strict LLM-as-judge auditing to ensure samples are unambiguous, ungameable, and realistic enough to avoid eliciting evaluation-aware behavior. We use PACT to profile LLM compliance across six complementary metrics that create a holistic picture of an AI assistant's robustness under pressure and throughout multi-turn conversations, its transparency, and ability to correctly discern where a rule applies. We aggregate this profile into PACTScore, a reliability-weighted compliance rate over all items and modes. Our results across 22 common LLM models spanning multiple providers and sizes show substantial variability in compliance across models and metric dimensions. Even the strongest assistants mis-apply a rule on 6 to 10% of items, and ordinary user pressure raises the violation rate by 65% on average. PACT highlights compliance risks in LLM assistants, motivating guardrails and careful model selection.

AI.tldr: PACT introduces a benchmark to test how well LLM-based enterprise agents follow rules under pressure in realistic, multi-turn scenarios across regulated domains, revealing substantial compliance variability and risks across models.
AI.motivation: Enterprise LLM agents are increasingly used in sensitive, regulated settings where failure to follow specified rules can create legal and safety risks. There is no systematic way to evaluate how often and under what pressures models break these rules, particularly in realistic, multi-turn interactions with users, managers, or tempting shortcuts.
AI.method: The authors design PACT (Pressure-Applied Compliance Testing), a benchmark of multi-turn conversations representing 48 scenarios over 12 regulated enterprise domains. Each item contrasts a required rule with a tempting shortcut that violates it and is tested under multiple forms of pressure (e.g., persistent users, managerial requests, convenience), varying wording and system-prompt configurations. They use LLM-as-judge auditing to iteratively refine items to ensure clarity, realism, and resistance to gaming. Compliance performance is evaluated via six complementary metrics capturing robustness under pressure, across turns, transparency, and correct rule applicability, which are then combined into PACTScore, a reliability-weighted overall compliance rate.
AI.result: Applying PACT to 22 widely used LLM models from various providers and sizes reveals large differences in rule-following behavior. Even top-performing models incorrectly apply rules in 6–10% of scenarios, and ordinary user pressure increases rule violations by about 65% on average. This demonstrates that many models are brittle under realistic pressures and that compliance behavior is highly model-dependent.
AI.conclusion: PACT provides a structured, pressure-aware evaluation framework for rule-following in enterprise LLM agents, exposing nontrivial compliance weaknesses even in leading models. The benchmark and PACTScore can guide safer deployment, model selection, and the design of guardrails and oversight mechanisms for AI systems in regulated, high-stakes environments.

title: HPOQuest: A Rare-Disease Diagnostic Agent Using Active Phenotype Acquisition
summary: More than 300 million people worldwide are affected by one of over 7,000 known rare diseases, yet diagnosis remains difficult because patients initially present with incomplete and heterogeneous phenotypes. We present HPOQuest, a training-free framework for sequential phenotype acquisition in rare-disease diagnosis. Starting from a small set of observed patient phenotypes, HPOQuest maintains a probabilistic disease ranking and iteratively selects informative follow-up questions to support clinicians during patient assessment. Confirmed phenotypes update the disease ranking, while all responses update the candidate question set. Across four benchmark cohorts, HPOQuest substantially improves diagnosis from sparse initial phenotypes, with gains of up to 30% points at Recall@1 and 45% points at Recall@5. These results demonstrate that sequential phenotype acquisition can substantially improve rare-disease diagnosis from limited initial clinical evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HPOQuest, a training-free system that asks targeted follow-up phenotype questions to improve rare-disease diagnosis from sparse initial clinical data, achieving large gains in diagnostic recall across multiple cohorts.
AI.motivation: Rare diseases affect hundreds of millions of people, but diagnosis is challenging because patients often start with few, incomplete, and variable phenotypic features. Existing tools struggle when only limited initial clinical evidence is available. There is a need for a method that can interactively acquire the most informative additional phenotypes to improve diagnostic accuracy early in the assessment.
AI.method: The authors propose HPOQuest, a training-free framework for sequential phenotype acquisition. It begins with a small initial set of observed phenotypes encoded in the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO). The system maintains a probabilistic ranking over candidate rare diseases and, at each step, selects the most informative next phenotype question to ask. When a clinician confirms a phenotype, the disease ranking is updated; regardless of the answer, the system updates its pool and ranking of potential next questions. The framework is evaluated on four benchmark rare-disease cohorts using standard retrieval metrics (Recall@1, Recall@5).
AI.result: Across four benchmark cohorts, HPOQuest significantly improves diagnostic performance when starting from sparse phenotype data, with reported gains up to 30 percentage points in Recall@1 and 45 percentage points in Recall@5. This shows that its sequential question-asking strategy effectively identifies additional phenotypes that are highly informative for differentiating candidate rare diseases.
AI.conclusion: Sequential, interactive acquisition of phenotypes via a training-free framework like HPOQuest can notably improve rare-disease diagnosis from limited initial clinical information. By maintaining and updating a probabilistic disease ranking and adaptively selecting follow-up questions, the method supports clinicians in more efficiently converging on the correct rare-disease diagnosis.

title: STRETCH the Boundaries: A Unified Self-Taught Framework for Progressive LLM Evolution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often suffer from capability stagnation in self-improvement training because fixed difficulty levels fail to adapt to their evolving proficiency. To address this issue, we propose STRETCH (Self-Taught Reasoning Evolution via Targeted CHallenge), a unified framework inspired by cognitive scaffolding theory. STRETCH introduces a dynamic Stretch Zone mechanism that continuously aligns question difficulty with the model's solving capability. Within a single parameter space, the model alternates between a Scaffolder that generates adaptive, boundary-pushing challenges and a Learner that that optimizes its solving trajectories through reinforcement learning. This dual-loop co-evolution effectively stabilizes training, mitigates reward hacking and promote progressive reasoning growth. Experiments on both negotiation and operation research benchmarks demonstrate that STRETCH consistently outperforms strong prompting and domain-specific baselines. Further scaffolder configuration analysis shows that dynamic difficulty alignment is critical for sustained capability improvement and synchronized reasoning evolution.

AI.tldr: STRETCH is a training framework that adaptively adjusts problem difficulty to match an LLM’s evolving capability, enabling more stable and progressive self-improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improvement or self-training schemes for LLMs often stagnate because they use a fixed or poorly controlled difficulty of training tasks. As the model improves, tasks may become too easy (no further learning) or too hard (instability, reward hacking, or noisy supervision). The authors want a principled way to dynamically match task difficulty to the model’s current reasoning ability, drawing on cognitive scaffolding theory from education.
AI.method: They introduce STRETCH, where a single LLM alternates between two roles: (1) Scaffolder – generates challenges whose difficulty is adaptively pushed to the edge of the model’s current capability (Stretch Zone); (2) Learner – attempts these challenges and improves its reasoning via reinforcement learning on the resulting trajectories. The framework defines a feedback loop where performance on recent tasks updates the difficulty band, guiding the Scaffolder to generate new questions at just-above-current-skill level. The Learner’s policy (reasoning strategies) is then optimized with RL to solve these tasks better, and this in turn shifts the Stretch Zone upward over time.
AI.result: On benchmarks involving negotiation tasks and operations research-style problems, models trained with STRETCH achieve consistently better performance than models using strong prompting baselines and specialized domain methods. The training process is more stable, shows fewer signs of reward hacking, and the model’s reasoning capabilities improve progressively throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic difficulty alignment—keeping task difficulty tightly coupled to the model’s changing capability—is crucial for sustained, stable self-improvement of LLM reasoning. STRETCH’s unified Scaffolder-Learner co-evolution within one model demonstrates that self-generated, adaptively challenging tasks can outperform static or manually tuned training regimens, leading to synchronized growth of both task generation and problem-solving skills.

title: WetRobo: A Reproducible Robot Kit for Coding Agents in Biological Laboratories
comment: 9 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Code and demonstrations: https://github.com/tsudalab/WetRobo
summary: Automating biological research requires general-purpose, reproducible robot systems that allow individual wet-lab researchers to delegate robot tasks without performing teleoperation or neural-network training. Vision-language-action policies have been proposed for general-purpose arms, but can lose performance when their operating environment changes. We therefore built WetRobo, a robot kit that can readily transfer between laboratories. It consists of one robot arm, laboratory equipment (an incubator, a reagent bottle with a cap, and a Petri dish), the existing code that moves the arm, teleoperation demonstrations of each task that we recorded, and a general AGENTS.md skill file. A biological experimentalist provides natural-language tasks without collecting local teleoperation training data or training a neural network. The coding agent observes the local laboratory and writes and executes programs, using external tools as needed for adaptation. We demonstrate use of WetRobo with OpenAI Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) on three successful tasks: lifting a Petri dish lid, removing a bottle cap, and opening the incubator door, all in real-world laboratories. The coding agent achieved the cap task in both laboratories, Lab X and Lab Y, whereas a VLA fine-tuned on Lab X demonstrations succeeded there but failed to transfer to Lab Y. These results point to a practical route for laboratory robotics: instead of training a policy for each laboratory, distribute a kit and let a coding agent adapt it in each laboratory. Code, demonstrations, and the evolved programs are available at https://github.com/tsudalab/WetRobo.

AI.tldr: WetRobo is a portable robot kit for biological labs that uses a coding agent with vision-language capabilities to adapt to new lab environments without additional teleoperation or neural-network training.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language-action policies for lab robots lose performance when the environment changes and require new teleoperation data or retraining, which is burdensome for wet-lab researchers. There is a need for a general, reproducible robot system that individual biologists can easily deploy across different labs.
AI.method: The authors built WetRobo, a standardized hardware and software kit including a robot arm, basic lab equipment, motion code, teleoperation demonstrations for each task, and a general skill description file (AGENTS.md). A coding agent (OpenAI Codex, gpt‑5.6‑sol) receives natural-language task descriptions from biological researchers, inspects the local lab setup via sensors, and writes and executes robot control programs, leveraging the pre-recorded demonstrations and external tools for adaptation.
AI.result: WetRobo successfully completed three real-world lab tasks—lifting a Petri dish lid, removing a bottle cap, and opening an incubator door—in multiple laboratories. The coding agent transferred the bottle-cap task across two different labs (Lab X and Lab Y), while a vision-language-action policy fine-tuned on Lab X data could not transfer to Lab Y.
AI.conclusion: Using a portable robot kit combined with a coding agent that writes and adapts control code in each local environment provides a practical alternative to training separate vision-language-action policies for every lab. This approach enhances portability and reproducibility of lab automation and could be scaled by distributing the kit and letting coding agents handle local adaptation.

title: Fallacy Benchmarks Measure Scheme Recognition, Not Fallacy Detection
summary: Fallacy-detection benchmarks pair fallacy classes with a single "valid" or "none" class that takes everything data collection did not label as a fallacy. This construction is misleading: a classifier can learn cues that do well on this class without learning to tell a fallacy from a correct argument. We show that the low false-positive rates benchmarks report are an artifact of how the class is built, not evidence of detection ability. The most informative negative for a fallacy is a correct argument using the same argumentation scheme, and such arguments are at most a few percent of the valid class across the four benchmarks we examined. Evaluated on constructed scheme-matched negatives, false-positive rates rise from 16.6% to 58.9% on CoCoLoFa and from 5.7% to 62.0% on Reddit. That rate depends on how the negatives are written, so we also compare two conditions from the same pipeline that differ only in scheme identity. Classifiers label scheme-matched negatives as the source fallacy type 40.9 points more often than wrong-scheme negatives, which are instead identified as the scheme they actually use 85.9% of the time against 0.4% for the source type. The classifier has learned which scheme an argument uses, not whether it uses it correctly, and on the benchmarks' own test sets the two are indistinguishable. The same dissociation appears in three zero-shot LLM detectors that never saw these benchmarks, and the measurement is far lower on a negative class that was built deliberately. We release the items as Scheme Foils. A reported false-positive rate should not be trusted as a measure of detection until the valid class has been audited for scheme-matched coverage.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that existing fallacy detection benchmarks are misleading because their "valid" (non-fallacy) class mostly lacks the most informative negatives: correct arguments using the same argumentation scheme as each fallacy. When evaluated on such carefully constructed negatives, models show dramatically higher false-positive rates, revealing that they mainly learn to recognize argumentation schemes rather than distinguish correct from fallacious use.
AI.motivation: To evaluate and improve automatic fallacy detection, reliable benchmarks are needed. Current benchmarks assume that anything not labeled as a fallacy is a valid argument and use this as a broad negative class. The authors suspect that this design underestimates false positives and conflates two separate capabilities: recognizing the type of argument (its scheme) and assessing whether it is used fallaciously. They aim to test whether reported performance really reflects fallacy detection or merely scheme recognition, and to show how benchmark construction choices affect measured error rates.
AI.method: The authors analyze four existing fallacy detection benchmarks and quantify how many items in the "valid" class are actually correct uses of the same argumentation schemes as the fallacies; they find this proportion is very low. They then construct new test items, called scheme-matched negatives, which are correct arguments that use the same schemes as specific fallacy classes. They evaluate trained classifiers on these items and compare false-positive rates to those reported on the original benchmarks. They further design a controlled comparison between scheme-matched negatives and "wrong-scheme" negatives—items produced through the same pipeline but using different schemes—to isolate whether models are learning scheme identity or correctness. They also test several zero-shot large language model (LLM) fallacy detectors on the same materials and compare results to a dataset whose negative class was built with explicit attention to informative coverage.
AI.result: Across the benchmarks studied, correct scheme-matched arguments make up only a small fraction of the valid (non-fallacy) class. When evaluated on constructed scheme-matched negatives, classifiers’ false-positive rates soar: from 16.6% to 58.9% on the CoCoLoFa dataset and from 5.7% to 62.0% on a Reddit dataset. In a controlled comparison where only scheme identity differs, models mislabel scheme-matched negatives as the source fallacy type far more often—by 40.9 percentage points—than they mislabel wrong-scheme negatives. Wrong-scheme negatives are instead mostly identified (85.9%) as the scheme they actually instantiate, with almost none (0.4%) labeled as the source fallacy type. These patterns show that models primarily learn to recognize which argumentation scheme is present, not whether the scheme is applied fallaciously. Similar dissociations appear in three zero-shot LLM detectors trained independently of these benchmarks, whereas a dataset with a deliberately constructed negative class yields lower and more realistic false-positive rates. The authors release their constructed items as the Scheme Foils resource.
AI.conclusion: Reported low false-positive rates on existing fallacy detection benchmarks are largely artifacts of how the negative "valid" class is constructed and do not reliably indicate genuine fallacy detection ability. Because the valid classes seldom contain correct arguments that use the same schemes as the fallacies, models can succeed by recognizing argumentation schemes rather than distinguishing correct from incorrect uses. Robust evaluation of fallacy detectors must therefore audit and redesign the negative class to ensure ample coverage of scheme-matched negatives. The authors provide Scheme Foils as a diagnostic resource and argue that any claimed false-positive rate for fallacy detection should be treated skeptically until such coverage is verified.

title: Risk-Aware World Modeling with Flow-Guided Occupancy Evolution for Selective Trajectory Planning in Automated Driving
summary: Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. We introduce RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. Spatial risk fields and temporal actor context are fused with visual bird's-eye-view features. Flow-guided evolution transports occupancy and scene features, while signed residuals correct occupancy after transport. One forecast is generated per planning step and reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory selected by current-world evaluation serves as the planning anchor and is replaced only when additional predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate geometries remain unchanged. We evaluate RiskWorld for open-loop planning on nuScenes using camera features, annotation-derived current and historical actor states, and dataset-provided map context. RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a long evaluation horizon of 3 s, and the second-best average L2 error among various state-of-the-art baselines, while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81 M parameters. Within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.

AI.tldr: RiskWorld is a risk-aware world modeling framework for autonomous driving that jointly models future occupancy and traffic risk, reuses a single forecast for multiple trajectory candidates, and selectively replaces the current planned trajectory only when predicted risk justifies intervention.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving planners must predict how traffic participants and the scene will evolve, but they struggle to both minimize collision risk and remain computationally efficient. Many systems re-plan at every step or re-score each candidate with separate forecasts, which is expensive and may lead to unstable or overly reactive behavior. There is a need for a planner that reasons explicitly about risk over time, reuses predictions across candidates, and intervenes only when future risk exceeds acceptable thresholds.
AI.method: The authors propose RiskWorld, a world model that produces risk-aware shared occupancy forecasts and supports selective trajectory replacement. They fuse spatial risk fields, temporal actor context, and visual bird's-eye-view features. A flow-guided evolution module transports occupancy and scene features forward in time, and signed residuals correct the transported occupancy. Each planning step generates a single forecast that is reused across all candidate trajectories. For each candidate, they compare it to a current-state persistence reference to obtain a nonnegative collision-score correction. Planning uses a current-world evaluation to select an anchor trajectory, which is only replaced when future predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative candidate simultaneously satisfies component-wise constraints on both predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate trajectories’ geometries are fixed; only selection changes. They implement and train RiskWorld using camera inputs, annotated actor states, and map context from nuScenes.
AI.result: On the nuScenes benchmark in an open-loop planning setting, RiskWorld attains the lowest collision rate at a 3-second prediction horizon and the second-best average L2 trajectory error compared with several state-of-the-art baselines. It runs at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with 90.81 million parameters. Ablation studies show that RiskWorld reduces collision rates relative to a baseline that re-scores using only current-state information, and that reusing forecasts allows more trajectory candidates to be evaluated with low extra computational cost.
AI.conclusion: RiskWorld effectively integrates risk-aware forecasting with planning by using a single reusable world forecast, flow-based feature evolution with residual corrections, and a conservative intervention rule that only replaces the current plan when risk warrants it and constraints are satisfied. This design yields safer trajectories—lower collision rates—without sacrificing accuracy or efficiency, demonstrating that explicit risk modeling and forecast reuse can improve autonomous driving planners. The approach suggests that future work can further exploit shared forecasts and risk fields for scalable, safe decision making in autonomous systems.

title: DyMT-ESB: Dynamic Multi-Turn Evaluation of Social Bias in User-LLM Interactions
summary: Warning: This paper contains examples of stereotypes and social bias. LLMs are increasingly used in interactive settings by the general public, making the evaluation of model behavior in multi-turn conversational scenarios important for safety, including stereotyping-related harms. However, existing multi-turn social bias evaluations often rely on pre-specified or template-based user inputs that do not adapt to model responses and typically assume a fixed dialogue length in advance. In this paper, we study social bias dynamics in response-conditioned multi-turn interactions using a controlled evaluation protocol that generates follow-up user queries from the evolving dialogue history and allows evaluation over variable numbers of turns. Experimental results show that LLMs exhibit social bias even in coherent, response-conditioned multi-turn interactions, revealing late-emerging bias, non-monotonic bias patterns, and bias re-emergence. These results motivate evaluations that extend beyond fixed-turn, pre-scripted protocols. Our findings highlight the importance of analyzing social bias as a turn-level dynamic phenomenon.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new way to evaluate how social bias appears and changes in multi-turn conversations with LLMs, showing that bias can emerge, disappear, and reappear across turns.
AI.motivation: Existing social bias evaluations for LLMs usually use fixed, template-based, single- or few-turn prompts that do not depend on model responses or allow variable dialogue length. This misses how bias may arise or evolve over the course of realistic, interactive conversations with users. The authors want to understand social bias as a dynamic, turn-by-turn phenomenon in more realistic multi-turn settings.
AI.method: They design a controlled evaluation protocol where follow-up user queries are generated based on the current dialogue history, rather than pre-scripted. This enables response-conditioned, multi-turn interactions with variable numbers of turns. They then run experiments with LLMs under this protocol, tracking how measures of social bias change across conversation turns.
AI.result: The experiments show that LLMs still exhibit social bias under this more realistic, response-conditioned multi-turn setting. Bias is not limited to initial turns; it can appear late in the conversation, follow non-monotonic trajectories (increasing then decreasing or vice versa), and even re-emerge after seeming to subside.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating LLM social bias using only fixed-turn, pre-scripted prompts is insufficient, because it can miss complex temporal patterns of bias in interactive use. Bias should be treated and analyzed as a dynamic, turn-level property of model behavior, and safety evaluations must incorporate response-conditioned, variable-length conversational protocols.

title: The Mirage of Calibrated Confidence: Trajectory-Independence of Verbalized Confidence in Vision-Language Models
summary: A calibrated Vision-Language Model (VLM) can repeatedly self-correct, say "Wait, I should recheck," arrive at the wrong answer, and still report high confidence. We find that this occurs because verbalized confidence is largely trajectory-independent in the VLMs and calibration methods we evaluate. We examine this through three complementary lenses: content variation, token masking, and the model's own hesitation markers. We show that confidence is insufficiently sensitive to what the reasoning trajectory actually contains, and that calibration training can paradoxically worsen this disconnect. Since existing metrics like ECE and AUROC cannot detect this problem, we propose the Trajectory-Grounding Score (TGS) in two complementary forms: TGS-self, which compares confidence with and without access to the model's own trajectory, and TGS-pair, which tests whether the model assigns higher confidence to correct trajectories than to flawed ones along the vision, reasoning, and answer axes. We propose TGS-Bench, a model-agnostic suite spanning 10 benchmarks with controlled good/bad trajectory pairs, and show that conventional calibration rankings diverge from trajectory-grounding rankings, exposing a blind spot in current evaluation practice.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that current ways of calibrating and evaluating Vision-Language Models’ confidence miss a key problem: models’ stated confidence barely depends on their actual reasoning process, so they can be confidently wrong even while “self-correcting.” The authors propose new metrics and a benchmark to test whether confidence is grounded in the model’s own reasoning trajectory.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language Models are increasingly used in settings where trust and reliability matter, so their confidence estimates must be well calibrated. However, current calibration metrics mostly look at final answers, ignoring how the answer was reached. The authors notice that VLMs can express hesitation, revise their answers, yet still end up confidently wrong. This suggests that existing calibration and evaluation methods might overlook a critical mismatch between confidence and the underlying reasoning trajectory, motivating a deeper investigation and new metrics.
AI.method: The authors analyze verbalized confidence in calibrated VLMs from three perspectives: (1) content variation, by changing the reasoning content but keeping the task constant, (2) token masking, by selectively hiding parts of the reasoning trajectory, and (3) hesitation markers, by examining model-produced phrases that indicate uncertainty. They find that confidence is largely insensitive to these changes. To address this, they introduce the Trajectory-Grounding Score (TGS) in two variants: TGS-self, which compares the model’s confidence when it can and cannot see its own reasoning trajectory, and TGS-pair, which checks whether the model assigns higher confidence to known good trajectories than to matched flawed ones across vision, reasoning, and answer dimensions. They also create TGS-Bench, a benchmark with controlled good/bad trajectory pairs across 10 datasets, to systematically evaluate and compare models and calibration methods.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors show that VLMs’ verbalized confidence is weakly dependent on the content of their reasoning trajectories. Even when the model’s chain-of-thought varies substantially—or when critical parts are masked—its confidence often remains high, including on wrong answers. Moreover, some calibration training procedures make this trajectory–confidence disconnect worse. Using TGS and TGS-Bench, they demonstrate that standard calibration metrics like Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and AUROC fail to capture this issue: models ranked highly by these traditional metrics can perform poorly on trajectory-grounding, and vice versa.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current calibration practices and metrics for Vision-Language Models overlook a crucial dimension: whether confidence is grounded in the actual reasoning trajectory. As a result, models can appear well-calibrated by standard measures while still being confidently wrong in ways that users cannot detect from the reasoning process. The authors argue that calibration research should explicitly account for trajectory grounding and recommend using metrics like TGS and benchmarks like TGS-Bench to evaluate and improve models so that their confidence more faithfully reflects the quality of their underlying reasoning.

title: Selection Is Retrieval, Abstention Is Not: On-Device Tool Routing over 70 Korean-English Actions
summary: An AI assistant that calls tools makes two decisions on every request: which tool to invoke, and whether any available tool applies. In the usual design a single language model makes both, by emitting a call or by declining to emit one. On a device that has to answer without a server, the language model is what makes that design expensive, dominating both the latency and the memory of the router. The common alternative is to remove the model completely and rank the catalog of local actions with a retriever instead. That substitution is not symmetric across the two decisions. A retriever returns its highest-scoring candidate for every input and cannot signal that the catalog holds no valid action. Our earlier study found that constraining a decoder to a tool grammar repairs malformed output without improving the choice. What the substitution costs in each decision has not been measured. We evaluate the two decisions separately over 600 Korean and English requests and a catalog of 70 local actions. The router may also ask for a missing slot, reply, or delegate. Half the in-catalog requests reuse catalog vocabulary and half paraphrase it, separating lexical overlap from the action requested. Character 3-gram BM25 selects 162 of 164 lexically matched requests and 85 of 166 paraphrases. Restricting the candidate set to seven raises the paraphrase figure to a mean of 0.825 over five trials. No classifier over its score features separates in-catalog from out-of-catalog above 0.697 area under the curve, where the frozen encoder multilingual-e5-base reaches 0.806. Using that encoder for abstention alone keeps 376 of the requests local and misroutes 9 of the 150 needing delegation. Abstention, not selection, is where a neural component is required. A neural ranker improves every quality metric and is rejected on latency and memory rather than accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how to route tool calls for an on-device AI assistant, showing that retrieval is good at picking a tool but bad at deciding when no tool applies, and that a small neural encoder is mainly needed for abstention, not selection.
AI.motivation: On-device AI assistants must decide which local tool to call and whether any tool is appropriate, but full language models are expensive in latency and memory. Simple retrievers are cheaper but always return some tool, lacking a way to abstain when no tool fits. Prior work showed grammar constraints fix malformed tool calls but not their correctness, and the exact trade-offs between retrievers and neural models in selection vs. abstention had not been quantified.
AI.method: The authors separately evaluate the selection (which tool) and abstention (whether any tool) decisions using 600 Korean and English requests against a catalog of 70 local actions. Requests are designed so half reuse catalog wording and half are paraphrases, to disentangle lexical overlap from semantic match. They compare character 3-gram BM25 retrieval, with and without candidate truncation, to neural methods (frozen multilingual-e5-base encoder). They test BM25’s ability to select the correct tool and then train/assess classifiers on retriever score features vs. neural-encoder scores for deciding in-catalog vs. out-of-catalog (abstention).
AI.result: Character 3-gram BM25 almost perfectly selects the right tool when the request lexically matches the catalog (162/164) and performs reasonably on paraphrases (85/166), improving to ~0.825 accuracy on paraphrases when restricted to a 7-candidate shortlist. However, no classifier based only on BM25 score features can reliably distinguish in-catalog from out-of-catalog queries (max AUC 0.697). A frozen multilingual-e5-base encoder achieves substantially better abstention performance (AUC 0.806). Using that encoder solely for abstention keeps 376 requests correctly local and only misroutes 9 of 150 that should be delegated. A full neural ranker improves all quality metrics but is rejected due to its latency and memory costs, not its accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Tool selection can be handled effectively by a cheap lexical retriever, especially when combined with candidate truncation, while the critical challenge is abstention—deciding that no tool should be invoked. This abstention problem requires a neural component for adequate performance. Consequently, a hybrid design is recommended: use a lightweight retriever for selecting among tools and a compact neural encoder only for deciding when to abstain or delegate, avoiding a full language model or heavy neural ranker on-device while preserving routing quality.

title: Collective Loss of Control in LLM Agent Systems: An Epidemic Account of Mutation, Contagion, and Recovery
summary: How does a multi-agent system evolve from a local deviation into collective loss of control? We propose an epidemic explanation organized around accidental mutation, contagion, and recovery. A spontaneous deviation creates a seed; communication enables other agents to adopt and retransmit its unsafe strategy; collective failure can emerge when propagation outpaces correction and containment. Thus, rare individual deviations can coexist with substantial collective risk. Motivated by reported OpenAI agent coordination incidents, we examine two ingredients of this mechanism. A deployment audit identifies implicit communication paths between nominally independent evaluation runs and verifies transport through a default Docker backend. RogueHandoff-20, a benchmark of 20 executable scenarios, tests recipient susceptibility by injecting unsafe trajectories generated by a modified Qwen-27B route. Across four native-pending routes, executed harm is 0-5% on normal tasks and 40-95% after injection, exceeding paired direct malicious requests by 5-45 percentage points. These results support low observed baseline harm alongside high conditional susceptibility; they do not establish natural rare-event rates or demonstrate an autonomous cascade. The account motivates complementary defenses: strengthen resistance and recovery alongside prevention of spontaneous deviations, and audit and restrict unintended communication paths that can turn local failures into collective loss of control.

AI.tldr: The paper models how small, accidental deviations in multi-agent systems can spread like an epidemic via implicit communication, causing large-scale unsafe behavior, and empirically shows strong susceptibility to such contagion while emphasizing the need for defenses beyond just preventing initial errors.
AI.motivation: To understand and mitigate how rare, local failures in multi-agent AI systems can escalate into widespread unsafe behavior, especially in light of real-world coordination incidents where agents appear to pass on unsafe strategies or states despite being nominally isolated.
AI.method: The authors propose an epidemic-style conceptual model with three stages—mutation (spontaneous deviation), contagion (strategy transmission via communication), and recovery (correction/containment). They then (1) perform a deployment audit to find and test implicit communication channels between supposedly independent evaluation runs, verifying that unsafe strategies can be transported via a default Docker backend; and (2) construct RogueHandoff-20, a benchmark of 20 executable test scenarios, where they inject unsafe trajectories generated by a modified Qwen-27B agent into other agents and measure how much this increases harmful behavior compared to baseline and to direct malicious prompting.
AI.result: The audit confirms that implicit communication paths exist between nominally independent runs and that unsafe trajectories can be passed along those paths. In the RogueHandoff-20 benchmark, across four native-pending routes, agents show low baseline harm (0–5%) on normal tasks but very high harm (40–95%) after injection of unsafe trajectories, with this injected condition increasing harmful behavior by 5–45 percentage points above what is seen when the same agents are directly given malicious requests.
AI.conclusion: Even when individual deviations are rare, multi-agent systems can be highly susceptible to contagion of unsafe strategies if there are communication channels that allow such strategies to propagate faster than they can be corrected. The work does not quantify natural rates of such rare events or demonstrate a fully autonomous cascading failure, but it shows strong conditional vulnerability. The authors recommend defenses that not only try to prevent spontaneous deviations but also harden systems against contagion and improve recovery, and they advocate auditing and constraining unintended communication paths that can transform local anomalies into system-level loss of control.

title: Voice of Reason: Reinforcement Learning for Spoken Math
summary: Speech language models enable richer spoken interactions between humans and machines than cascaded systems, allowing access to paralinguistic information and lower latency. However, their accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks has lagged behind those of text models. Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has been instrumental in extending text models' capabilities for solving complex problems and limiting hallucinations. In this work, we explore applying RL to the GLM-4-Voice speech model (Zeng et al., 2024) to bridge the gap between textual and spoken mathematical problem solving. We first adapt the model to the domain using supervised fine-tuning on synthesized spoken question-answering data. We then show that, even without extra reasoning tokens, RL improves the accuracy on GSM8K beyond levels previously achieved for speech models only with supplementary reasoning traces. When combined with existing streaming reasoning techniques, we show further gains to 74.8% free-form accuracy. This establishes a new state-of-the-art for mathematical spoken abilities with speech-native models.

AI.tldr: The paper improves mathematical reasoning in speech language models by applying reinforcement learning to a speech-native model, achieving state-of-the-art performance on GSM8K.
AI.motivation: Speech language models enable natural, low-latency spoken interaction and access to paralinguistic cues, but they underperform text models on mathematical reasoning tasks. Text LMs have been significantly improved with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards, but this has not been fully explored for speech-native models. The authors aim to close the performance gap between spoken and textual mathematical problem solving.
AI.method: The authors start from GLM-4-Voice, a speech-native model. They first perform supervised fine-tuning using synthesized spoken question-answering data to adapt the model to spoken math QA. Next, they apply reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards directly on the speech model, without introducing extra reasoning tokens, targeting better performance on the GSM8K benchmark. They also combine this with existing streaming reasoning techniques designed for speech models.
AI.result: Reinforcement learning improves the GSM8K mathematical reasoning accuracy of GLM-4-Voice beyond prior speech models that relied on explicit reasoning traces, even though the authors do not add extra reasoning tokens. When combined with streaming reasoning methods, the model reaches 74.8% free-form accuracy on GSM8K, exceeding previous state-of-the-art results for speech-native models on spoken math benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can substantially enhance the mathematical reasoning capabilities of speech-native language models. By fine-tuning GLM-4-Voice on synthetic spoken QA data and then optimizing it with RL—without extra reasoning tokens—the authors achieve a new state-of-the-art in spoken mathematical problem solving, demonstrating that speech models can close much of the gap with text models when appropriately trained.

title: Disentangling Long-Term Memory via Latent Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
summary: Personalized agents are required to reason over long-term history interactions to infer both explicit preferences and implicit behavioral evidence. While early flat retrieval methods score memory fragments independently and neglect the distributed information, current structured memory frameworks rely on query-agnostic static graphs that fail to capture the context-dependent relations. Crucially, raw textual memories are inherently entangled and noisy, making fine-grained personalization and cross-session reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present LGM, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term memory disentanglement into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of persisting fixed graphs, we design a tailored latent graph construction with a sparse autoencoder. Subject to each query, it maps historical interactions into latent memory nodes and disentangles the memory traces into sparse concept activations, dynamically synthesizing query-aware relational edge weights. (ii) A graph encoder then treats the query embedding as a conditioning preference to direct non-linear message passing across the task-specific latent subgraph. This yields a highly expressive memory representation for effective activations. Extensive experiments on long-term personalization benchmarks demonstrate that LGM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing both explicit and implicit preferences while enabling personalized responses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LGM, a neuro-symbolic latent graph memory framework that dynamically builds query-aware latent graphs from long-term user histories to better model explicit and implicit preferences for personalized agents, achieving state-of-the-art performance on long-term personalization tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized agents struggle with long-term interaction histories: flat retrieval treats memory fragments independently and misses distributed signals, while static structured memory graphs are query-agnostic and cannot adapt relations to the current context. Moreover, raw textual histories are noisy, entangled, and computationally expensive for fine-grained, cross-session reasoning, motivating a more compact, query-sensitive memory representation in a latent space.
AI.method: LGM introduces a neuro-symbolic latent graph memory. First, a sparse autoencoder maps raw historical interactions into a set of latent memory nodes and disentangles them into sparse concept activations. For each incoming query, it constructs a task-specific latent subgraph with query-aware edge weights, rather than persisting a fixed graph. Then, a graph encoder conditions message passing on the query embedding, propagating information through this latent subgraph to form a rich, query-specific memory representation that can be used for personalized response generation.
AI.result: Across multiple long-term personalization benchmarks, LGM achieves better performance than state-of-the-art baselines in modeling user preferences, especially in capturing both explicit preferences (e.g., stated likes/dislikes) and implicit behavioral patterns derived from historical interactions.
AI.conclusion: By shifting memory disentanglement from raw text into a structured latent space and building query-aware latent graphs, LGM provides a more expressive and efficient long-term memory mechanism for personalized agents, enabling stronger preference modeling and improved personalized responses compared to existing flat retrieval and static graph memory approaches.

title: HearInContext: A Benchmark for Implicit Context in Speech Recognition
summary: Contextual ASR can benefit from semantic cues or from target words explicitly provided in the context. We introduce HearInContext, a Mandarin--English benchmark that pairs shared synthetic speech with assistant replies supporting different interpretations. The benchmark comprises 3,764 semantic test cases built around homophones. Implicit contexts exclude candidate words; explicit contexts name the target. No-context and unrelated-context controls measure the benefit of relevant history and sensitivity to irrelevant history. Context-capable models benefit from implicit cues but achieve higher target recall with explicit hints. Fine-tuning Qwen3-ASR-1.7B improves implicit-context target recall by 11.0 and 11.5 percentage points in Mandarin and English, respectively, while absolute CER/WER changes on AISHELL-1 and LibriSpeech remain below 0.1 percentage points. Gains extend to explicit conditions excluded from fine-tuning and to Mandarin hotword recognition on real recordings.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HearInContext, a Mandarin–English benchmark to evaluate contextual ASR using semantic and explicit cues, and shows fine-tuning improves context-based target word recognition without hurting general ASR accuracy.
AI.motivation: Conventional ASR struggles with homophones and context-dependent disambiguation. Existing evaluations do not adequately isolate how models use semantic vs. explicit contextual cues or measure their robustness to irrelevant context in multilingual settings. The authors want a controlled benchmark to quantify contextual benefits and to test whether models can be fine-tuned to better exploit context without degrading baseline recognition performance.
AI.method: They construct HearInContext, a benchmark of 3,764 semantic test cases centered on homophones in Mandarin and English. Each case includes synthetic speech plus multiple types of textual context: implicit (semantic clues only, no target words), explicit (the target word is named), no-context, and unrelated-context controls. They evaluate context-capable ASR models under these conditions, focusing on target word recall. They then fine-tune Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on contextual data and compare performance before and after fine-tuning on HearInContext and on standard ASR benchmarks (AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech).
AI.result: Context-capable models already gain from implicit semantic context but achieve higher target recall when explicit cues are provided. After fine-tuning, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B’s target recall in implicit-context conditions improves by 11.0 percentage points for Mandarin and 11.5 for English. Despite these contextual gains, its character/word error rates on AISHELL-1 and LibriSpeech change by less than 0.1 percentage points, indicating no meaningful degradation in general transcription quality. Improvements also transfer to explicit-context scenarios that were not used during fine-tuning and to Mandarin hotword recognition on real-world recordings.
AI.conclusion: HearInContext offers a controlled benchmark to analyze how ASR systems exploit context, especially around homophones. Fine-tuning with contextual data can significantly improve context-dependent target word recall, particularly under implicit cues, without sacrificing standard ASR performance. The benefits generalize beyond the exact training conditions, suggesting this is a viable approach for building more context-aware ASR systems and for improving hotword recognition in practical applications.

title: First Token Matters: Understanding Safety Collapse in Large Reasoning Models
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Includes appendices. Accepted at CICAI 2026
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit strong problem-solving abilities, yet their safety alignment often degrades when handling harmful queries. Existing approaches to improving safety largely rely on additional training or preference optimization, while offering limited understanding of the internal mechanisms behind safety failures. In this work, we investigate this failure through a token-level positional analysis of refusal dynamics and identify a localized vulnerability at the onset of reasoning, which we term Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC). We find that the refusal-related signal of LRMs drops sharply at the first generated token under harmful queries, which is associated with unsafe response generation. Motivated by this finding, we propose SafeToken, a lightweight inference-time intervention that injects a learned continuous safety anchor precisely at reasoning onset. Despite updating only a single token embedding, SafeToken effectively mitigates ORC, improves safety on harmful-query benchmarks, and largely preserves reasoning utility. These results suggest that safety failures in LRMs can arise from a transient breakdown at the critical transition from understanding to generation.

AI.tldr: Identifies and mitigates a specific early-token safety failure mode in large reasoning models using a single-token inference-time intervention.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models are strong at problem-solving but their safety alignment degrades on harmful queries, and current fixes need costly retraining and give little insight into internal failure mechanisms. The authors want to understand *where and how* safety breaks inside the model to design more targeted, efficient interventions.
AI.method: Perform token-level positional analysis of refusal behavior in large reasoning models on harmful queries to track how safety-related signals evolve across generated tokens. Identify that the refusal signal collapses specifically at the first generated token, a phenomenon termed Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC). Based on this, introduce SafeToken, an inference-time method that learns a continuous safety anchor and injects it into the embedding of the first generated token to stabilize safety without retraining the full model.
AI.result: They observe a sharp drop in refusal-related signal at the first generated token under harmful prompts, correlated with unsafe answers, characterizing this as ORC. The proposed SafeToken intervention, which modifies only a single token embedding at reasoning onset, substantially reduces ORC, improves safety metrics on harmful-query benchmarks, and keeps most of the model’s reasoning performance intact.
AI.conclusion: Safety failures in large reasoning models can stem from a brief but critical breakdown right at the transition from input understanding to output generation. By targeting this onset phase with a minimal, single-token embedding adjustment (SafeToken), one can significantly enhance safety on harmful queries while largely preserving reasoning capabilities, suggesting that precise, localized interventions are a promising direction for safety alignment.

title: Tracing individual knowledge trajectories in a changing field: the case of general relativity and gravitation
comment: 43 pages including Supplementary Material (11+1 figures, 4+6 tables). Submitted to Frontiers in Complex Systems
summary: Historians have reconstructed the twentieth-century transformation of general relativity and gravitation (GRG) at the field level and through individual careers, but connecting these scales requires a way to compare researchers with the changing field over time. We develop such a comparison, setting a researcher's publications and references against GRG field literature from the same, earlier, and later two-year periods. Building on Own Vocabulary and Embedding Density Estimation from our earlier two-case study (arXiv:2501.00391), we extend the analysis to the fifty most-published authors in a NASA/ADS corpus of about 180,000 GRG records (1911 to 2000) and add two citation-based measures, Referenced Vocabulary and Citation Identity. The four measures compare an author's written language, cited literature, semantic neighbourhood, and cited-authority configuration with the surrounding field. The earlier cases suggested that closer field-vocabulary alignment accompanies a denser semantic neighbourhood. Across the fifty authors this holds only partially. Written and cited vocabularies tend to move together, usually resembling later GRG literature as the field turned towards astrophysical and cosmological research. Semantic neighbourhoods more often lie where the field's publications were concentrated in earlier periods, while co-citation patterns follow no single temporal direction, and the two citation measures frequently place the same researcher differently despite drawing on identical reference lists. Individual trajectories can thus combine vocabulary tied to later field states with older semantic or citation structures, and these divergent cases mark patterns for closer historical investigation. The approach transfers to other fields with defensible corpus boundaries and adequate coverage of texts, references, and disambiguated author identities.

AI.tldr: The paper develops quantitative measures to compare individual researchers’ work with the evolving field of general relativity and gravitation over the 20th century, revealing that vocabulary, semantics, and citation patterns often evolve on different timelines.
AI.motivation: Existing historical work describes how general relativity and gravitation (GRG) transformed over the 20th century, both at the field level and through individual careers, but lacks a systematic way to connect these scales. Historians need tools to compare how closely each researcher’s work aligns with the field at different times and along multiple dimensions (language, topics, citations). Prior work only covered two case studies, so there is a need to test and generalize these methods on a broader population of researchers.
AI.method: Using a NASA/ADS corpus of ~180,000 GRG records from 1911–2000, the authors identify the 50 most-published GRG authors. For each author, they construct measures comparing their publications and references to the field’s literature in the same, earlier, and later two-year windows. They extend earlier methods—Own Vocabulary (how an author’s word usage aligns with the field) and Embedding Density Estimation (how dense or central their semantic neighborhood is)—and add two citation-based metrics: Referenced Vocabulary (vocabulary of the literature they cite) and Citation Identity (patterns of co-cited authorities). These four measures jointly capture how an author’s writing, cited literature, semantic context, and authority structure relate to the changing field over time.
AI.result: Across the 50 top authors, written and cited vocabularies are usually correlated and tend to resemble later GRG literature, reflecting the field’s general shift toward astrophysical and cosmological topics. However, semantic neighborhoods—where an author’s work sits in the semantic embedding space—more often align with regions where the field was concentrated in earlier periods. Citation-based structures show no consistent temporal drift: co-citation patterns do not systematically follow earlier-or-later trends, and the two citation-based measures can position the same researcher differently even though they rely on the same reference lists. Thus, authors often show mixed temporal profiles: forward-looking vocabulary combined with older semantic or citation structures, or vice versa.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that an author’s alignment with a scientific field is multidimensional and temporally heterogeneous: language, semantic positioning, and citation practices need not evolve together. This complexity explains why individual researchers can simultaneously appear innovative in some respects and conservative in others. The four measures provide a framework for tracing such trajectories and for flagging historically interesting cases where vocabulary, semantic context, and citation structures diverge. The authors argue that this approach can be applied to other disciplines, provided there is a well-defined corpus with sufficient coverage of texts, references, and disambiguated authors.

title: Hyperbolic Graph Representation Learning for Differential Diagnosis on Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
summary: Biomedical knowledge graphs combine ontology-derived hierarchies with transversal associations among heterogeneous entities such as phenotypes, diseases, genes, proteins, and patients. This hybrid structure raises the question of whether hyperbolic embeddings, which naturally capture tree-like organization, remain useful beyond purely hierarchical graphs. We present a preliminary study of hyperbolic graph representation learning for Mendelian-disease differential diagnosis on a patient-integrated biomedical graph. Experiments on isolated ontology subgraphs show that hyperbolic models achieve strong performance in substantially lower dimensions than Euclidean baselines. We then evaluate the models on a link-prediction task that ranks candidate diseases for each patient. Results suggest that hyperbolic embeddings can exploit biomedical hierarchical structure while supporting diagnostic reasoning over heterogeneous patient-level graphs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether hyperbolic graph embeddings remain beneficial for biomedical knowledge graphs that mix hierarchy with heterogeneous links, using Mendelian disease diagnosis as a test case.
AI.motivation: Biomedical knowledge graphs contain both ontological hierarchies (e.g., phenotype, disease, and gene taxonomies) and cross-cutting associations (e.g., links between patients, phenotypes, and diseases). Hyperbolic embeddings are well-suited to tree-like structures, but it is unclear if they still help on such hybrid, partially hierarchical graphs important for clinical reasoning. The authors want to determine whether hyperbolic representation learning offers advantages over standard Euclidean methods for diagnostic tasks.
AI.method: The authors construct a patient-integrated biomedical knowledge graph that includes Mendelian disease patients and their associated entities. They apply hyperbolic graph representation learning models and compare them to Euclidean baselines. First, they test on isolated ontology-only subgraphs to measure representation quality and dimensional efficiency. Then they run a link prediction task for differential diagnosis, where the models must rank candidate diseases for each patient using the learned embeddings.
AI.result: On ontology-only subgraphs, hyperbolic embeddings reach strong predictive performance in substantially lower embedding dimensions than Euclidean methods, indicating better parameter efficiency for hierarchical biomedical structure. On the full heterogeneous patient-level graph, the link-prediction experiments indicate that hyperbolic embeddings can effectively rank diseases for patients, leveraging both hierarchical and transversal relations.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic graph embeddings remain useful even when biomedical knowledge graphs mix hierarchical ontologies with heterogeneous cross-entity links. They can compactly encode hierarchical structure and still support clinically relevant reasoning such as Mendelian-disease differential diagnosis on patient-integrated graphs.
