By proactively allocating targeted training samples to agents based on their evolving competence, CERA-MoA promotes capability differentiation. Extensive experiments across various domains demonstrate that CERA-MoA outperforms state-of-the-art static-agent routing and fix-workflow fine-tuning baselines.

AI.tldr: They propose CERA-MoA, a framework where both the query router and multiple agents are jointly and continually learned, yielding better routing, specialization, and performance than previous static MoA systems.
AI.motivation: Existing Mixture-of-Agents systems train the router and the agents separately. Once trained, the router is static and cannot adapt as agents are further fine-tuned, and agents do not specialize based on data routed to them. This misalignment wastes capacity and limits performance and efficiency, especially as agent capabilities evolve during post-training.
AI.method: They introduce CERA-MoA, an iterative reinforcement learning-based framework in which a dynamic router and multiple independent agent policies co-evolve. The system uses a predictive familiarity estimator that inspects mid-layer hidden states to estimate each agent's semantic competence on a query without running full rollouts. Using these familiarity scores, a cumulative-threshold adaptive routing strategy selects a minimal subset of agents to activate, balancing performance and computational cost. Training data is proactively allocated to agents based on their evolving competence, encouraging data-driven specialization and capability differentiation.
AI.result: Across multiple domains and benchmarks, CERA-MoA consistently yields better task performance and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art baselines that use static routers with frozen agents or fixed fine-tuning workflows. It shows improved routing quality, clearer specialization of agents, and better trade-offs between accuracy and compute.
AI.conclusion: Jointly evolving the router and agents in a Mixture-of-Agents setup, guided by a familiarity-based adaptive routing mechanism, leads to more specialized agents, more efficient computation, and superior performance versus conventional static-agent routing and fixed fine-tuning approaches.

title: LangSelect: Cost-Aware Target-Language Routing for LLM Code Generation
summary: LLM code-generation systems usually choose a target programming language before decoding and treat that choice as fixed. We show that, for language-flexible programming tasks -- tasks where several target languages are acceptable and checkable by the same tests -- this choice is a measurable cost lever: verified implementations of the same task can differ substantially in generated-token length. We introduce LangSelect, a verification-aware router that selects the target language before generation and falls back when the first attempt fails. To separate offline routing opportunity from end-to-end behavior, we evaluate verified-solution replay, which chooses among already accepted corpus solutions, and live GPT-5 generation, which charges every generation attempt, including failures and fallbacks. On MultiLang-Bench, a 3,000-task, 8-language verified corpus, replay shows substantial language-routing headroom. In live evaluation on 450 held-out tasks, a train-split Domain heuristic baseline reduces harness-proxy tokens, which include wrapper and entrypoint overhead, by 50.3\% at 92.9\% pass after fallback, while a learned CodeBERT+metadata selector reaches the highest pass after fallback, 93.8\%, with a 3.7\% token increase. These results show that output-language routing can define a practical cost-correctness frontier for unit-test-verifiable code generation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how choosing the programming language for LLM-based code generation affects token cost and correctness, and introduces a routing method that picks the best language per task to optimize this tradeoff.
AI.motivation: Current LLM code generators commit to a single target language (e.g., Python) before decoding, even though many benchmarks accept solutions in multiple languages using the same test harness. Different languages can yield implementations of different lengths and costs. The authors want to understand and exploit this variability to reduce token usage while preserving or improving correctness on unit-test-based evaluation.
AI.method: They define "language-flexible" programming tasks where many languages are acceptable. They build MultiLang-Bench, a 3,000-task corpus with verified solutions in 8 languages. They propose LangSelect, a verification-aware routing framework that selects a target language before generation and can fall back to other languages if the first attempt fails. They analyze two settings: (1) offline "verified-solution replay," where they pick among existing accepted solutions per task to estimate the upper bound of routing gains, and (2) live GPT-5-based generation, where each attempt, including failed attempts and fallbacks, incurs token cost. They compare heuristic language selectors based on domain information with a learned selector using CodeBERT plus metadata.
AI.result: On the MultiLang-Bench corpus, replay experiments show substantial potential gains ("headroom") from routing tasks to languages with shorter verified solutions. In live experiments on 450 held-out tasks, a simple train-split domain-based heuristic reduces harness-proxy tokens (including wrapper and entrypoint overhead) by 50.3% while achieving 92.9% pass rate after fallback. A more sophisticated learned selector based on CodeBERT and task metadata obtains the best accuracy, 93.8% pass rate after fallback, at the cost of a modest 3.7% increase in token usage compared to a baseline.
AI.conclusion: Choosing the output programming language is an effective control knob for trading off token cost and correctness in LLM-based, unit-test-verifiable code generation. Language routing via their LangSelect framework can significantly reduce token usage for a given accuracy or increase accuracy for a similar token budget, establishing an explicit cost-correctness frontier for multi-language code generation systems.

title: Compositional Policy Violations: When Step-Level Compliance Fails In Agentic AI Workflows
summary: Agentic workflows now make consequential decisions in regulated settings, and the governance placed around them is almost entirely step-scoped: input-output classifiers, per turn rails, and span-level evaluators. The policies organizations actually hold, such as referral thresholds, authority limits, and review requirements, are properties of the whole execution rather than of any one step. This mismatch admits a failure mode we call a Compositional Policy Violation (CPV): every individual step passes its own check while the composed execution violates the governing policy. A predicate over a single step cannot evaluate a property that step does not determine, so no improvement in the accuracy of the step-scoped monitors detects this class. We define CPVs as the failure of step-level compliance to compose, and present a taxonomy of four types: Authority Creep, Threshold Laundering, Cumulative Sum Violation, and Context Collapse. We show that the correct repair for each class is dictated by where the guarded quantity mutates. We then introduce a provenance-aware runtime architecture that evaluates policies over complete execution traces, recomputing guarded quantities from raw provenance rather than the pipeline's derived representation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and addresses a new failure mode in governing multi-step AI agent workflows, where each step individually complies with policy but the overall execution violates it.
AI.motivation: As AI agents are deployed in regulated, high-stakes environments, governance and safety mechanisms are mostly applied at the step or turn level (e.g., per-call filters, classifiers). However, real-world organizational policies—like spending limits, escalation rules, or cumulative risk thresholds—apply to the overall workflow or case, not to individual steps. This mismatch can allow subtle but serious policy violations that are invisible to step-level monitors, demanding a framework that reasons about entire execution traces instead.
AI.method: The paper conceptually defines Compositional Policy Violations (CPVs) as cases where step-level compliance does not compose to end-to-end compliance. It develops a taxonomy of four CPV types—Authority Creep, Threshold Laundering, Cumulative Sum Violation, and Context Collapse—based on how and where the relevant 'guarded quantity' (such as authority, thresholds, or cumulative metrics) changes during the workflow. Building on this taxonomy, the authors design a provenance-aware runtime architecture that records detailed execution traces and recomputes guarded quantities from raw provenance. This architecture evaluates policies over complete executions rather than trusting intermediate, derived representations from the workflow itself.
AI.result: The paper shows that accurate step-level monitors are inherently unable to detect CPVs, since no predicate over a single step can capture properties determined only by the full execution. It demonstrates that each of the four CPV types arises from specific patterns in where and how guarded quantities mutate. For each class, the authors identify the appropriate 'repair' strategy—i.e., how policies should be enforced over traces so that step-level compliance becomes compositional. They then implement or at least specify a provenance-aware runtime that can track and recompute these guarded quantities over full traces, enabling policy enforcement that closes the CPV gap.
AI.conclusion: Step-scoped governance for agentic AI workflows is fundamentally insufficient to enforce real organizational policies that apply at the level of whole cases or executions. The paper formalizes this gap as Compositional Policy Violations, classifies key patterns of such violations, and argues that the correct enforcement locus depends on where guarded quantities change in the workflow. By introducing a provenance-aware trace-based runtime that evaluates policies over entire executions and recomputes relevant quantities from raw provenance, the authors provide a path toward closing this compositionality gap and achieving end-to-end policy compliance for complex AI agents.

title: When Audit Quality Fails to Predict Downstream Utility: A Counterfactual Study of Synthetic-Data Selectors for Low-Resource African NLP
summary: Quality-aware synthetic-data selection rests on a proxy: examples that an LLM judge rates as good should also help a downstream model learn. In a controlled replay in low-resource African-language classification, we show that this proxy breaks. Across four languages (Amharic, Hausa, Swahili, Yoruba), two classification tasks (MasakhaNEWS, AfriSenti), and five matched-budget selectors, audit rankings and downstream rankings diverge. Within each cell, the Spearman between judged label correctness and Macro-F1 across selectors has mean $ρ{=}0.04$ (median $0.00$), showing that the mismatch is not an aggregation artifact. \method{}-V2, our counterfactual audit framework, produces the cleanest selected pool on three audit channels at once: highest judged label correctness ($0.904$ vs.\ $0.767$ for naive, a $17.9\%$ relative gain), lowest shortcut score, and a hard-reject rate of $0.162$ vs.\ $0.486$ for naive. AlpaGasus nevertheless leads downstream Macro-F1 ($0.202$ vs.\ $0.163$ for \method{}-V2), and the inversion persists on the five non-degenerate cells. The lesson is methodological: in this controlled setting, audit quality is a property of the selected pool, not a guarantee of downstream utility. Synthetic-data evaluation should therefore report audit and downstream metrics on the same retained sets. We release the audit tables, per-selector retained pools, and a claim ledger that links every reported number to its source row.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that high-quality synthetic data as judged by LLM audits does not necessarily translate into better downstream performance for low-resource African-language text classification, and argues that both audit and downstream metrics must be reported on the same data subsets.
AI.motivation: To test the widely used assumption that synthetic examples rated as high-quality by LLM-based judges are also the most useful for training downstream models, especially in low-resource settings where synthetic data is appealing but risky.
AI.method: They run a controlled replay experiment on low-resource African-language classification (Amharic, Hausa, Swahili, Yoruba) across two datasets (MasakhaNEWS, AfriSenti). They compare five synthetic-data selection strategies under matched data budgets. For each strategy, they compute LLM-based audit metrics (label correctness, shortcut score, and hard-reject rate) using their counterfactual audit framework (METHOD-V2), and also train downstream classifiers to measure Macro-F1. They then analyze rank correlations (Spearman) between audit-based rankings and downstream performance across selectors and settings.
AI.result: Audit-based rankings of selectors and downstream-performance-based rankings diverge strongly: within each language–task–setting cell, the Spearman correlation between judged label correctness and downstream Macro-F1 averages only 0.04 (median 0.00). METHOD-V2 selects pools with substantially better audit metrics (e.g., judged label correctness 0.904 vs. 0.767, lower shortcut scores, and lower hard-reject rates), yet another selector (AlpaGasus) consistently yields higher downstream Macro-F1 (0.202 vs. 0.163). This inversion persists across five non-degenerate experimental cells.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based audit quality reflects properties of the selected synthetic data pool but does not guarantee downstream utility; clean, high-audit-quality synthetic data can underperform “messier” data for actual learning. Therefore, synthetic-data evaluation should jointly report both audit metrics and downstream task performance on the exact same retained data, and the authors release detailed audit tables, retained pools, and a claim ledger to support transparent analysis.

title: Infinite-Parameter LLMs: Generating and Adapting Weights from Live Data
summary: The scaling laws hold that a language model grows more capable with more parameters and more training data, and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have ridden these laws to remarkable results, activating only a fraction of an enormous stored parameter bank for each token. That success is built on static pretraining data. A deployed model faces a different world, where much of the data that would make it more useful is not in its training set but in the live interaction it is currently handling, such as the facts a user supplies or the corrections they give. A conventional model cannot learn from this data, because its weights are frozen after training. Instead, the knowledge and behaviour supplied at run time are placed in the prompt, by retrieval or instruction, and re-read on every request only to be discarded once the request ends. We ask how an architecture could learn from live interaction by writing it into its weights. Taking inspiration from MoE, we propose the \textbf{Infinite-Parameter LLM}. A compact hypernetwork turns the data given at run time into a low-rank modulation of a shared base network, so the feed-forward weights are generated from live data rather than stored in a fixed bank. Where prior weight generators read the context once and freeze, we carry a Bayesian belief over the generator's latent code and update it online, so the effective weight is re-derived from that evolving belief as the session proceeds rather than fixed after one read. The stored footprint stays fixed, yet the weights the model can compile are effectively infinite. For the knowledge and behaviour supplied at run time, carrying them in the weights rather than the prompt is amortized in compute, frees the context window, persists across turns, and can generalise better than in-context use. We specify an evaluation protocol that tests exactly this against in-context learning and retrieval.

AI.tldr: Proposes an ‘Infinite-Parameter LLM’ that dynamically writes interaction-time information into generated weights instead of prompts, enabling continual adaptation without increasing stored parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing scaling laws and MoE models rely on static pretraining data and frozen weights; they cannot permanently learn from live user interactions, which are instead repeatedly re-fed via prompts or retrieval, wasting context and compute and limiting generalization.
AI.method: Introduce a compact hypernetwork that maps live interaction data into low-rank modulations of a shared base network’s feed-forward weights. Maintain a Bayesian belief over the hypernetwork’s latent code and update it online over a session so that effective weights are regenerated as the belief evolves, allowing dynamic, session-long adaptation while keeping the stored parameter footprint fixed.
AI.result: Conceptually shows that live interaction information can be encoded into dynamically generated weights rather than prompts, yielding an effectively unbounded (‘infinite’) space of realizable weights without increasing stored parameters; defines an evaluation protocol comparing this approach to in-context learning and retrieval for knowledge and behavior supplied at run time.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, hypernetwork-generated weight modulation with Bayesian online updating can turn interaction-time information into persistent, generalizable model behavior during a session, amortizing compute, freeing context window space, and potentially outperforming standard in-context learning and retrieval, all without growing the model’s stored parameter count.

title: MechSparse: Mechanism-Guided Sparse PEFT Selection Is Task-Shaped
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability identifies sparse subsets of heads and MLP blocks that carry specific behaviors. We ask whether such causal signals can guide where to place a small PEFT budget more effectively than the cheap heuristics practitioners already use. \method{} scores attention heads and MLP blocks by normalized activation-patching recovery on clean/corrupted probes and trains LoRA/QLoRA only on the selected sites; \methodc{} adds bounded credit for small within-layer joint subsets.
  We compare against random, magnitude, activation-norm, and gradient/Fisher on Ministral-8B/NF4 in three cells: Swahili span-JSON information extraction (IE) at $b{=}0.25\%$ and $1.0\%$, and English$\to$Swahili machine translation (MT) at $b{=}1.0\%$. The causal selectors never win the primary metric. On the headline IE cell (3 seeds, paired-bootstrap CIs over $600$ predictions), \methodc{} beats random by $+0.079$ span+type F1 and gradient/Fisher by $+0.174$, but trails activation-norm by $0.028$, with the smallest cross-seed std ($\pm 0.003$). On MT all four selectors lie within $0.30$ BLEU and every paired CI includes zero. A schema-versus-span decomposition explains the IE gap: activation-norm captures the rigid JSON routine, while causal scores track content-sensitive sites. We distill a preliminary diagnostic -- prefer activation-norm when output structure dominates, treat causal selectors as a hypothesis for content-dominated tasks -- and release masks, scores, predictions, and evaluation files for direct replay.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether mechanistic-interpretability-based “causal” scores for attention heads/MLP blocks help allocate a tiny PEFT (LoRA/QLoRA) budget better than standard heuristics, and finds they do not clearly outperform simpler activation-based methods, while offering insights about when each selector is preferable.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA require choosing where in a model to place a very small number of trainable parameters. Practitioners typically rely on simple, cheap heuristics (e.g., activation norms, gradients) or even random selection. Mechanistic interpretability has identified specific heads/MLPs as causally responsible for behaviors; if such causal signals could guide PEFT placement, they might substantially improve performance at fixed budget. The paper wants to test this hypothesis empirically and understand whether these more expensive, causally-motivated selectors actually provide an advantage over existing heuristics.
AI.method: The authors introduce two selectors: (1) a base method (\method{}) that scores each attention head and MLP block by a normalized activation-patching recovery metric using clean vs. corrupted probes, then allocates LoRA/QLoRA only to the highest-scoring sites; (2) an extended method (\methodc{}) that additionally assigns bounded credit to small joint subsets of components within a layer. They then evaluate these causal selectors against four baselines—random, weight-magnitude, activation-norm, and gradient/Fisher-based scoring—on the Ministral-8B/NF4 model in three experimental settings ("cells"): Swahili span-to-JSON information extraction at 0.25% and 1.0% PEFT budget, and English-to-Swahili machine translation at 1.0% budget. Performance is examined across multiple seeds, with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals, and a decomposition of IE performance into schema vs. span components to analyze where each selector helps.
AI.result: The causal selectors (\method{} and \methodc{}) never achieve the best performance on the main metrics compared to the baselines. In the headline Swahili IE setup, \methodc{} improves over random selection by +0.079 span+type F1 and over gradient/Fisher by +0.174, but still lags behind the simple activation-norm heuristic by 0.028 F1, though it shows the lowest cross-seed variance (±0.003). For machine translation, all four selectors (including causal ones and baselines) fall within 0.30 BLEU of each other, and all paired confidence intervals include zero, indicating no significant differences. A more detailed decomposition of IE performance shows that activation-norm tends to favor components handling rigid JSON structure, while causal scores favor content-sensitive components, explaining the observed performance trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic-interpretability-based causal scoring provides a principled way to identify behaviorally important components for PEFT placement, but in these experiments it does not consistently outperform simpler, cheaper heuristics like activation-norm. The evidence suggests that activation-norm is preferable when the task is dominated by rigid output structure (e.g., JSON formatting), while causal selectors may be more promising for content-dominated tasks, though this remains a hypothesis. The authors position their work primarily as a diagnostic study: they clarify when different selectors may be advantageous, highlight stability benefits of causal selectors, and publicly release masks, scores, predictions, and evaluation artifacts to facilitate direct replication and further analysis.

title: Suppressed, Not Erased: A Representational Trace of Edited Facts Survives Even Weight-Free Knowledge Editing
summary: Knowledge-editing benchmarks certify local correctness, whether an edited model produces the new fact on near-edit prompts but not how much of the original fact remains decodable inside the model. We study residual knowledge directly with a linear trace probe: after editing a fact, we ask whether the original object is still recoverable from the model's hidden states. On GPT-2-XL, across three mechanistically distinct editors applied to 50 CounterFact edits, the original object remains linearly decodable well above chance after a successful edit (probe accuracy 0.96 for ROME, 0.86 for constrained fine-tuning, and 0.79 for the memory-based editor GRACE, against a chance level of 0.50; all edits reach 100% generation-based success). The GRACE result is the most informative: GRACE changes zero base-model weights, overriding the fact through an external memory, yet the original object is still decodable from the underlying network, so the residual trace cannot be attributed to an incomplete weight update. We read this as evidence that editing, even when behaviorally successful, suppresses rather than erases the original association in representational space. We also report a relearning-savings instrument that did not behave reliably in our setting and discuss why; we treat it as a negative methodological result rather than evidence. Code and data are released.

AI.tldr: They examine what remains of old knowledge inside language models after applying different knowledge-editing methods, finding that the original facts are still strongly linearly decodable from hidden states, so edits suppress rather than erase internal representations.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge-editing benchmarks focus on whether a model outputs the updated fact on specific prompts, but they do not measure how much of the old fact persists internally. This paper aims to directly probe residual knowledge to better understand what editing actually does to the model’s representations and to compare different editing methods on this internal criterion.
AI.method: Use a linear probe ("linear trace probe") on GPT-2-XL’s hidden states to test decodability of the original object after edits. Apply three distinct editing methods—ROME (weight-level causal editing), constrained fine-tuning, and GRACE (an external memory-based editor that leaves base weights unchanged)—on 50 CounterFact factual edits. For each method, they measure probe accuracy at predicting the original object from hidden activations post-edit, alongside standard generation-based success. They also explore a relearning-savings metric as an additional instrument, though it proves unreliable here.
AI.result: All three editors achieve 100% success on the usual generation-based editing metric (they output the new fact correctly), but the original fact remains strongly linearly decodable from hidden states after editing: probe accuracy 0.96 for ROME, 0.86 for constrained fine-tuning, and 0.79 for GRACE, versus 0.50 chance. The GRACE result is especially telling because GRACE does not modify base-model weights, yet the old fact’s representation is still accessible, showing that residual traces are not simply due to partial weight updates. The attempted relearning-savings measure does not produce stable or interpretable results.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge edits that look perfect behaviorally do not erase old facts from a model’s internal representations; they mainly suppress their expression, leaving a linearly decodable trace. This holds across very different editing paradigms, including one that leaves the base model unchanged. Linear probing is therefore an informative complement to standard editing benchmarks. The negative result on the relearning-savings instrument suggests that not all proposed metrics reliably capture residual knowledge, underlining the need for careful methodology when assessing knowledge editing.

title: A Benchmark Suite and Ground-Truth Methodology for Formal Verification of IEC 61131-3 Ladder Diagram Programs
summary: We present the first benchmark suite for formal verification of Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) programs that combines controlled ground truth with coverage of both textual (Structured Text, ST) and graphical (Ladder Diagram, LD) IEC 61131-3 encodings. Despite growing support for tools, the field lacks standard evaluation benchmarks: existing corpora omit formal properties or graphical dialects, and private program sets preclude reproducible measurement of progress. Our suite comprises 50 programs in 83 variants across ten industrial domains, provided in PLCopen Extensible Markup Language (XML) and ST, each paired with a formal property, machine-checkable expected verdict, and violation witness in the Software Verification Competition (SV-COMP) format. The central methodological contribution is a tripartite ground-truth discipline - verdicts are established by construction, fault injection, or audited cross-tool consensus - motivated by a concrete failure mode where the obvious safety property misclassifies all attacks from two public logic-bomb corpora as safe due to invisible non-termination. Reference verdicts are obtained with the Efficient SMT-Based Context-Bounded Model Checker (ESBMC) v8.4 from source: all 25 graphical benchmarks execute, and 43 of 45 accepted variants match recorded verdicts. On the finite-state fragment (21 benchmarks), nuXmv - a model checker with unrelated decision procedures - agrees on all 24 interlock variants and resolves two benchmarks ESBMC-PLC leaves unknown, confirming tool-neutral ground truth and discriminative power. Porting exposes format and semantics fragmentation: front-ends accept different serializations, and timer semantics vary across tools - phenomena the suite is designed to reveal. The corpus, schema, validator, and recheck harness are released as open artifacts.

AI.tldr: They introduce the first open benchmark suite for formally verifying PLC programs, covering both textual and graphical IEC 61131-3 languages with ground-truth verdicts and artifacts for reproducible evaluation.
AI.motivation: Formal verification for PLC programs is increasingly supported by tools, but the community lacks common, openly-available benchmarks that include formal properties, ground-truth answers, and coverage of both textual (ST) and graphical (LD) PLC languages. Existing corpora either lack formal properties or omit graphical dialects, and many industrial program sets are proprietary, preventing reproducible comparison and progress tracking. There is also a concrete failure mode where naive safety properties miss logic-bomb attacks due to non-termination, highlighting the need for carefully constructed and validated ground truth.
AI.method: They construct a benchmark suite of 50 PLC programs across ten industrial domains, yielding 83 variants expressed in PLCopen XML and Structured Text (ST). Each benchmark is paired with a formal property, an expected machine-checkable verdict, and a violation witness compliant with the SV-COMP format. To ensure reliable ground truth, they apply a tripartite discipline: (1) establishing verdicts by construction, (2) injecting faults to generate known violations, and (3) using audited consensus across multiple verification tools. They use ESBMC v8.4 to obtain reference verdicts from source code, and cross-check a finite-state subset with nuXmv, which uses different decision procedures, to validate tool-neutrality and discriminative power. They also analyze tool behavior when porting benchmarks, observing differences in accepted serializations and timer semantics.
AI.result: The resulting suite spans 50 PLC programs in 83 variants across ten industrial domains, each with associated properties and SV-COMP style verdicts/witnesses. ESBMC-PLC successfully executes all 25 graphical benchmarks and confirms 43 of 45 accepted variants against the recorded verdicts, leaving two as unknown. On the finite-state fragment of 21 benchmarks, nuXmv agrees with ESBMC-PLC on all 24 interlock variants (including multiple variants per benchmark) and is able to resolve two benchmarks that ESBMC-PLC leaves unknown. Porting the benchmarks to different tools reveals practical issues: format fragmentation (different tools accept different XML/ST serializations) and semantic fragmentation (notably differing timer semantics). All artifacts, including the corpus, schema, validator, and recheck harness, are made publicly available.
AI.conclusion: They conclude that their benchmark suite fills a critical gap for the formal verification of PLC software by providing open, reproducible, and tool-neutral benchmarks with strong ground truth, spanning both textual and graphical PLC languages. The tripartite ground-truth methodology and cross-checking with independent model checkers demonstrate that the suite is discriminative and reliable. Additionally, the observed fragmentation in formats and timer semantics underscores the need for standardized representations and semantics, which the suite is explicitly designed to expose. The open artifacts enable community-wide evaluation, comparison, and future extension of PLC verification tools.

title: Function Lives Where Variance Doesn't: Task-Weighted Charts of a Language Model's Computation
summary: How many dimensions does a language model's computation actually use? The question is ill-posed until one names a functional. Task-weighted charts make it well-posed: low-dimensional coordinate systems fit against a chosen functional of the representation, under the functional's own metric, turning distillation into plain least squares. Across six models from three families, spanning 70m to 7B parameters, next-token prediction needs 70--90% of the residual stream's width to stay within 5% of intact perplexity, a width consumed by the rare tail of language, and the variance profile predicts none of it: two directions carry 90% of GPT-2's activation variance and almost none of its function. Dimension is per-functional: the model's own uncertainty reads from six coordinates where the full predictive distribution needs hundreds; and it grows with depth. The dissociation is exploitable: when only a few dimensions can be kept, charts trained under the functional's metric preserve the model's predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how many effective dimensions language models use for different tasks by defining task-specific low-dimensional coordinate systems (task-weighted charts) based on chosen functionals, showing that functional dimensionality is high for full prediction but much lower for some internal quantities, and that function-based compression outperforms variance-based compression.
AI.motivation: Traditional notions of dimensionality (e.g., variance explained by principal components) fail to capture how many directions in representation space actually matter for a model’s behavior. There is a need for a behaviorally grounded, task-specific measure of dimensionality that reflects the computations a language model performs, rather than just its activation variance profile.
AI.method: Introduce task-weighted charts: learn low-dimensional linear coordinate systems that best approximate a chosen functional of the model’s internal representations, under a metric induced by that functional. Apply this framework to the residual streams of six language models of varying sizes and families. Compare the dimensionality needed to preserve different functionals (e.g., next-token predictive distribution, model uncertainty) and contrast it with variance-based dimensionality measures such as PCA. Evaluate compression by measuring perplexity degradation when restricting computation to the learned low-dimensional coordinates.
AI.result: For next-token prediction, models require 70–90% of the residual stream’s width to keep perplexity within 5% of the original, meaning most dimensions are functionally important, largely due to modeling rare tokens. In contrast, activation variance is highly concentrated: in GPT-2, two principal components capture ~90% of variance but contribute negligibly to predictive performance, indicating a strong mismatch between variance and function. Different functionals have different effective dimensionalities: model uncertainty can be read from only about six dimensions, while representing the full predictive distribution requires hundreds. Functional dimensionality tends to increase with depth. Functionally trained charts preserve predictions better than PCA-based or theoretically optimal linear compression when aggressive dimensionality reduction is required.
AI.conclusion: Functional dimensionality in language models is task-dependent and cannot be inferred from activation variance alone. Many more dimensions are behaviorally relevant for next-token prediction than variance analyses would suggest, whereas some internal quantities like uncertainty live in very low-dimensional subspaces. This reveals a dissociation between where variance lies and where function lies. By training low-dimensional charts under the metric of a given functional, one can compress model computations in a way that better preserves behavior than variance-based methods, especially when only a small number of dimensions can be retained.

title: WordPolo: Evaluating Language Models Through Iterative Semantic Feedback
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are typically evaluated on challenging benchmarks through dataset accuracy alone, providing no insight into the quality or faithfulness of their reasoning processes. We present WordPolo, a word-finding task where participants must discover an unknown target word using semantic similarity feedback. Players start with zero knowledge, make guesses, and receive distance scores (1 = correct, higher = further away). Success requires interpreting scores to navigate semantic space and systematically narrow the search. This design makes iterative reasoning and adaptive search strategies both directly observable and necessary for success. We evaluate recent LLMs (GPT-4.1, Llama 4, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Qwen 3), LRMs (o4-mini, Deepseek-R1), humans, and a novel heuristic on 1,500 puzzles. Beyond solve rates (which range from 4% to 62%), we introduce progression-based metrics that reveal models often make meaningful progress, insights that accuracy alone would miss. Our analysis shows how reasoning models can be hindered by overthinking and underthinking, while successful models exhibit human-like strategies. WordPolo demonstrates the need for benchmarks that test both reasoning process and outcomes, providing holistic measurements of model capabilities. Our code and dataset can be found at https://wordpolo-demo.vercel.app/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WordPolo, a semantic word-finding game used as a benchmark to evaluate not just whether LLMs and LRMs get the right answer, but how they reason their way toward it.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks mainly measure dataset accuracy and give little insight into the quality, faithfulness, or dynamics of models’ reasoning processes. The authors want a setting where reasoning steps and search strategies are observable, comparable to humans, and essential to success, so they can analyze how models actually think rather than only whether they are right.
AI.method: They design WordPolo, where a player must guess an unknown target word using iterative feedback in the form of semantic distance scores. The player starts with no information, proposes guesses, and receives a numerical distance (1 if correct; larger means semantically further). This forces a process of interpreting feedback, adjusting hypotheses, and exploring semantic space. They then run large-scale experiments on 1,500 puzzles, comparing multiple state-of-the-art LLMs (e.g., GPT-4.1, Llama 4, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Qwen 3), LRMs (o4-mini, Deepseek-R1), humans, and a custom heuristic baseline. In addition to simple solve rate, they define progression-based metrics that track how guesses move closer or further from the target over time.
AI.result: Models’ solve rates vary widely (4%–62%), but progression metrics show that even when they fail to solve a puzzle, they often make non-trivial, structured progress in semantic space—information that accuracy metrics would overlook. Analysis highlights that reasoning-focused models can suffer from both “overthinking” (unnecessary or unproductive complexity) and “underthinking” (shallow or premature guesses), whereas better-performing systems tend to exhibit search patterns similar to human strategies. The heuristic provides a baseline for what simple, explicit strategies can achieve.
AI.conclusion: WordPolo serves as an effective benchmark that evaluates both reasoning processes and final outcomes, enabling richer, more diagnostic assessments of LLMs and LRMs than raw accuracy alone. The observed behaviors—like overthinking, underthinking, and human-like search strategies—underscore the importance of progression-based, process-aware benchmarks for future model development. The authors release code and data to facilitate further research using this framework.

title: Lost in Perception: Isolating Perceptual and Reasoning Failures in Multimodal Physics and Geometry Reasoning
summary: Multimodal LLMs report strong performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks, yet most treat perception and reasoning as a single measurable process. We introduce a five-task diagnostic experiment across physics and geometry benchmarks that isolates failures to perception, reasoning, or both. Incorrect diagram interpretation degrades performance even on problems models solve correctly from text alone, and accuracy generally rises from raw images to human-authored captions. Recovery under corrected captions is high for some models, separating perception-blocked failures from genuine reasoning bottlenecks. Which reasoning error follows a perception failure depends on domain: physics failures resolve into calculation errors, geometry into conceptual misapplication. As a discussion beyond our core experiments, InternS1-mini, despite heavy scientific pretraining and thinking capabilities, falls below the weakest model from experiments on every task, with reasoning traces frequently truncating before completion.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses how multimodal LLMs fail on scientific reasoning by disentangling perception errors from reasoning errors using a five-task benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal LLM evaluations conflate visual perception and symbolic reasoning, making it unclear whether failures stem from misreading diagrams or flawed reasoning. The authors want a clearer diagnostic framework for scientific problems that combine text and images.
AI.method: They design a five-task diagnostic suite in physics and geometry that compares model performance across different input forms: raw images, human-written captions of those images, text-only versions of problems, and corrected captions. By observing how accuracy changes under these conditions, they attribute errors to perception, reasoning, or both, and analyze error types (e.g., calculation vs conceptual mistakes). They also qualitatively examine an additional model, InternS1-mini, outside the main experiments.
AI.result: They find that misinterpreting diagrams substantially harms performance even on problems the models can solve from text alone. Accuracy improves when moving from raw images to high-quality human captions, and many models recover strongly when given corrected captions, indicating that some failures are purely perceptual. Error patterns differ by domain: in physics, perception issues tend to surface as calculation mistakes; in geometry, as conceptual misapplications. InternS1-mini underperforms all benchmarked models and often produces truncated reasoning traces.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal LLM benchmarks must separate perception and reasoning to properly understand model weaknesses. High recovery under corrected captions shows that many current limitations are in visual understanding rather than core reasoning, and error taxonomies differ by domain. Diagnostic setups like this can guide more targeted improvements in both perception modules and reasoning architectures, and prevent overestimating multimodal scientific reasoning capabilities.

title: TalkMatrix: Generating Character Dialogue that is Both Consistent and Diverse
summary: Candidate-based decoding typically selects a completion for each prompt independently, but many applications require a collection of outputs that satisfies global, non-decomposable requirements. We formulate this setting as structured multi-prompt, multi-completion selection: given a candidate pool for every prompt, select one completion per prompt to optimize a collection-level objective. We instantiate the problem in character dialogue, where each character should remain consistent across situations, each line should fit its situation, and characters and situations should remain distinguishable. Our method, TalkMatrix, generates multiple candidates for every character--situation pair and jointly selects a complete matrix using four embedding-based consistency and diversity objectives. Because a weighted sum can improve some dimensions by sacrificing another, TalkMatrix maximizes the worst-performing objective through a two-level minimax formulation. We approximately optimize the resulting discrete objective with multi-start coordinate ascent, and compare it with local, partial-matrix, and generic combinatorial search baselines. We run experiments on $50$ synthetic role-playing scenarios and $25$ curated board game scenarios where multiple characters interact in predefined situations. An LLM-as-a-judge rates matrix-level selection higher than random and independent cell-level selection baselines. These results show the value of structured selection for globally controlled dialogue generation, while our empirical validation remains specific to role-playing scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TalkMatrix, a method for jointly selecting one completion per prompt across many prompts to satisfy global dialogue-level constraints, rather than choosing each completion independently.
AI.motivation: Standard candidate-based decoding in language models selects the best completion for each prompt in isolation, which fails when we need a whole set of outputs to jointly satisfy non-decomposable, global constraints (e.g., consistent characterization across many lines of dialogue). The authors are motivated by applications like multi-character role-playing or board-game dialogue, where each character must remain consistent in personality and style across situations, each utterance must be appropriate for its situation, and different characters and situations must remain distinguishable. Independent selection cannot guarantee these properties, motivating a structured selection framework over all prompts and candidates together.
AI.method: They formalize a structured multi-prompt, multi-completion selection problem: given multiple candidate completions for every prompt (here, every character–situation pair), choose exactly one candidate per prompt to optimize a collection-level objective. For the dialogue instantiation, they propose TalkMatrix, which: (1) generates multiple candidate utterances for each character–situation pair; (2) defines four embedding-based objectives capturing character consistency, situation appropriateness, character distinguishability, and situation distinguishability; (3) combines these via a two-level minimax formulation that maximizes the worst-performing objective instead of a simple weighted sum, avoiding trade-offs that overly sacrifice one dimension; and (4) approximately optimizes this discrete, combinatorial objective using multi-start coordinate ascent. They compare against baselines including independent (local) selection, partial-matrix optimization, and generic combinatorial search methods.
AI.result: On 50 synthetic role-playing scenarios and 25 curated board-game scenarios, each involving multiple characters across predefined situations, TalkMatrix is evaluated with an LLM-as-a-judge. The judge rates the matrices selected by TalkMatrix higher at the whole-matrix level than outputs produced by random selection and by independent cell-level selection. This suggests that structured, joint selection improves global dialogue quality and control. However, evidence is limited to these particular role-playing/board-game settings.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that moving from independent, per-prompt candidate selection to structured, joint selection over many prompts enables better global control of dialogue properties such as character consistency, situational fit, and distinctiveness. TalkMatrix demonstrates that a minimax multi-objective formulation with approximate combinatorial optimization can yield higher-quality dialogue matrices than local or random baselines. Nonetheless, the authors acknowledge that their empirical validation is currently confined to role-playing scenarios, and broader generalization to other tasks or domains remains to be established.

title: Compiled Agency: Frontier General-Purpose Coding Agents Build Winning Game Players from Bare Interaction - from Flappy Bird to StarCraft II and Civilization
summary: LLM agents have repeatedly struggled to convert knowledge of a game into competent play, even when researchers build the agent around the model - supplying perception, memory, skill libraries, planners, or executable-policy scaffolds. Rapid progress in coding agents raises two sharper questions: can frontier models now win games at all, and can they win them unaided, building the entire player themselves? We introduce Gauntlet, a develop-freeze-evaluate framework that ports games from small arcades to full commercial-scale titles, behind one deliberately bare contract: a general-purpose coding agent receives a game description, a raw observation/action interface, and an empty policy file - no strategy, no algorithm, no architecture. In a single autonomous session the agent experiments with the live game and engineers a standalone controller; we freeze the result and score it on held-out instances with zero model calls during play. On an unpublished procedural roguelike, held-out success spans 0-86 percent and exposes a sharp generational threshold: every observed session of a newest-generation system outperforms the best session of its predecessor. At full-game scale, a compiled raw-API controller defeats every fair StarCraft II built-in AI and two cheating variants, and single-session programs win complete games of Civilization (Freeciv) by total conquest on held-out seeds. Though at modest rates against novice AI, this is a first: no prior language-agent system had won full games of this genre standalone, without per-turn model calls and a hand-crafted tactical layer. Frontier coding agents begin to track long-horizon strategy. The frozen programs are inspectable. We call this capability compiled agency: development experience compiled into a persistent executable agent whose architecture is built by the model.

AI.tldr: Gauntlet tests whether modern coding-capable LLMs can, in a single autonomous session, build game-playing agents from scratch that then play without further model calls.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can often describe how to play games but fail to translate that knowledge into strong, autonomous gameplay, especially over long horizons. Prior work usually gives the model extensive scaffolding like planners, memory, or custom policies, making it unclear whether the model itself can construct competent agents. With rapid gains in coding abilities, the authors want to know if current frontier models can independently engineer persistent, high-performing game controllers.
AI.method: They propose Gauntlet, a develop-freeze-evaluate framework. A general coding LLM is given: (1) a description of a game, (2) a raw observation/action API, and (3) an empty policy file. In a single uninterrupted session, the model can experiment with the live game and write a program (controller) that interfaces with the game. After this development phase, the resulting controller is frozen (no more model calls) and evaluated on held-out game instances. They test on an unpublished procedural roguelike, StarCraft II (against built-in AIs), and Freeciv (a Civilization-like game), without extra strategic scaffolding beyond the coding agent itself.
AI.result: On the procedural roguelike, frozen controllers achieve held-out success rates ranging from 0% to 86%, with a clear generational jump: every run with the newest-generation model beats the best run from its predecessor. At full-game scale, a controller compiled via this method beats all fair StarCraft II built-in AIs plus two cheating variants, and single-session controllers win full Freeciv games by total conquest on test seeds, albeit at modest win rates versus novice AI.
AI.conclusion: Frontier coding-capable LLMs can now autonomously construct persistent game-playing agents that exhibit nontrivial long-horizon strategy, without hand-crafted tactical layers or per-turn model calls. The authors term this "compiled agency": the model’s one-shot development experience is compiled into an inspectable executable whose architecture and logic are designed by the model itself. This demonstrates a new level of agentic capability and offers a transparent way to study learned strategies.

title: Entropy in Conversational AI: Structured Unpredictability as Inferrable Interiority
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Ancillary files contain the complete artifact: code, frozen protocol, per-sequence and per-item outcome files, and deterministic analysis scripts. Code archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21462383 Final-grid pre-registration: https://osf.io/dyt3w/
summary: Sampling can increase response diversity without producing history-dependent behavior. We formalize a different design target, structured unpredictability, as conditional dependence between an output and a persistent hidden state beyond what an observer can infer from the transcript. A selection layer updates a low-dimensional style-and-attention state from a capacity-limited stream, generates several responses with a fixed base model, and selects for novelty and state affinity. Evaluation uses scripted sequences of independent prompt turns: the base model receives the current turn and rendered state, but not the preceding dialogue; cross-turn dependence resides in the wrapper state and response selector. A synthetic implementation validates the pipeline and matches four prospectively hash-frozen divergence features at point level. In the final real-model grid (mlx-community/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-4bit; 56 sequences per arm), the mechanism increased lexical novelty over the low-variance and consistency-only controls by 0.073 and 0.023, respectively. Its stylometric-consistency contrast with novelty-matched sampling was equivalent to zero under the registered smallest-effect rule, so the joint novelty-consistency criterion failed. The original two-part accumulation criterion also failed; a revised final-grid contrast, frozen after the powered grid, found higher consistency than the memory-reset ablation (0.028, 95% CI [0.018,0.039]), but does not establish path dependence. Twin separation was not established (0.003, 95% CI [-0.011,0.019]); the mean curve's saturating curvature matched the frozen prediction, which without separation does not support path dependence. Probe-level capability equivalence held within +/-0.10 on a near-ceiling battery, while output quality was not evaluated. All outcomes are machine-scored; no claims about perceived mind or consciousness are tested.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and tests a wrapper mechanism that adds structured, stateful unpredictability to a base language model by using a persistent hidden style/attention state and a selection layer for candidate responses, aiming to boost diversity while preserving consistency, and empirically finds modest novelty gains but limited evidence for true path-dependent behavior.
AI.motivation: Standard sampling-based methods to increase diversity in language model outputs can lead to uncontrolled randomness and history-dependent behavior that may be undesirable or hard to characterize. The authors want a design that provides 'structured unpredictability': outputs that are partly shaped by a persistent internal state in ways that an external observer cannot fully infer from the visible dialogue, but that do not rely on changing the base model itself. They are also motivated by interest in whether such mechanisms can produce signatures sometimes associated with 'mind-like' properties (e.g., path dependence, twin separation) without making any claims about consciousness.
AI.method: They introduce a wrapper architecture around a frozen base model. A low-dimensional hidden 'style-and-attention' state is updated turn by turn from a capacity-limited stream of information, independent of the full dialogue history. For each user prompt, the wrapper uses the current state to produce multiple candidate responses from the unchanged base model. A selection layer then scores these candidates for both novelty and affinity to the current hidden state, and selects one to present. The authors evaluate this mechanism using scripted sequences of independent prompts: the base model only sees the current prompt and a rendering of the hidden state, never the full past dialogue. Cross-turn dependence is thus carried solely in the wrapper state and selection process. They run both synthetic simulations and experiments with a real quantized model (mlx-community/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-4bit), structured as preregistered power and confirmatory grids, with multiple control conditions (low-variance control, consistency-only control, sampling-based novelty-matched control, and memory-reset ablation). They compute machine-scored metrics of lexical novelty, stylometric consistency, divergence features, path dependence signatures (e.g., twin separation, saturating curves), and probe-level task capabilities.
AI.result: In synthetic tests, the proposed pipeline behaves as intended and reproduces a set of hash-frozen divergence features at the level of individual points. In experiments on the real model (56 scripted prompt sequences per experimental arm), the wrapper increases lexical novelty by 0.073 compared to a low-variance control and by 0.023 compared to a consistency-only control, indicating that it successfully boosts diversity. However, when compared to a sampling-based condition adjusted to match novelty, the stylometric consistency advantage is effectively zero under the preregistered smallest-effect-size-of-interest, so the combined novelty-plus-consistency goal is not met. The preregistered two-part criterion for cumulative divergence (path dependence) also fails. A revised, post-hoc contrast (final-grid comparison frozen after observing a powered grid) shows higher consistency than a memory-reset ablation (difference 0.028, 95% CI [0.018, 0.039]), but this alone does not demonstrate true path-dependent behavior. Tests of 'twin separation'—whether initially identical systems diverge meaningfully over time—find no significant effect (0.003, 95% CI [-0.011, 0.019]). The observed saturating curvature of divergence over time matches preregistered predictions, but without twin separation this pattern does not support claims of path dependence. Probe-level task performance remains within ±0.10 of controls on a nearly ceiling-level capability battery, and the study does not evaluate perceived output quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed wrapper can modestly increase lexical diversity in a language model's outputs using a persistent, low-dimensional state and a novelty-plus-state-affinity selection mechanism, without degrading measured task capabilities. However, under preregistered criteria, it fails to demonstrate the desired combination of greater novelty and stylometric consistency or convincing behavioral evidence of path-dependent internal dynamics such as twin separation. Post-hoc analyses hint that the persistent state may contribute to consistency beyond simple memory reset baselines, but this does not amount to strong evidence of structured, mind-like path dependence. The authors emphasize that all metrics are automated and that the work does not address or support claims about subjective experience or consciousness.

title: MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-Modal Understanding in Situated Education
summary: Large vision-language models have achieved remarkable progress in multi-modal understanding, yet their capabilities in educational settings remain insufficiently evaluated. In AI-assisted language learning, models must interpret artistic imagery, understand its semantic, affective, and cultural content, and reason about visual context to support meaningful interaction. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on real-world images or domain-specific educational reasoning, providing limited coverage of artistic educational content. To address this gap, we introduce MUSE, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on artistic image understanding in situated educational applications. MUSE decouples image annotation from question generation, enabling diverse tasks with controllable difficulty while reducing annotation effort. It comprises twelve tasks spanning visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, culture understanding, and compositional reasoning, together with diverse artistic images deliberately curated to center Singaporean and Southeast Asian multicultural contexts alongside Western art traditions, covering multiple themes and difficulty levels. Evaluation of open-source and proprietary models reveals substantial disparities across capability dimensions, particularly in affective interpretation and compositional reasoning. Our analysis further identifies common failure modes and key challenges for developing trustworthy multi-modal models for education. We hope MUSE will serve as a standardized benchmark for advancing multi-modal understanding in situated educational applications.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MUSE, a benchmark to evaluate large vision-language models on understanding artistic images in educational contexts, especially with multicultural (Singaporean and Southeast Asian plus Western) content.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language benchmarks focus mainly on real-world images or narrow educational reasoning tasks and largely ignore artistic imagery used in language learning. Educational use demands rich interpretation of semantic, affective, and cultural aspects of art, which current benchmarks do not adequately test. The authors aim to fill this evaluation gap to better understand and improve models used in AI-assisted language learning.
AI.method: The authors design MUSE, a benchmark specifically targeting artistic image understanding for situated educational applications. They decouple image annotation from question generation so they can systematically vary task types and difficulty while saving annotation effort. MUSE includes 12 tasks that cover visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, cultural understanding, and compositional reasoning. The image set mixes diverse artistic images with an emphasis on Singaporean and Southeast Asian multicultural contexts alongside Western art, and is organized by themes and difficulty. They evaluate a range of open-source and proprietary large vision-language models on these tasks and analyze their performance and failure modes.
AI.result: Evaluation shows that current large vision-language models have uneven abilities across the different task dimensions. They perform notably worse on affective interpretation (understanding emotions, moods) and on compositional reasoning (handling complex relations and multi-step inferences) than on simpler perception or semantic tasks. The benchmark exposes substantial capability disparities and recurring patterns of errors on artistic, educationally grounded tasks.
AI.conclusion: MUSE provides a standardized, task-diverse benchmark for assessing and comparing large vision-language models on artistic image understanding in realistic educational settings. The observed weaknesses in affective and compositional reasoning highlight important challenges for building trustworthy multimodal models for AI-assisted language learning. The authors propose MUSE as an evaluation foundation that can guide future model development and research on multi-modal educational applications.

title: MIRAGE: How Conversation State Shapes Historical Evidence Use in Multimodal Personal Agents
summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents are increasingly used as personal assistants for long-running tasks. Their utility depends on continuity: agents must retrieve and use earlier evidence across dialogue, files, and workspace state. However, agents can generate plausible answers even when access to that history has degraded, causing outcome-only evaluation to overestimate true evidence use. We present MIRAGE (Multimodal Interaction Retrieval, Attribution, and Grounding Evaluation), a controlled study of historical evidence use under conversation-state variation in multimodal personal agents. MIRAGE holds evidence objects, questions, and scoring fixed while varying only conversation state, and evaluates whether an agent can determine answerability, recover the correct source, and answer from it. Across seven frontier and open-weight multimodal backbones, we find that: 1) pre-compaction depth and post-compaction continuation form distinct, non-monotonic failure regimes rather than a single degradation curve; 2) open-weight models rely heavily on context continuity and are reluctant to spontaneously switch to tool-mediated retrieval when provenance fails; and 3) retrieval pressure improves source attribution in deep pre-compaction states for tool-compliant models, but consistently regresses after compaction, where stored evidence has already degraded. These findings show that historical evidence use should be evaluated under state variation, rather than inferred from outcome-only correctness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MIRAGE, a benchmark and methodology to test how well multimodal LLM-based agents actually retrieve and use historical evidence under changing conversation states, rather than just judging them by whether their final answers look correct.
AI.motivation: MLLM agents are used as long-running personal assistants that must rely on past dialogue, files, and workspace state. Existing evaluations often only check whether the final answer is correct, which can be misleading because models can guess plausible answers even when they have lost access to the true historical evidence. This creates a gap between apparent performance and real evidence-based reasoning, especially when conversation state is compacted or context windows are exceeded.
AI.method: The authors propose MIRAGE, a controlled evaluation framework where evidence objects, questions, and scoring are held fixed but the conversation state is systematically varied (e.g., different depths before and after context compaction). They test seven advanced multimodal backbones, probing whether agents can: (1) judge if a question is answerable given the available history, (2) identify and retrieve the correct evidence source, and (3) answer grounded in that source. They specifically manipulate pre-compaction depth and post-compaction continuation, and observe how models use tools and retrieval under these conditions.
AI.result: The study finds: (1) evidence-use failures are not a simple monotonic degradation with depth; instead, there are two distinct failure regimes: deep pre-compaction and post-compaction continuation. (2) Open-weight models are highly dependent on continuous context and generally do not switch on their own to tool-based retrieval when provenance information is missing. (3) For models that do use tools, stronger retrieval prompts improve source attribution in deep pre-compaction settings, but this benefit disappears or reverses after compaction, where the stored evidence is already degraded.
AI.conclusion: Historical evidence use in multimodal assistants cannot be reliably inferred from outcome-only correctness. Proper evaluation must vary conversation state and explicitly test answerability judgments, source recovery, and grounded answering. MIRAGE demonstrates that compaction and long interaction histories create distinct, non-trivial failure patterns, highlighting the need for state-aware evaluation and better integration of retrieval tools to maintain robust evidence use over time.

title: Flag Game: A Toy Model for Mechanistic Swarm Interpretability
summary: Emergent coordinated behaviors of AI agents are starting to present critical safety risks. A key phenomenon driving these behaviors is the rapid formation and spread of beliefs about the world, and mechanistic understanding is crucial for collective alignment. To this end, we introduce the Flag Game, a toy model for studying the mechanisms of collective belief formation. Concretely, a hidden country flag defines the ground truth, and each bounded agent directly observes only a private crop but can exchange beliefs and weigh social evidence from peers. Despite its simplicity, the Flag Game reproduces rich collective phenomenology: non-monotonic scaling of performance with population size, accuracy gains from social-awareness prompting and team diversity, and strong effects of organizational structure. In particular, we identify that collective belief collapse at small population sizes turns into collective belief polarization as the population grows. This polarization causes the performance decline at large population sizes, but creates diversity in collective beliefs. Finally, we dissect the mechanisms underlying collective belief collapse and polarization with two complementary approaches. We first introduce social circuit attribution, a technique to predict which agent, and what view, matters most to collective dynamics, and verify its predictions by causal interventions on agents, tracing how agent patching changes collective outcomes. However, the efficacy of causal interventions on agents decreases as the population grows. We therefore develop a statistical mechanical theory for larger populations and verify that it matches the empirical phase diagram. Together, these results take a first step toward mechanistic swarm interpretability, a science of how the properties of individual agents and their communication give rise to emergent collective behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Flag Game, a toy model to study how AI agents form collective beliefs and how this can lead to safe or unsafe emergent behaviors.
AI.motivation: Emergent coordinated behaviors in AI multi-agent systems can pose safety risks due to rapid, poorly understood formation and spread of beliefs. The authors want a mechanistic, interpretable setting to study how individual agent properties and communication patterns produce collective beliefs, collapses, and polarizations, which is crucial for collective alignment and safety.
AI.method: They design the Flag Game, where a hidden country flag is the ground truth. Each bounded agent sees only a private crop of the flag but can exchange beliefs and weigh peers' social evidence. They run multi-agent experiments varying population size, prompting (social-awareness), team diversity, and organizational structure. They analyze emergent behaviors using two methods: (1) social circuit attribution, which predicts which agents and which views most influence collective dynamics, validated via causal interventions and agent patching; and (2) a statistical mechanical theory to model large-population behavior and reproduce the empirical phase diagram of belief collapse vs. polarization.
AI.result: The Flag Game reproduces complex collective phenomena: performance scales non-monotonically with population size; social-awareness prompting and team diversity improve accuracy; organizational structure strongly affects outcomes. Small populations exhibit collective belief collapse, while larger ones display collective belief polarization. Polarization both degrades performance at large scales and introduces diversity in collective beliefs. Social circuit attribution successfully identifies influential agents/views and predicts intervention effects, but direct causal interventions on agents become less effective as populations grow. The statistical mechanical model accurately matches the phase behavior observed in large populations.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an interpretable testbed and initial mechanistic tools for understanding emergent collective behavior in AI swarms. By connecting individual agent properties and communication patterns to macroscopic phenomena like belief collapse and polarization, and by introducing social circuit attribution and a statistical mechanical framework, the paper takes a first step toward "swarm interpretability" aimed at improving safety and alignment of large multi-agent AI systems.

title: Reading Between the Lines: Can LLMs Discover the Question Behind the Text?
summary: This paper introduces ``question archaeology'', a specific evaluation task focused on inferring the single, authentic "genesis question" that motivated the creation of a complete text. Distinct from question generation, which targets any plausible question, or discourse frameworks that model utterance-level acts, our task assesses a model's grasp of authorial intent. We present a new dataset of commissioned texts paired with their original research questions and plausible distractors. Our evaluation of both proprietary models, like Gemini Flash and Pro, as well as open source models like Mistral and Qwen, reveals significant progress in this task, with the newer versions outperforming the earlier ones, while BERT-based models performed poorly. Notably, our findings indicate that current LLMs surpass human performance on this task, suggesting advanced understanding of authorial intent. This capability has important implications for AI's role in tasks requiring nuanced interpretation of human communication. Our work thus provides a new framework and a challenging benchmark for future models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates a new NLP task, “question archaeology,” which aims to recover the original research question that motivated a text.
AI.motivation: Existing work on question generation and discourse analysis does not directly target the recovery of the specific motivating question behind a text, which is crucial for assessing models’ understanding of authorial intent. The authors aim to formally define and benchmark this capability.
AI.method: They define the task of “question archaeology,” construct a dataset of commissioned texts paired with their true genesis questions and carefully designed distractor questions, and evaluate multiple models—including proprietary LLMs (Gemini Flash/Pro), open-source LLMs (Mistral, Qwen), and BERT-based models—on selecting the correct genesis question.
AI.result: Newer LLMs (both proprietary and open-source) substantially outperform earlier versions and BERT-based models on the question archaeology task. Performance of current LLMs exceeds that of human annotators, indicating that they are particularly strong at inferring underlying authorial intent from text.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces question archaeology as a novel evaluation framework and benchmark for measuring models’ grasp of authorial intent. Current LLMs already show impressive, even superhuman, performance on this task, implying that they may be well-suited for applications requiring fine-grained interpretation of human communication and setting a challenging standard for future models.

title: Cognitive Extensions for Dual-Process Language Agents: Memory and Self-Reflection in Interactive Environments
summary: Language agents remain brittle in interactive environments, where success requires long-horizon state tracking, valid action execution, and recovery from failed steps. We extend SwiftSage, a dual-process agent that combines a fast action proposer with a slower planner, using two modular cognitive extensions: an Adaptive Memory Module (AMM) for salience-gated episodic storage and trigger-driven retrieval, and a Self-Reflection Module (SRM) for bounded execution-time validation and corrective intervention. Both modules are implemented as feature-flagged extensions over the same execution substrate, enabling controlled ablations on ScienceWorld. Across four configurations---baseline, baseline+AMM, baseline+SRM, and the full system---the full system achieves the best mean final score (64.62), success rate (43.17%), and successful-step efficiency (19.33 steps), while SRM is the strongest standalone contributor. The results suggest that execution-time control is the dominant bottleneck in this setting, while episodic memory becomes most useful once the runtime loop is stabilized.

AI.tldr: The paper enhances SwiftSage, a dual-process language agent, with adaptive memory and self-reflection modules to improve interactive task performance, finding that execution-time control is the main performance bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Language agents struggle with brittle behavior in interactive, long-horizon environments requiring accurate state tracking, valid actions, and recovery from errors. The authors aim to address these limitations by adding cognitive-like abilities—episodic memory and self-reflective control—to an existing dual-process agent architecture.
AI.method: They extend the SwiftSage dual-process agent with two modular components: (1) an Adaptive Memory Module (AMM) that performs salience-gated episodic storage and trigger-based retrieval, and (2) a Self-Reflection Module (SRM) that validates and intervenes on actions during execution. These modules are implemented via feature flags on a shared execution substrate, allowing controlled ablation experiments across four configurations (baseline, baseline+AMM, baseline+SRM, full system) evaluated on the ScienceWorld benchmark.
AI.result: On ScienceWorld, the full system (SwiftSage + AMM + SRM) achieves the best performance in terms of mean final score (64.62), task success rate (43.17%), and efficiency measured as successful steps (19.33 steps). Among individual extensions, SRM contributes more to performance than AMM on its own.
AI.conclusion: Execution-time control via self-reflection is identified as the primary bottleneck in this interactive setting, with episodic memory providing maximal gains only after the agent’s runtime decision loop is stabilized. Modular cognitive extensions like AMM and SRM can substantially improve language agent robustness and efficiency in complex environments.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Biomedical Relation Extraction
summary: Extracting SNP-phenotype associations from biomedical literature is vital but challenging. We benchmarked diverse NLP models, including MLMs, hybrid architectures, and state-of-the-art LLMs (Gemini 2.0, OpenAI O-series, Qwen, Mistral), on the SNPPhenA corpus across three tasks: sentence-level, abstract-level, and association strength classification. OpenAI O1 achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) results using few-shot learning for non-finetuned sentence-level classification (F1 0.89) and established a new SOTA for abstract-level classification (F1 0.82). Association strength classification proved difficult, though fine-tuned Gemini 2.0 Pro performed best (F1 0.60) in the first LLM evaluation of this task. Proprietary LLMs, especially in few-shot (O1) or fine-tuned (Gemini 2.0 Pro) settings, significantly outperformed other models. These findings confirm the power of modern LLMs for genomic knowledge extraction.
